items.title: Comparison of intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) and intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for oropharyngeal cancer: efficacy and toxicity differ by outcome measure
items.authors: You J, You J, Xu B, et al.
items.abstract: Aim: Whether intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) offers measurable clinical benefits over intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for oropharyngeal cancer remains debated. Methods: We pooled data from two phase III randomized trials and one matched cohort study comparing IMPT with IMRT and analyzed disease-control, survival, acute toxicity, and nutritional outcomes. Results: The hazard ratio for locoregional recurrence was 1.37 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.56-3.36, I2 = 0%]; for progression-free survival, 0.90 (95% CI 0.61-1.33, I2 = 0%); and for overall survival, 0.79 (95% CI 0.32-1.98, I2 = 47%). Acute grade 3 dysphagia occurred in 24% of patients receiving IMPT, compared with 40.9% receiving IMRT [risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95% CI 0.51-0.84, I2 = 0%]. Grade 3 xerostomia or oral/pharyngeal dryness occurred in 19.9% and 32.5%, respectively (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.95, I2 = 0%). Exploratory nutritional outcomes showed no definitive benefit, including 12-month gastrostomy dependence (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.08-1.28, I2 = 0%), weight loss ≥20% (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.12-9.38, I2 = 85.7%), and composite nutritional endpoints (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.12-7.07, I2 = 87.7%). Conclusions: IMPT's primary advantage is reducing acute toxicity, not improving efficacy.

items.title: Carbon ion radiotherapy for non-metastatic pancreatic cancer: final results of the prospective phase 2 PACK-study (NCT04194268)
items.authors: Liermann J, Naumann P, Jäkel C, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) in patients with non-metastatic, inoperable pancreatic cancer in a prospective phase 2 setting. Methods: In this single-center investigator-initiated phase 2 trial, 25 patients with locally advanced or locally recurrent pancreatic cancer were included. CIRT was performed using an intensity-controlled rasterscanning system for beam application [total dose: 48 Gy (RBE), 12 fractions]. Concurrent chemotherapy with Gemcitabine 300 mg/m2 was administered weekly. The primary endpoint was the 1-year OS rate, defined as time from study inclusion. 1y- and 2y-OS and -PFS were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method, 95 % confidence intervals are shown. Toxicity was evaluated using CTCAEv5.0. Results: Twenty-three patients were included in the final analysis. After the completed 12-month follow-up of the last patient, the 1- and 2-year OS rates were 78 % [CI 63 %; 97 %] and 59 % [CI 41 %; 84 %]. The median OS was 26.5 months. The 1- and 2-year PFS rates were 26 % [CI 13 %; 52 %] and 10 % [CI 3 %; 37 %] with a median PFS of 8.1 months. Study treatment was well tolerated with three treatment-related CTCAE grade 3 toxicities, including one case of abdominal pain, one upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage and one ureteric stricture. No treatment-related CTCAE grade 4-5 toxicities were observed. Conclusion: Chemoradiation with carbon ions demonstrated encouraging overall survival and acceptable toxicity in non-metastatic pancreatic cancer patients. A subsequent randomized Phase 3 trial should investigate OS superiority of CIRT compared to conventional chemoradiotherapy or chemotherapy.

items.title: PET-Guided Dose Escalation for Stage III Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Raman S, Bissonnette JP, Palma DA, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Uniform radiation dose escalation has not improved outcomes in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and locoregional failure remains common despite multimodal therapy. We evaluated whether fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET)-guided dose escalation to metabolically active tumor subvolumes reduces locoregional failure compared with standard chemoradiation. Methods And Materials: PET-BOOST was a multi-institutional, open-label, phase 2 randomized trial conducted at 7 Canadian centers (January 2017-May 2022). Eligible patients had inoperable, FDG-avid stage IIIA/IIIB NSCLC and an achievable boost dose of at least 65 Gy. Patients were randomized 1:1 to standard chemoradiation with 60 Gy in 30 fractions or metabolically adaptive radiotherapy with an integrated boost to FDG-avid subvolumes to a maximum of 85 Gy in 30 fractions. Concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy was planned, and consolidation durvalumab was permitted after 2018. The primary endpoint was 2-year locoregional failure; secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicity, and quality of life (QOL). Results: Seventy-eight patients were randomized: 40 to standard radiotherapy and 38 to dose escalation, with a median follow-up of 5.0 years. Median age was 64.4 years; 53% were male, 62% had stage IIIA disease, and 76% received consolidation durvalumab. Median prescription boost dose was 75 Gy. Two-year locoregional failure was 27.5% with standard radiotherapy versus 18.4% with dose escalation (P=.13). Two-year OS (72.5% vs. 73.7%; P=.91) and PFS (52.5% vs. 57.9%; P=.74) did not differ between arms. Grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicities occurred in 25% versus 37% of patients (P=.26), with one grade 5 pulmonary hemorrhage in the dose-escalation arm. QOL did not differ between arms. Conclusions: Metabolically adaptive PET-guided radiotherapy dose escalation was feasible in the context of consolidation immunotherapy and resulted in a numerically lower rate of locoregional failure, but did not significantly improve locoregional control or survival. The lower-than-anticipated event rate may have limited statistical power, and larger studies would be required to determine whether selective dose escalation provides a clinically meaningful improvement in locoregional control.

items.title: Perioperative chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy versus perioperative chemotherapy alone in patients with high-risk, localised pancreatic cancer (MASTERPLAN): an open-label, phase 2, multicentre, randomised trial of the Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group
items.authors: Oar A, Kneebone A, Sjoquist KM, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has poor outcomes and high rates of locoregional recurrence. MASTERPLAN evaluated whether stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) reduced locoregional recurrence in patients with high-risk, localised PDAC. Methods: MASTERPLAN was an open-label, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted across 14 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand. Eligible participants were aged 18 years or older with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1, and had previously untreated localised PDAC with at least one high-risk feature, including tumour size more than 4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, node-positive disease, borderline resectable disease, or locally advanced disease. Participants were randomly assigned (2:1) using the method of minimisation to investigator-choice chemotherapy, with or without SBRT, stratified by participant cohort (potentially operable vs inoperable), planned chemotherapy regimen, randomisation before or within the first 28 days of chemotherapy, and institution. Chemotherapy consisted of mFOLFIRINOX (day 1 oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2, irinotecan 150 mg/m2, leucovorin 50 mg, and fluorouracil 2400 mg/m2 over 46 h every 14 days for six cycles; all intravenous) or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (gemcitabine 1000 mg/m2 and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2 on days 1, 8, and 15 every 28 days for three cycles; both intravenous). SBRT was delivered as 40 Gy in five fractions, with two to four fractions delivered per week, with real-time radiotherapy quality assurance. Surgical resection was considered following induction therapy, followed by a planned further 12 weeks of adjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus capecitabine (28-day cycles of 1000 mg/m2 intravenous gemcitabine administered on days 1, 8, and 15 with 830 mg/m2 oral capecitabine twice daily administered on days 1-21). Participants deemed not suitable for surgery continued the same chemotherapy for an additional 12 weeks with reassessment for surgical suitability permitted, for a total planned duration of chemotherapy of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was 12-month locoregional recurrence in the intention-to-treat population, with safety endpoints analysed by treatment received. The trial planned to recruit 120 patients but due to slow accrual closed to recruitment early on Jan 6, 2025. Trial closure and database lock occurred on July 21, 2026. This trial was registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trial Registry (ACTRN12619000409178) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04089150), and is complete.…

items.title: Hypofractionated Versus Conventionally Fractionated Postmastectomy Radiotherapy With Internal Mammary Node Irradiation for High-Risk Breast Cancer (HypoMast-IMNI): A Randomized Phase III Trial
items.authors: Wang X, Zhang X, Chen X, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: When coverage of internal mammary nodes (IMN) is required, the efficacy and safety of hypofractionated regimens within postmastectomy radiotherapy (PMRT) remain to be established. This study evaluated hypofractionated radiotherapy (HypoRT) in patients with high-risk, operable breast cancer undergoing PMRT with IMN irradiation (IMNI). Methods: In this phase III noninferiority trial, eligible patients with high-risk disease after mastectomy (including pT1-4N2-3, pT3-4N1, or pT1-2N1 disease with additional high-risk factors) were randomly assigned (1:1) to HypoRT (42.56 Gy in 16 fractions) or conventionally fractionated radiotherapy (ConvRT; 50 Gy in 25 fractions), both targeting the chest wall and regional lymph nodes, including the IMN. The primary end point was locoregional recurrence (LRR). Secondary end points were distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), breast cancer recurrence-free survival (BCRFS), disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), and treatment-related toxicity. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrial.gov (identifier: NCT03856372). Results: Between September 2018 and July 2022, 1,494 patients were randomly assigned. After a median follow-up of 58.1 months in the modified intention-to-treat population (n = 1,429), the 5-year cumulative incidence of LRR was 1.7% (95% CI, 0.9 to 2.9) with HypoRT and 2.2% (95% CI, 1.3 to 3.5) with ConvRT (hazard ratio, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.32 to 1.51]), meeting the noninferiority criterion (P = .017). No significant differences were observed in 5-year DMFS, BCRFS, DFS, or OS. Grade 3 acute skin toxicity was significantly lower with HypoRT (1.7% v 12.2%, P < .001). The incidence of grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis was low and comparable between arms, with no ischemic cardiac events recorded. Conclusion: For patients with high-risk, operable breast cancer requiring PMRT with IMNI, the 16-fraction HypoRT regimen is noninferior to ConvRT for locoregional control, offers a superior acute toxicity profile, and demonstrates excellent cardiopulmonary safety.

items.title: Organ Preservation With Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (OPTNT) for Early Low Rectal Cancer: Short-Term Outcomes of a Nonrandomized Phase 2 Clinical Trial
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Xian Z, Feng Q, Qian Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Total mesorectal excision (TME) is standard for low rectal cancer (≤5cm from anal verge) but causes permanent stomas, functional impairments and surgical risks. Local excision (LE) suits early tumors (cTis-T1N0) but has higher recurrence in cT2+; watch-and-wait (WW) after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy risks residual disease. Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) improves outcomes, but prior LE trials had limitations. Objective: To evaluate TNT combined with planned LE for organ preservation in selected low rectal adenocarcinoma patients. Design: Prospective single-arm phase 2 trial (June 2022-March 2024, tertiary center) enrolled 57/60 patients (cT1-3N0M0 nonmucinous adenocarcinoma, etc.). TNT: 50 Gy + 2 cycles of CapoX (standard capecitabine + oxaliplatin) + 4 consolidation CapoX. Clinical complete response (cCR)/near-complete clinical response (ncCR) patients had LE; others got TME. Patients with high-risk residual disease after LE also had additional TME. Results: Median age was 61 years (28-79); 66.7% were male. cT3 tumors were present in 78.9%, and 78.9% had tumors ≤3 cm from the anal verge. After TNT, 47.4% achieved cCR and 38.6% achieved ncCR. Among surgically treated patients, the pathological complete response (pCR) rate was 68.6%; in the overall population, with WW counted as non-pCR, it was 61.4%. The total complete response rate, including pCR and cCR managed with WW, was 68.4%. Sphincter preservation was 94.7%. LE was associated with lower median blood loss (7 vs 50 mL; P<0.001) and shorter median hospitalization (7 vs 14 days; P=0.001) than TME. Grade 3 adverse events occurred in 22.8%, most commonly lymphocytopenia; no grade 4 or 5 events occurred. Low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) scores were assessed after TNT and at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. At 6 months, LARS outcomes favored LE (80.0% vs 53.8% reporting no LARS; P=0.027). Wexner incontinence scores did not differ significantly between groups at any time point. Conclusion: TNT with planned LE is feasible in cT1-3N0M0 low rectal cancer, yielding a pCR rate of 61.4% in the overall population, 94.7% sphincter preservation, and acceptable toxicity. However, the non-randomized design and immature 3-year organ-preservation endpoint limit this study to a feasibility assessment and do not permit conclusions regarding comparative effectiveness versus WW. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05563922.

items.title: A randomized Phase 1 study of telisotuzumab adizutecan (ABBV-400, Temab-A) in combination with bevacizumab versus trifluridine-tipiracil with bevacizumab in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer
items.authors: Cecchini M, Cruz-Correa M, Han SW, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Telisotuzumab adizutecan (ABBV-400, Temab-A) is an antibody-drug conjugate targeting c-Met (MET) protein with adizutecan, a novel topoisomerase 1 inhibitor payload. In monotherapy dose escalation, Temab-A demonstrated a manageable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in advanced colorectal cancer (CRC; NCT05029882). Based on these results, a randomized cohort of Temab-A + bevacizumab (Bev) versus trifluridine-tipiracil (FTD-TPI) + Bev (standard-of-care) was added with the hypothesis that addition of Bev would enhance efficacy. Patients And Methods: Patients unselected for c-Met protein expression with advanced CRC were enrolled in 2 parts. In dose escalation, patients received Temab-A 1.6, 2.0, or 2.4 mg/kg + Bev 7.5 mg/kg Q3W. In dose optimization, patients were randomized 1:1:1 to Temab-A 2.0 or 2.4 mg/kg + Bev 7.5 mg/kg Q3W, or FTD-TPI 35 mg/m2 Days 1-5 and 8-12 Q4W + Bev 5.0 mg/kg Q2W. Primary objectives were safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of Temab-A + Bev. Results: Overall, 83 patients received treatment with Temab-A + Bev (n=63) or FTD-TPI + Bev (n=20) with median 3 (range, 1-8) prior lines of treatment and median follow-up of 18.2 months. Treatment-related adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and hematological with low discontinuation rates (Temab-A 2.0: 3/26 [12%]; Temab-A 2.4: 1/30 [3%]). Objective response rate was 19% and 30% with Temab-A 2.0 and 2.4 + Bev, respectively, and 0% with FTD-TPI + Bev. For Temab-A 2.0 and 2.4 + Bev vs FTD-TPI + Bev, median progression-free survival was 5.6 and 6.8 months vs 4.2 months; median overall survival was 11.2 (HR=0.75) and 14.7 months (HR=0.62) vs 10.2 months, respectively. Conclusion: Temab-A 2.4 mg/kg + Bev demonstrated the most favorable risk-benefit profile, was tolerable, and had clinically meaningful improvements in efficacy versus FTD-TPI + Bev for advanced CRC. The regimen is being evaluated in the global randomized Phase 3 trial AndroMETa-560 (NCT07525206).

items.title: 14-day versus 28-day trifluridine-tipiracil plus bevacizumab for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (PRABITAS): a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial in Japan
items.authors: Sakakida T, Taniguchi H, Asayama M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Trifluridine-tipiracil (FTD-TPI) plus bevacizumab is the standard treatment for refractory metastatic colorectal cancer. However, the conventional schedule is frequently associated with haematological and gastrointestinal toxicity, which is clinically significant and relevant to patients. A simplified 14-day schedule has been proposed to reduce toxicity, but whether this treatment preserves survival has not been established in a randomised trial. We therefore aimed to assess whether the 14-day schedule is non-inferior to the conventional schedule for overall survival. Methods: PRABITAS was a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3, non-inferiority trial conducted in 178 hospitals in Japan. Patients with refractory metastatic colorectal cancer were randomly assigned (1:1) using a minimisation algorithm, stratified by Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, RAS mutational status, and institution, to FTD-TPI (35 mg/m2 orally twice daily) plus bevacizumab (5 mg/kg intravenously) on either a conventional 28-day (FTD-TPI on days 1-5 and 8-12; bevacizumab on days 1 and 15) or 14-day schedule (FTD-TPI on days 1-5; bevacizumab on day 1). Eligibility criteria were broadened compared with those of conventional explanatory trials, and trial procedures were aligned with routine clinical practice. The primary endpoint was overall survival, analysed in the intention-to-treat population, with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1·25. Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose. Missing data were not imputed. This trial is registered with the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials, jRCTs041230120, and is closed to enrolment. Findings: Between Dec 26, 2023, and May 20, 2025, we randomly assigned 972 patients, of whom 970 (99%) constituted the intention-to-treat population after two were excluded because they were randomly assigned before site approval (486 [50%] to the 28-day treatment group, 292 [60%] men and 194 [40%] women]; and 484 [50%] to the 14-day treatment group, 264 [55%] men and 220 [45%] women). Median follow-up was 17·9 months (IQR 14·3-22·6). Median overall survival was 10·3 months (95% CI 9·5-11·6) in the 28-day group and 11·3 months (10·2-12·5) in the 14-day group (stratified hazard ratio 0·93 [95% CI 0·80-1·08]). The 12-month overall survival rates were 44·0% (95% CI 39·5-48·5) in the 28-day group and 47·5% (42·9-52·0) in the 14-day group.…

items.title: Pembrolizumab with or without platinum-based chemotherapy as first-line treatment in advanced NSCLC expressing PD-L1 ≥50%: The PERSEE randomized phase III trial (GFPC 01-2020)
items.authors: Descourt R, Mogenet A, Consigny M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Pembrolizumab, alone or combined with platinum-based chemotherapy, is a standard first-line treatment for patients with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without actionable oncogenic alterations and with high programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression. We conducted a head-to-head comparison of these two treatment strategies. Methods: In this multicenter, phase III trial (PERSEE, NCT04547504), adult patients with treatment-naïve stage IV or unresectable stage III NSCLC not amenable to definitive radiotherapy and PD-L1 expression ≥50% were randomly (1:1) assigned to receive pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks, for up to 35 cycles) or pembrolizumab in combination with four cycles of induction chemotherapy, stratified according to the presence of brain metastases and histologic subtype. Patients with non-squamous histology received cisplatin or carboplatin (AUC 5) plus pemetrexed, followed by pembrolizumab-pemetrexed maintenance; patients with squamous histology received carboplatin (AUC 6) plus paclitaxel, followed by pembrolizumab maintenance. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), assessed by blinded central review according to RECIST v1.1. Key secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), objective response rate, duration of response, and safety. Results: A total of 321 patients underwent randomization, with 160 assigned to pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy and 161 to pembrolizumab monotherapy. At a median follow-up of 38.7 months, median PFS was significantly longer with combination therapy than with monotherapy (16.1 months [95% CI, 11.0-34.1] vs. 6.9 months [95% CI, 5.5-9.3]; hazard ratio (HR), 0.56; 95% CI, 0.43-0.74; P<0.001). Median OS was 50.2 months versus 29.9 months, respectively (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.56-1.05). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 54% and 19% of patients, respectively; grade ≥3 immune-related adverse events occurred in 13% of patients in each group. Conclusions: Among patients with treatment-naïve advanced NSCLC and high PD-L1 expression, the addition of platinum-based chemotherapy to pembrolizumab significantly prolonged PFS compared with pembrolizumab monotherapy.

items.title: Cognitive outcomes of low-dose whole-brain radiation therapy in mild Alzheimer's disease: A multicenter, randomized, sham-controlled phase II clinical trial
items.authors: Hong EH, Kim A, Kim KY, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) has shown potential in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) models, but controlled clinical evidence is limited. We evaluated two whole-brain LDRT regimens in mild AD. Materials And Methods: In this multicenter, participant-blinded, three-arm phase II trial, amyloid-positive participants were randomized 1:1:1 to sham irradiation, 0.04 Gy per fraction (0.24 Gy total), or 0.5 Gy per fraction (3 Gy total), delivered twice weekly for 3 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-cog) score from baseline to 6 months. Twelve-month analyses were exploratory. Longitudinal outcomes were estimated using mixed-effects models. Results: Forty-one participants were randomized; 36 were included in the modified intention-to-treat population and 30 completed 12-month follow-up. At 6 months, adjusted between-group differences in ADAS-cog change versus sham were -2.08 points (95% CI, -7.06 to 2.89; p = 0.401) for 0.24 Gy and -2.92 points (95% CI, -6.72 to 0.89; p = 0.129) for 3 Gy. At 12 months, the corresponding exploratory differences were -3.02 points (95% CI, -10.00 to 3.96; p = 0.386) and -5.36 points (95% CI, -10.58 to -0.14; nominal p = 0.044). No treatment-related adverse events or radiologic safety concerns were identified. Conclusions: The prespecified 6-month primary endpoint was not met. Exploratory 12-month and secondary analyses showed differences in selected cognitive outcomes, although the findings varied across doses and outcomes. These findings did not establish efficacy or a dose-response relationship and warrant confirmation in a larger trial with longer follow-up.

items.title: From contouring variability to dosimetric impact: a comprehensive assessment of online adaptive MR-guided SBRT for pancreatic cancer
items.authors: Poeta S, Gulyban A, Paquier Z, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To quantify inter-physician contouring variability and evaluate its dosimetric impact in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients treated with daily online adaptive MR-guided stereotactic body radiotherapy (MRgSBRT), to assess safety and clinical robustness of online contouring. Methods: Fifty treatment sessions from ten PDAC patients treated with 50 Gy in five fractions on a 1.5 T MR-Linac were retrospectively analyzed. During each treatment session ("online"), targets and organs-at-risk (OARs) within 3 cm of the tumor were delineated by seven physicians working on the MR-Linac. All structures were re-contoured offline by a single pancreatic-expert radiation oncologist ("reference"). Geometric agreement was assessed using Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Mean Distance to Agreement (MDA), and 95 % Hausdorff Distance (HD95). Dosimetric analyses were performed on delivered treatment plans using both online and reference contours, with evaluation based on fraction-wise worst-case dose metrics. Results: High geometric concordance was observed for stomach and duodenum, whereas smaller or anatomically complex structures (GTV, major vessels, bile duct) showed greater variability. Online GTVs were larger than reference contours. Despite these differences, target coverage (V50Gy and V35Gy) was maintained with online contours. While occasional per-fraction gastrointestinal (GI) dose constraint exceedances were identified using reference contours, fraction-wise worst-case analysis showed GI doses remained within clinical tolerance for nearly all patients. Conclusion: Daily online adaptive MRgSBRT for PDAC provides robust target coverage and clinically acceptable OAR sparing, despite contouring variability. Multi-physician online contouring appears safe in clinical practice, although further improvements may be achieved through standardized contouring guidelines and harmonization strategies.

items.title: Harmonizing Radiotherapy Data Standards: A Comparative Analysis of OMOP, CDISC, FHIR, NAACCR, and OBO Foundry with an O3-Anchored Mapping Framework
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Xiao Y, Kennedy G, Baker RL, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This Special Report analyzes current radiotherapy data standards, determines which radiotherapy data elements should propagate between them, and identifies the barriers to that propagation to improve interoperability and data utilization in clinical care and research. Methods: We compared five data standards-OMOP, CDISC SDTM, FHIR, NAACCR, and the Operational Ontology for Oncology (O3)-and one ontology framework, the OBO Foundry, for radiotherapy data representation, strengths, limitations, and implementation maturity, and examined harmonization initiatives including NRG's O3-based conversion frameworks, CodeX mCODE, and ESTRO and IAEA efforts. We then scored a 90-item benchmark drawn from radiotherapy operational and trial-reporting requirements, partitioned the radiotherapy items by whether and where they should propagate, and matched each barrier to a remediation route and owning body. Results: Counting only unqualified matches, O3 covered 46 of 62 radiotherapy-specific items (74%) versus 15 (24%) for OMOP, 12 (19%) for NAACCR, 11 (18%) for FHIR, and none for OBO Foundry; on the 28 general clinical items the ordering reversed (OMOP 79%, FHIR 71%, NAACCR 46%, O3 25%, OBO Foundry 4%). Each standard is strongest on the items its target function was built to serve. Wholesale propagation is therefore unwarranted: 20 course-summary elements should converge across standards, 26 planning and adaptive elements warrant selective adoption, and 16 voxel- and machine-level artifacts should be referenced by DICOM unique identifier rather than replicated. Conclusions: Harmonization requires ontology-driven approaches using O3 as the semantic backbone with mappings to FHIR, OMOP and CDISC, applied to a defined tier of elements rather than the full element set. The principal barriers are process barriers-structural, terminological, burden-related and tooling-related-each with a named owner and an existing route. Standardized formats alone are insufficient; they require robust information systems, validation, and governance. Harmonization improves real-world data utility but cannot resolve biases inherent to nonrandomized data. Coordinated international collaboration remains critical for advancing precision radiation oncology.

items.title: Active surveillance versus standard surgery after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for oesophageal cancer: long-term results of a cluster-randomised controlled trial (SANO)
items.authors: Panday SSGG, van der Wilk BJ, Lagarde SM, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The Surgery As Needed for Oesophageal cancer (SANO)-trial demonstrated that active surveillance is non-inferior to standard surgery in terms of two-year overall survival in patients with a complete clinical response after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT). Active surveillance resulted in improved quality of life. Here, we report five-year outcomes. Methods: From 2017 to 2021, a multicentre stepped-wedge cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial was conducted. Patients with locally advanced oesophageal cancer who achieved complete clinical response (defined as no tumour detected on endoscopic biopsies, -ultrasound, or PET-CT) underwent active surveillance or standard surgery. Cox regression was used to compare five-year overall and disease-free survival, and the cumulative incidence of distant metastases was estimated using competing risk analysis. Results: A total of 309 patients were included, 198 underwent active surveillance and 111 underwent standard surgery. Median follow-up was 76 months (IQR 67-86). Five-year overall survival was not statistically significantly different between active surveillance and standard surgery (50%, 95%CI 43-57 vs. 54%, 95%CI 46-64; HR 1.17, 95%CI 0.77-1.77) with similar results across histologic subtypes. Disease-free survival was not statistically significantly different (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.94-2.06). The cumulative incidence of distant metastases at five years was significantly higher in the active surveillance group compared to the standard surgery group (46%, 95%CI 39-53 vs. 29%, 95%CI 21-37; P<.01). Overall, 85 of 198 patients (43%) avoided oesophagectomy, including those with sustained complete clinical response at last follow-up or distant metastases detected within six months after nCRT. Conclusions: Overall survival at five years is not statistically significantly different between active surveillance and standard surgery in patients with oesophageal cancer and a complete clinical response after nCRT, despite a higher incidence of distant metastases in the active surveillance group. These findings support active surveillance as a feasible treatment strategy in selected patients.

items.title: Neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and chemotherapy versus standard of care for locally advanced rectal cancer (UNION): a prespecified interim analysis of a multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial
items.authors: Tao K, Lin Z, Zhang P, et al.
items.abstract: Background: To our knowledge, UNION is the first phase 3 trial to assess a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy compared with standard care in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer, which reported positive results for the primary endpoint (blinded independent review committee [BIRC]-assessed pathological complete response rate; 39·8% vs 15·3%). Here, we present a prespecified interim analysis of event-free survival. Methods: This open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial was conducted at nine hospitals in China. Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years with untreated cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (≤10 cm distance from the anal verge) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1; stratified by clinical T stage and N stage), using permuted blocks, to receive neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy (25 Gy in five fractions) followed by two cycles of intravenous camrelizumab (200 mg on day 1) plus CAPOX (oral capecitabine 1000 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1-14 and intravenous oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 on day 1; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50·4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent oral capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily) followed by two cycles of CAPOX (standard-of-care group). After surgery, both groups received six cycles of adjuvant CAPOX, and the experimental group additionally received adjuvant camrelizumab for up to 15 cycles. The primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pathological complete response rate in the intention-to-treat population, which has been previously reported. Here, we performed a prespecified interim analysis of investigator-assessed event-free survival (one of the key secondary endpoints, defined as time from randomisation to radiographic progression precluding surgery, local recurrence or distant metastasis, or death) in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients) with a boundary of a two-sided p values less than 0·0102. Safety was evaluated in all patients who received at least one dose of the study treatment according to the assigned regimen. The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04928807, and is active, but no longer recruiting. items.title: Locoregional and distant recurrence after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy versus chemoradiotherapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a focused meta-analysis
items.authors: Ruan Y, Cao W, Long C, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NCIT) is used for locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but its effect on postoperative recurrence patterns remains uncertain. We compared overall, locoregional, and distant recurrence after NCIT versus neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT). Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched through 01 May 2026. Eligible studies included patients with resectable or potentially resectable locally advanced ESCC who received NCIT or NCRT followed by radical esophagectomy. Recurrence outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RRs), and disease-free survival or recurrence-free survival (DFS/RFS) and overall survival (OS) as hazard ratios (HRs), using random-effects models. Post hoc sensitivity analyses excluded studies with marked between-group follow-up imbalance. Results: Twenty comparative studies, all conducted in China, were included; 19 were retrospective observational studies and one was a randomized phase 2 trial. Five studies contributed to the overall-recurrence analysis, and six studies contributed to each of the locoregional- and distant-recurrence analyses. NCIT was associated with lower overall recurrence (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49-0.95; P = 0.03) and distant recurrence/metastasis (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.89; P = 0.009), whereas locoregional recurrence did not differ significantly (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.67-1.55; P = 0.92). In post hoc analyses excluding studies with marked follow-up imbalance, the locoregional estimate remained nonsignificant (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.15), and the distant-recurrence/metastasis estimate was attenuated and no longer significant (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.36-1.17). Ten studies contributed to OS, which favored NCIT (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93; P = 0.02; I² = 77%), whereas eight contributed to DFS/RFS, which did not differ significantly (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.59-1.13; P = 0.21; I² = 74%). Conclusions: Compared with NCRT, NCIT was associated with fewer overall recurrences after radical esophagectomy for locally advanced ESCC. The primary distant-recurrence signal was not robust after excluding studies with marked follow-up imbalance, and no locoregional advantage was demonstrated. These findings do not establish therapeutic superiority and should be interpreted cautiously given the predominance of retrospective evidence, risk of bias, and substantial heterogeneity in survival analyses.

items.title: Drivers of Change in Radiotherapy Practice: Lessons From a UK Tertiary Cancer Centre (2013-2023)
items.authors: Kapadi A, Price G, Faivre-Finn C, et al.
items.abstract: Aims: There is a dearth of systematic analysis regarding the introduction of changes in radiotherapy practice and how they are evaluated, potentially limiting understanding of how future radiotherapy development could be improved. Using The Christie NHS Foundation Trust (Manchester, UK), a tertiary cancer centre, as a site exemplar, we summarise the types of radiotherapy changes introduced across five cancer sites for which radiotherapy is a crucial component of curative treatment. Along with identifying where and how practice has changed, we also examine the rationale underpinning changes introduced. Materials And Methods: Interviews were conducted with key radiotherapy professionals based at The Christie to elicit changes introduced over the period 2013-2023 across the following cancer sites: Upper Gastro-Intestinal, Head and Neck, Breast, Bladder and Prostate, and Brain and Central Nervous System. Analysis involved mapping changes across the radiotherapy pathway, categorising changes according to the evidence base and identifying key factors associated with driving change and evaluation in practice. Results: Advances across computing and engineering have supported the development of radiotherapy techniques, enabling the refinement of patient set-up, dose fractionation and margin definition. Other drivers for change include alignment with national standards, improving patient experience and clinical trial participation. The pace of change can be further dictated by service culture and readiness, influenced by clinician interest, expertise and consensus. Notably, several changes were introduced into the routine setting without systematic evaluation of their impact, under assumptions of benefit. Conclusion: Changes in radiotherapy are underpinned by diverse sources of evidence, yet evaluation of impact remains crucial for delivering high quality, evidence-based care. Developing quick, accessible and novel ways to monitor and evaluate modifications in radiotherapy planning or delivery is crucial for fostering more evidence-based and efficient practice, especially with the rapidly developing use of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Androgen Synthesis Inhibitors vs Androgen Receptor Inhibitors and Survival in Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer
items.authors: Gebrael G, Jo Y, Nandakumar V, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: In metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC), randomized clinical trials directly comparing androgen deprivation therapy intensification using androgen synthesis inhibitors (ASIs) vs next-generation androgen receptor inhibitors (ARIs) are lacking. Objective: To compare the outcomes associated with ASI vs ARI intensification therapy among patients with mHSPC in community or academic clinical practices. Design, Setting, And Participants: This was a retrospective cohort study of patients diagnosed with mHSPC between February 4, 2013, and April 29, 2024, with follow-up through the July 2024 data cut, providing a median (IQR) follow-up of 25.6 (24.5-26.6) months. Patient-level data were extracted from the nationwide US-based Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived deidentified research database of community and academic practices. Patients with evidence of an mHSPC diagnosis initiating treatment with an ASI (abiraterone acetate) or ARI (apalutamide or enzalutamide) within 3 months prior to or 6 months after an mHSPC diagnosis were eligible. Patients with prior docetaxel receipt were excluded. Exposure: Treatment with an ASI vs an ARI. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), defined as time in months from mHSPC diagnosis to death or censoring at last recorded activity. Results: Of 3404 patients (median [IQR] age, 73 [66-80] years), 1830 received treatment with an ASI (abiraterone), and 1574 with an ARI (507 apalutamide, 1067 enzalutamide). Following inverse probability of treatment weighting, patients receiving an ARI had significantly longer OS (median, 67.9 months [95% CI, 67.5 months to not reached]) compared with patients treated with the ASI (median, 57.2 months [95% CI, 52.7-63.3 months]) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.74 [95% CI, 0.64-0.87]); P < .001). Results were similar in sensitivity analyses using therapy initiation as the index date (HR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.62-0.84]; P < .001) and when restricted to index dates on or after December 16, 2019 (HR, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.56-0.81]; P < .001). The association was not modified by insurance status or socioeconomic status. Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study of 3404 patients with mHSPC, treatment intensification with an ARI was associated with significantly longer OS compared with an ASI. These findings may help guide clinical treatment selection and patient counseling. However, given conflicting clinical practice data across differing database populations, only a randomized clinical trial can definitively answer this question.

items.title: Harmonizing spatially fractionated radiation therapy: consensus and roadmap from an ESTRO workshop
items.authors: Wang X, Bargalló HV, Griffin RJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) intentionally delivers nonuniform dose distributions characterized by alternating high-dose peaks and low-dose valleys, with therapeutic potential for complex, inoperable bulky tumors. Although clinical adoption is expanding, clinical implementation and practices remain heterogeneous across institutions. This consensus aims to identify system-level barriers to harmonized clinical implementation of SFRT and formulate consensus-based recommendations to enable reproducible multi-institutional integration. Methods: The 2025 ESTRO Physics Workshop convened multidisciplinary international experts to evaluate current implementation practices and develop harmonization priorities through structured consensus discussions. Twenty-eight delegates participated, representing centers across Europe, the United States, China, and Australia. Core domains included dose recording and reporting specifications, commissioning and quality assurance (QA), motion management, registry infrastructure, and governance. Results: Five principal domains were identified as barriers to harmonized implementation: (1) inconsistent dose recording and reporting conventions; (2) variability in commissioning and QA practices for heterogeneous small-field dose distributions; (3) uncertainty in motion management and geometric robustness evaluation in the presence of anatomical changes; (4) fragmented data infrastructure limiting multi-institutional outcome analysis; and (5) limited coordinated governance and standardization infrastructure. Consensus recommendations and a phased roadmap with measurable milestones were formulated to address these domains. Conclusion: Harmonization of clinical implementation is essential to ensure reproducibility, support prospective multi-institutional trials, and safeguard consistent patient care across institutions. Coordinated international collaboration will be critical to establish standardized definitions, QA benchmarks, registry infrastructure, and governance frameworks for safe and effective clinical integration.

items.title: Rilvegostomig Plus Trastuzumab-Deruxtecan for Early-Stage Breast Cancer: The I-SPY2.2 Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: I-SPY2 Trial Investigators and Advocates, O'Sullivan CC, Kalinsky KM, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: The I-SPY2.2 trial tests personalized treatment strategies to improve outcomes while reducing exposure to standard chemotherapy in patients with high-risk early breast cancer (EBC). Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of trastuzumab-deruxtecan (T-DXd), an antibody drug conjugate targeting low ERBB2 (formerly HER2) expression, combined with rilvegostomig (R), a bispecific antibody targeting programmed cell death 1 protein and T-cell immunoglobulin and ITIM domain as initial therapy in I-SPY2.2 (RT-DXd). Design, Setting, And Participants: This phase 2, multicenter, adaptively randomized neoadjuvant trial enrolled patients with high-risk stage II/III ERBB2-negative EBC (including those with ERBB2 low/ultralow tumors), as stratified by hormone receptor (HR) status and response-predictive subtypes. It was conducted at 30 sites in the US; efficacy data were analyzed continuously during the trial to update probabilities and other analyses before publication. Interventions: Participants received up to 3 sequential treatment blocks, based on response and subtype: RT-DXd (block A), taxane-based therapy with/without immunotherapy (block B), and doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide (AC) with/without immunotherapy (block C). Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary end point was pathologic complete response (pCR). Safety assessments included adverse events (AEs), with focused monitoring for interstitial lung disease (ILD). Results: A total of 182 individuals (mean [SD] age: RT-DXd, 48.1 [13.1] years; control, 50.9 [12.0] years) participated in the trial. Eighty-eight were randomized to the contemporary control arm, and 108 of 289 remaining participants (37%) were randomized to RT-DXd; 3 participants did not receive block A treatment, and 11 did not receive the assigned control treatment, leaving the intention-to-treat population with 105 and 77 evaluable participants. Among 105 patients treated with RT-DXd in block A, the modeled pCR rate was 54% in immune-positive tumors, which met the predefined threshold for success. Similar pCR rates were observed in HR-positive, immune-positive disease (57%) and HR-negative, immune-positive disease (52%). Across all treatment blocks, overall pCR rates were similar to control regimens; however, among immune-positive patients who experienced pCR, 21 (62%) required only block A, and 33 (97%) avoided anthracycline-based chemotherapy. Enrollment was paused twice to evaluate grade 2 or higher ILD and resumed after data safety monitoring board approval. The most common AEs were fatigue and nausea.…

items.title: Perioperative pembrolizumab or placebo plus neoadjuvant cisplatin and gemcitabine in participants with muscle-invasive bladder cancer who are eligible for cisplatin: the double-blind, phase III KEYNOTE-866 study
items.authors: Bedke J, Arkosy P, Nishiyama H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Perioperative PD-(L)1 inhibitors, either combined with cisplatin-based chemotherapy or enfortumab vedotin, have improved outcomes in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) who are cisplatin eligible. The double-blind, phase III KEYNOTE-866 study evaluated perioperative (neoadjuvant and adjuvant) pembrolizumab versus placebo added to neoadjuvant cisplatin plus gemcitabine (chemotherapy) and radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection (cystectomy) in MIBC. Patients And Methods: Eligible participants were aged ≥18 years, had centrally assessed clinical stage T2-T4aN0M0 or T1-T4aN1M0 MIBC with ≥50% urothelial histology, and were eligible for cisplatin-based chemotherapy and cystectomy. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to neoadjuvant pembrolizumab or placebo plus chemotherapy every 3 weeks for 4 cycles, followed by cystectomy, and adjuvant pembrolizumab or placebo every 3 weeks for 13 cycles (pembrolizumab or placebo group, respectively). Primary end point was event-free survival (EFS) by investigator assessment. Pathological complete response (pCR) rate by blinded independent central pathological review and overall survival (OS) were key secondary end points. Safety was a secondary end point. Results: Overall, 907 participants were randomly assigned (pembrolizumab, n = 453; placebo, n = 454). Median follow-up was 60.9 months (range, 40.7-78.7). At 60 months, the estimated EFS rate was 63.5% with pembrolizumab versus 61.9% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.71-1.10; one-sided P = 0.1366). The pCR rate was 44.4% versus 35.8% (estimated difference 8.9%; 95% CI 2.5-15.1); median OS was not reached in both groups (hazard ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.79-1.27). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 99.8% of participants in the pembrolizumab group (grade ≥3 in 80.2%) and 98.7% in the placebo group (grade ≥3 in 75.1%). Conclusions: The addition of perioperative pembrolizumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and cystectomy did not confer a statistically significant EFS benefit in participants with MIBC who are cisplatin eligible. The safety profile of pembrolizumab was manageable and consistent with prior reports.

items.title: Capivasertib plus abiraterone in PTEN-deficient de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: updated survival analysis from CAPItello-281
items.authors: Fizazi K, Clarke NW, De Santis M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Patients with phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN)-deficient de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) have poor prognosis and reduced benefit from current standard of care. The phase III CAPItello-281 study (NCT04493853) showed a statistically significant benefit in radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) with capivasertib plus abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone (combined with prednisone/prednisolone and androgen deprivation therapy): hazard ratio (HR) 0.81, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.66-0.98; P=0.034. The HR for interim overall survival (OS; 26% maturity) was 0.90, 95% CI 0.71-1.15. Here, we report ad hoc, descriptive analyses at 42% OS data maturity. Patients And Methods: Patients with de novo mHSPC and PTEN-deficient tumors (defined as ≥90% of viable malignant cells with no specific cytoplasmic staining by immunohistochemistry) received capivasertib plus abiraterone or matched placebo (randomized 1:1) plus abiraterone. Analyses performed at this ad hoc data cut-off, including the alpha-controlled key secondary endpoint of OS as well as the primary endpoint of investigator-assessed rPFS, were descriptive and not prespecified in the protocol. Results: 1012 patients received capivasertib plus abiraterone (n=507) or placebo plus abiraterone (n=505). At this ad hoc analysis at 42% OS maturity (data cut-off: March 9, 2026), with 17 months' additional follow-up (median follow-up 39 months in both arms), HR for OS favored capivasertib plus abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68-0.99, P=0.044) and OS medians were reached: 57.4 versus 46.5 months. Updated rPFS (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70-0.99, nominal P=0.033; median 35.5 versus 26.0 months) was consistent with the primary analysis. The safety profile remained consistent with the primary findings. Conclusions: With longer follow-up, findings from this updated descriptive analysis support the clinically meaningful OS benefit of adding capivasertib to abiraterone in the treatment of patients with PTEN-deficient mHSPC. Capivasertib plus abiraterone represents a first-in-class targeted treatment approach for this poor prognosis population with high unmet need.

items.title: Nivolumab plus relatlimab with platinum-doublet chemotherapy versus nivolumab with platinum-doublet chemotherapy in stage IV or recurrent non-small cell lung cancer: clinical, translational, and patient-reported outcomes results from the phase II RELATIVITY-104 study
items.authors: Girard N, Burotto M, Paz-Ares LG, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Programmed death 1-blocking antibody, nivolumab, plus lymphocyte-activation gene 3-blocking antibody, relatlimab, is approved for advanced melanoma. We report results from Part 2 of RELATIVITY-104, the first phase II, proof-of-concept, head-to-head study to evaluate first-line nivolumab plus relatlimab plus platinum doublet chemotherapy (PDCT) versus nivolumab plus PDCT in patients with stage IV/recurrent non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Patients And Methods: In Part 2, patients were randomized 1:1 to nivolumab plus relatlimab plus PDCT or nivolumab plus PDCT. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) per blinded independent central review (BICR). Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS) and duration of response (DOR) per BICR, ORR and PFS by subgroups, and safety. Exploratory analyses included overall survival (OS), biomarker, translational, and patient-reported outcomes. Results: In part 2, the primary endpoint was not met (ORR, 51.3% for nivolumab plus relatlimab plus PDCT versus 45.0% for nivolumab plus PDCT); PFS hazard ratio (HR; 90% confidence interval [CI]) was 0.89 (0.72 to 1.09). A trend towards improved clinical benefit was seen with nivolumab plus relatlimab plus PDCT in a subgroup of patients with programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) ≥1% and nonsquamous histology (ORR: 58.0% versus 39.6%; PFS: HR, 0.68; 90% CI 0.46 to 1.01). A potential improvement in OS was observed with nivolumab plus relatlimab plus PDCT in the PD-L1 ≥1% nonsquamous subgroup (HR, 0.60; 90% CI 0.38 to 0.94). The safety profile of nivolumab plus relatlimab plus PDCT was manageable and consistent with previous reports. Conclusion: In RELATIVITY-104, the addition of relatlimab to standard-of-care did not improve outcomes in the unselected all-randomized population. However, positive trends observed in the subgroup of patients with tumor PD-L1 ≥1% and nonsquamous NSCLC supports further investigation in these patients in the phase III RELATIVITY-1093 study. items.title: Lymph node-targeted, mKRAS-specific amphiphile vaccine in pancreatic cancer: the randomized phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial
items.authors: George B, Singh H, Devoe CE, et al.
items.abstract: Camupepimut (ELI-002 7P) drives mutated KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell responses that correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with mKRAS pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in the phase 1 AMPLIFY-201 trial. In the phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial, patients with stage I-III KRAS-mutated PDAC without recurrence within 6 months of standard therapy were randomized 2:1 to camupepimut (n = 96) or standard-of-care/observation (n = 48). Stratification balanced nodal status. The primary DFS endpoint was not met (median 23.8 versus 21.2 months; HR 0.85, P = 0.5329). However, prespecified and exploratory analyses were informative. A numerical DFS advantage at 6 months of 14.0% (75.7% versus 61.7%; HR 0.55, P = 0.0557) corresponded to camupepimut dosing. Post hoc multivariate Cox regression analysis of DFS indicated an improved outcome for camupepimut (adjusted HR 0.47, P = 0.0086), a worse outcome for stage III disease (adjusted HR 2.29, P = 0.0127), an elevated baseline CA19-9 (adjusted HR 3.16, P < 0.0001) and baseline circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) positivity (adjusted HR 5.99, P < 0.0001). Prespecified subgroup analyses addressing prognostic and predictive factors suggested DFS benefit for camupepimut (ctDNA negative: HR 0.51, P = 0.0280; no prior radiation: HR 0.59, P = 0.0221). Exploratory analysis demonstrated that ex vivo mKRAS-specific T cell responses were robust (98.9%, 89/90) and associated with antigen spreading (86.7%, 13/15). In camupepimut-treated patients, mKRAS-specific T cell response >9.17-fold over baseline (82.2%, 74/90) correlated with improved DFS (HR 0.22, P < 0.0001), with the median DFS not reached versus 6.08 months for above and below 9.17-fold, respectively. Camupepimut safety was similar to observation, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 10.4% (10/96) versus 14.6% (7/48), and few serious AEs (6.3%, 6/96 versus 8.3%, 4/48; reflecting progression/surgical complication). These efficacy and immunogenicity signals will inform a refined strategy for a confirmatory phase 3 trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05726864 .

items.title: Efficacy and toxicity of antibody-drug conjugates in older adults with breast cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Margolis S, Kalbasi TR, Zektser Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: : Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have reshaped breast cancer treatment, yet their efficacy and toxicity in older adults (≥65 years) remain poorly characterized. Methods: : We searched PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase (Elsevier) through November 17, 2025 for phase 2 or 3 randomized trials comparing ADCs versus non-ADC therapies in metastatic or early-stage breast cancer. The primary analysis assessed progression-free survival (PFS) in metastatic disease and invasive disease-free survival (IDFS) in early-stage disease, stratified by age (≥65 vs. <65 years), using pooled hazard ratios (pHRs). Age-by-treatment interaction was assessed using the ratio of HRs. Secondary outcomes included overall survival (OS) and grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs). Results: Of 3,045 records identified, 20 trials (14 metastatic, 6 early-stage; 13,055 participants, 18% aged ≥65 years) met inclusion criteria. In metastatic trials, ADCs improved PFS in both older (pHR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.51-0.79) and younger participants (pHR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.51-0.66), with no significant age-by-treatment interaction (pooled ratio of HRs, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.91-1.33). ADCs also improved OS in the metastatic setting, though no trial reported age-stratified OS. In early-stage trials, only two reported age-stratified IDFS, with discordant results precluding pooled analysis. Grade ≥3 AEs were reported across all trials, but only three provided age-stratified data, and none stratified AEs jointly by treatment arm and age. Conclusion: ADC efficacy in metastatic breast cancer was similar across age groups, though data in early-stage disease were limited. Insufficient age- and treatment-stratified toxicity reporting precludes meaningful safety assessment of ADCs in older adults with breast cancer.

items.title: ENZARAD (ANZUP 1303): Phase 3 Trial of Enzalutamide With Androgen Deprivation Therapy and Radiation Therapy in High-Risk Localized or Locally Advanced Prostate Cancer
items.authors: Williams S, Sweeney CJ, Thomas H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The effects of adding enzalutamide to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and radiotherapy for high-risk localized or locally advanced prostate cancer were unknown. Methods: Open-label, phase 3 trial of definitive prostate radiotherapy with 24 months of ADT and 1:1 randomization to either enzalutamide (160mg daily for 24 months) or an older nonsteroidal antiandrogen (NSAA) for 6 months. The primary endpoint was metastasis-free survival on conventional imaging (MFS-CI) with computerized tomography and/or 99mTc-bone scintigraphy. Radiation to pelvic lymph nodes was required for cN1 disease but optional for cN0. Results: 802 participants were randomized. After a median follow-up of 92 months, 207 MFS-CI events were reported (98 enzalutamide, 109 NSAA) with 8-year MFS-CI rates 74% vs 72%, hazard ratio [HR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.67 to 1.15; P=0.34). Prespecified subgroup analyses noted enzalutamide was associated with a possible MFS-CI benefit in the subgroup undergoing planned pelvic nodal radiotherapy, N=324 (HR 0.47, 95% CI: 0.29 to 0.76 Padjusted =0.004). Grade 3-5 adverse events were reported in 185 participants in each arm. Conclusions: The use of enzalutamide rather than NSAA in addition to radiotherapy and ADT for 2 years showed no significant MFS-CI or OS improvement at 8 years.

items.title: COMPANION-002: A Randomized Phase 2/3 Trial of Tovecimig Plus Paclitaxel versus Paclitaxel Alone as a Second-line Therapy in Patients with Advanced Biliary Tract Cancer
items.authors: Azad NS, Hu I, Pathak P, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Patients with previously treated biliary tract cancer (BTC) have a short median overall survival (OS), and few treatment options. Tovecimig, a bispecific antibody to delta-like ligand-4 and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-A, was evaluated in combination with paclitaxel in COMPANION-002, a randomized phase 2/3 study in pretreated patients with advanced BTC. Methods: Patients with advanced BTC with one prior systemic therapy were randomized to paclitaxel (80 mg/m2; days 1, 8 and 15) with or without tovecimig (10 mg/kg; days 1 and 15). The primary endpoint was RECIST v1.1-defined objective response rate (ORR) as assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS) and OS. Crossover from the paclitaxel control arm to tovecimig plus paclitaxel was permitted following BICR-confirmed progression. Results: 168 patients were randomized 2:1 to tovecimig+paclitaxel (n=111) or paclitaxel alone (n=57). Tovecimig+paclitaxel significantly improved BICR-assessed ORR (18.0% vs 5.3%; P=.0228) and PFS (4.7 vs 2.6 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.44; P<.0001). Among 31 patients (54%) who crossed over, post-progression PFS (time from crossover to subsequent second progression) exceeded initial PFS (PFS from randomization to initial progression on paclitaxel; 3.5 vs 1.9 months; HR, 0.40; P=.0035). Overall, 142 patients (85%) received tovecimig; no difference in OS was observed (HR, 1.05; P=.779). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) with tovecimig+paclitaxel were hypertension (69.4%) and fatigue (66.7%). Grade ≥3 TEAEs occurred in 93.5% and 64.2% of patients treated with tovecimig+paclitaxel and paclitaxel alone, respectively. Conclusion: Tovecimig combined with paclitaxel significantly improved ORR and PFS versus paclitaxel alone as second-line therapy for patients with BTC.

items.title: Adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine compared to standard of care after curative intent resection of cholangiocarcinoma and muscle invasive gallbladder carcinoma (ACTICCA-1/AIO-HEP-0112 trial)
items.authors: Stein A, Bridgewater J, Klümpen HJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Despite curative resection and adjuvant capecitabine, about 50% of biliary tract cancer (BTC) patients have tumour recurrence or die within two years. Combination chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine (CisGem) is an established palliative chemotherapy regimen BTC, which has been evaluated in the adjuvant setting here. Patients And Methods: ACTICCA-1 is a randomized, phase III investigator-initiated trial. Patients were enrolled at 67 sites across 8 countries between September 2017 and January 2023 and randomized to CisGem or capecitabine as adjuvant treatment regimen, each for a planned duration of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint is disease-free survival (DFS). Secondary endpoints include overall survival, safety and tolerability. Results: 591 patients have been randomized. Median follow-up was 4.8 years. Median age was 63, 46.9% were female, and median interval between surgery and enrolment was 67 days. Primary tumour location was intrahepatic in 28.3%, perihilar in 19%, distal in 36.5%, and gallbladder in 16.2%, 47.9% of patients had lymph node positive disease (N+). CisGem showed a median DFS of 25.7 months compared to 17.9 months for capecitabine (log rank p=0.097). As pre-defined in the statistical analysis plan (SAP), due to violation of proportional hazard assumption a Cox model was not feasible and restricted mean survival time (RMST) was analysed. Patients receiving CisGem experienced on average 2.6 additional DFS months (95% CI 0.6-4.68) compared to capecitabine (RMST in the first 3 years, p=0.011), but no significant improvement in overall survival (RMST p=0.076; median 58.1 vs. 48.2 months). Toxicity showed a higher number of Severe Adverse Events (SAE) (130 vs. 113 with 51 vs. 47 assessed as treatment related) and a higher AE rate of 74.7% vs. 69.5% with CisGem compared to capecitabine. Conclusion: CisGem did not statistically improve DFS compared to capecitabine and should thus not be applied as standard of care in the adjuvant setting. Trial Registration: The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02104882) and the EudraCT Nr: 2012-005078-70 / EU-CT-Nr.: 2024-517340-61-00.

items.title: Final results of nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab or chemotherapy in microsatellite instability-high/mismatch repair-deficient metastatic colorectal cancer from CheckMate 8HW
items.authors: Lonardi S, Lenz HJ, Elez E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The phase III CheckMate 8HW trial met its dual primary endpoints of superior progression-free survival (PFS) with nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NIVO+IPI) versus chemotherapy (first-line [1L]) and versus NIVO (all lines) in patients with centrally confirmed microsatellite instability-high/mismatch repair deficient (MSI-H/dMMR) metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). We report prespecified final overall survival (OS) analyses and updated efficacy outcomes. Methods: Immunotherapy-naïve adults with mCRC across different lines and MSI-H/dMMR by local testing were randomized 2:2:1 to NIVO (240 mg) plus IPI (1 mg/kg) Q3W for four doses, then NIVO 480 mg Q4W; NIVO (240 mg) Q2W (six doses), then 480 mg Q4W; or chemotherapy ± targeted therapies. Secondary endpoints include PFS in NIVO+IPI versus NIVO (1L), and OS and objective response rate (ORR) in the centrally confirmed MSI-H/dMMR population. Results: 839 patients across all lines were randomized; efficacy analyses were conducted in those with centrally confirmed MSI-H/dMMR. Median follow-up across all lines and treatment groups was 68.0 months (range 37.6-81.4). NIVO+IPI demonstrated significant OS benefit versus NIVO across all lines (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.46-0.82; P=0.0009) and versus chemotherapy in 1L (HR 0.37; 95% CI 0.24-0.57; P<0.0001]). Clinically meaningful OS benefit was noted with 1L NIVO+IPI versus NIVO (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.44-0.99; P=0.0432), not meeting the prespecified threshold for significance (P<0.006). PFS continued to favor NIVO+IPI across all three comparisons: NIVO (all lines; HR 0.60), chemotherapy (1L; HR 0.21), and NIVO (1L: HR: 0.68). Grade 3/4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 78 (22%) versus 50 (14%) patients treated with NIVO+IPI versus NIVO across all lines, with no new safety concerns or additional treatment-related deaths from the previous follow-up. Conclusions: NIVO+IPI showed significant OS benefit versus NIVO across all lines and versus chemotherapy in 1L, while providing a clinical OS benefit versus NIVO in 1L, reinforcing its standard-of-care status in MSI-H/dMMR mCRC.

items.title: Relatlimab plus nivolumab versus nivolumab for advanced melanoma: 5-year survival and biomarker analyses of the phase 3 RELATIVITY-047 trial
items.authors: Long GV, Dolfi S, Hodi FS, et al.
items.abstract: Nivolumab plus relatlimab is approved for advanced melanoma based on the RELATIVITY-047 trial; however, long-term data are needed. Here, we report data from RELATIVITY-047 with the longest follow-up at present. In this phase 2-3, double-blind trial, patients with metastatic/unresectable melanoma were randomized 1:1 to nivolumab 480 mg plus relatlimab 160 mg (n = 355) or nivolumab 480 mg (n = 359) intravenously every 4 weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review. Secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), response, and safety. Additional post-hoc analyses such as melanoma-specific survival (MSS), and exploratory biomarker analyses are also reported. This analysis shows clear separation in survival curves with the largest absolute differences to date in PFS, OS, and MSS. In this prespecified 5-year analysis, with a minimum follow-up of 57.3 months, nivolumab plus relatlimab demonstrated continued clinically significant benefit versus nivolumab for PFS (hazard ratio = 0.77; 95% confidence interval: 0.65-0.92), OS (hazard ratio = 0.78; 95% confidence interval: 0.64-0.95), and MSS (hazard ratio = 0.71; 95% confidence interval: 0.57-0.88). The safety profile remained consistent with prior reports. Among biomarker-evaluable patients in the programmed death ligand 1 ≥1% subgroup, analyses revealed an association between worse outcomes with nivolumab and high peripheral or tumor lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG-3)+ CD8 cell levels. The addition of relatlimab to nivolumab was associated with a lower prevalence of primary resistance than nivolumab alone. These data support the hypothesis that relatlimab can overcome LAG-3-mediated resistance to nivolumab and provides evidence for differential efficacy patterns observed across biomarker subgroups linked to primary versus acquired resistance states. items.title: A randomised phase III trial of adjuvant treatment intensification with mFOLFIRINOX versus mFOLFOX6 in high-risk stage III colon cancer: Results of the international IROCAS study
items.authors: Bennouna J, André T, Martin E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Patients with pT4 and/or pN2 stage III colon cancer remain at high risk of recurrence despite oxaliplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy. We evaluated whether intensification with modified FOLFIRINOX improved outcomes compared with modified FOLFOX6. Patients And Methods: In this international, academic, open-label, randomised phase III trial conducted by PRODIGE in France, CCTG in Canada, and GONO in Italy, patients with stage III colon adenocarcinoma after R0 resection presenting T4 and/or N2 were randomly assigned (1:1) to mFOLFIRINOX or mFOLFOX6 every 2 weeks for 12 cycles. The primary endpoint was 3-year disease-free survival (DFS) in the intention-to-treat population. Results: Between May 2017 and June 2023, 795 patients were assigned to mFOLFIRINOX (n=398) or mFOLFOX6 (n=397). Median age was 59 years (range 19-75); 39.7% were women, 52.8% had pT4 disease, 72.2% had pN2 disease, and 25.3% had both. At a median follow-up of 55 months (IQR 42.6-65.9), 284 DFS events had occurred: 146 with mFOLFIRINOX and 138 with mFOLFOX6. Three-year DFS was 65.6% versus 66.3%, respectively (hazard ratio [HR] 1.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84-1.36; P=0.61). Although Overall survival (OS) data remain immature, 3-year OS was 91.2% versus 86.7% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.61-1.21; P=0.37); no significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction was observed. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 62.2% and 62.1% of patients, respectively. Grade ≥3 diarrhoea (15.6% versus 3.8%) and fatigue (7.3% versus 1.8%) were more frequent with mFOLFIRINOX, whereas grade ≥3 neutropenia was less frequent (18.0% versus 23.9%). G-CSF use was 37.8% versus 19.1%. Conclusion: Adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX triplet chemotherapy did not improve DFS compared with standard doublet mFOLFOX6 in patients with high-risk stage III colon cancer. These findings do not support empirical chemotherapy intensification and highlight the need for novel adjuvant strategies. Gov Identifier: NCT02967289.

items.title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin followed by postsurgical adjuvant nivolumab versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine-cisplatin in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer: final results from the phase III CA017-078 trial
items.authors: Sonpavde G, van der Heijden MS, Gupta S, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Perioperative immune-checkpoint inhibition improves outcomes in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). The phase III, randomized CA017-078 (ENERGIZE) trial evaluated perioperative nivolumab plus neoadjuvant gemcitabine-cisplatin (GC) versus neoadjuvant GC alone for previously untreated, resectable MIBC. Patients And Methods: Adults with previously untreated cT2-T4aN0M0 MIBC eligible for radical cystectomy (RC) and cisplatin were randomized to neoadjuvant nivolumab plus GC followed by RC and adjuvant nivolumab (nivolumab plus GC arm), or neoadjuvant GC followed by RC alone (GC arm). Co-primary endpoints were pathological complete response (pCR; defined as ypT0N0) and event-free survival (EFS). Overall survival (OS) was a secondary endpoint within the prespecified hierarchical testing strategy, and formal testing was contingent on a statistically significant EFS result. Results: At this final analysis with 54.5 months of median follow-up, 325 patients were randomized to the nivolumab plus GC arm, 328 to the GC arm. pCR rates were 39.1% and 29.6%, respectively (adjusted difference 9.5%, 99.91% CI -2.6-21.6). EFS was not improved in the nivolumab plus GC versus GC arm (104 events in each arm; HR 0.94, 95.74% CI 0.71-1.25; P=0.6697). OS was summarized descriptively because EFS did not meet the testing criterion (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.64-1.21). Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 50.0% versus 49.5%; one treatment-related death occurred with nivolumab plus GC. Pretreatment ctDNA was positive in 229/416 tested patients (55%) overall, 108/211 (51%) in the GC arm, and 121/205 (59%) in the nivolumab plus GC arm. Clearance by cycle 4 day 1 (C4D1) occurred in 153/199 patients (76.9%) overall, 87/107 (81.3%) with nivolumab plus GC, and 66/92 (71.7%) with GC. ctDNA detection at baseline and at C4D1 was associated with shorter EFS and OS. Conclusions: The addition of perioperative nivolumab to neoadjuvant GC did not improve outcomes and was associated with predictable toxicity. Exploratory analysis showed ctDNA was strongly prognostic.

items.title: Oral Health Behavior-Cognition-Awareness education is associated with improved short-term knowledge and long-term oral hygiene in head and neck cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy: a two-phase study
items.authors: Sun C, Lin Q, Zhang F, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC) has increased steadily, and radiotherapy remains a primary treatment modality. However, radiotherapy may induce severe oral complications, including radiation-related caries and osteoradionecrosis of the jaw (ORN). Consequently, comprehensive pre-treatment oral care and patient education are essential. This two-phase study conducted in Guangzhou, China, evaluated the effects of a structured oral health education program on short-term knowledge, behaviors, and long-term oral hygiene outcomes in HNC patients undergoing radiotherapy. Methods: In Phase 1, 63 HNC patients were prospectively enrolled and received a standardized, single-session Oral Health Behavior-Cognition-Awareness (OHBCA) education. Questionnaires assessed knowledge, awareness, and behaviors at baseline and 6 weeks post-intervention. In Phase 2, a retrospective cohort analysis was performed, comparing 24 patients from Phase 1 who completed 12-month follow-up (intervention group) with 19 historical controls who received standard care. Oral hygiene behaviors and clinical indices (e.g., Debris Index, Gingival Index) were evaluated at 12 months post-radiotherapy. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the use of a convenience sample, formal sample size calculation was not performed. Statistical analyses included paired and independent samples tests as appropriate. Results: In Phase 1, the OHBCA education led to significant, large-magnitude improvements in oral health knowledge, awareness, and self-reported behaviors (all p < 0.01), including reduced tobacco/alcohol use and enhanced hygiene practices. In Phase 2, at the 12-month follow-up, the intervention group demonstrated significantly better oral hygiene indices (e.g., lower plaque and gingival scores; all p < 0.0001) and more favorable self-care behaviors compared to the historical control group. Conclusion: This exploratory study suggests that a structured pre-radiotherapy oral health education program is associated with significant short-term improvements in patient knowledge and behaviors, as well as superior long-term clinical oral hygiene outcomes. These preliminary, hypothesis-generating findings support the potential value of integrating systematic patient education into the HNC radiotherapy care pathway and underscore the need for validation through prospective randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Pan-Asian adapted ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with renal cell carcinoma
items.authors: Kanesvaran R, Gruenwald V, Wong A, et al.
items.abstract: The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with renal cell carcinoma (RCC) were published in May 2024 and adapted in December 2025 according to previously established standard methodology to produce the Pan-Asian adapted ESMO consensus guidelines for the management of Asian patients with RCC. The adapted guidelines presented in this manuscript represent the consensus opinions reached by a panel of Asian experts in the treatment of patients with RCC representing the oncological societies of China [Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO)], Indonesia [Indonesian Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (ISHMO)], India [Indian Society of Medical and Paediatric Oncology (ISMPO)], Japan [Japanese Society of Medical Oncology (JSMO)], Korea [Korean Society of Medical Oncology (KSMO)], Malaysia [Malaysian Oncological Society (MOS)], The Philippines [Philippine Society of Medical Oncology (PSMO)], Singapore [Singapore Society of Oncology (SSO)], Taiwan [Taiwan Oncology Society (TOS)] and Thailand [Thai Society of Clinical Oncology (TSMO)], coordinated by ESMO and the SSO. The voting was based on scientific evidence and was independent of the current treatment practices, drug access restrictions and reimbursement decisions in the different regions of Asia. The latter are discussed separately in the manuscript. The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with RCC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in drug approvals and reimbursement strategies between the different regions.
