items.title: Denosumab Therapy Duration and Osteonecrosis of the Jaw and Skeletal Events in Bone-Metastatic Prostate Cancer
items.authors: Kim S, Jung S, Bu S, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Denosumab reduces skeletal-related events in bone-metastatic prostate cancer but carries a cumulative risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ). The treatment duration that best balances these risks has not been established in clinical settings. Objective: To evaluate the association between duration of denosumab treatment and the 3-year cumulative incidence of ONJ and skeletal events. Design, Setting, And Participants: This nationwide retrospective cohort study emulated a target trial using Korean Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service data from January 1, 2009, through August 31, 2024; patients were not randomized. A clone-censor-weight approach with inverse probability of censoring weighting estimated 3-year cumulative incidence and risk ratios (RRs), with death as a competing event. Men included in the analysis had bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and initiated oncologic-dose denosumab therapy; men with castration-sensitive disease were excluded. Exposures: Six strategies defined by 3 durations (≤6, 7-12, and ≥13 months), each as a schedule-flexible group and a schedule-adherent subgroup (intervals ≤12 weeks). Main Outcomes And Measures: Three-year cumulative incidence of ONJ and skeletal events (pathologic fracture, spinal cord compression, and surgery to bone) was the primary outcome; a radiotherapy-inclusive conventional composite of skeletal-related events was assessed as a secondary outcome. Results: Among 3307 men included in the analysis (mean [SD] age, 72.6 [8.6] years; median follow-up, 42.6 [IQR, 26.5-57.4] months), the overall 3-year cumulative incidence was 9.8% (95% CI, 8.7%-11.0%) for ONJ and 4.9% (95% CI, 4.2%-5.7%) for skeletal events. Relative to treatment for 6 months or less, treatment for 7 to 12 months showed a lower risk of skeletal events (3.82% [95% CI, 3.04%-4.80%] vs 5.76% [95% CI, 4.23%-7.79%]; RR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.45-0.97]) and higher risk of ONJ (3.28% [95% CI, 2.41%-4.44%] vs 1.47% [95% CI, 0.86%-2.50%]; RR, 2.22 [95% CI, 1.21-4.11]). Compared with 7 to 12 months, treatment for 13 months or longer was associated with higher risk of ONJ (12.20% [95% CI, 10.86%-13.68%]; risk difference, 8.93 [95% CI, 7.16-10.64] percentage points), without further reduction in risk for skeletal events (3.99% [95% CI, 3.30%-4.82%]; risk difference, 0.17 [95% CI, -1.03 to 1.31] percentage points).…

items.title: Implementation and sustainability of surgical randomized trials in gynecologic oncology: Adoption beyond publication
items.authors: Agusti N, Bercow A, Ramirez PT, et al.
items.abstract: Surgical randomized trials have transformed gynecologic oncology by redefining the extent and route of surgery, nodal assessment, and multimodality care. However, the effect of a surgical trial does not end at publication. Unlike medical therapies, surgical interventions depend on operator expertise, team coordination, pathology support and perioperative infrastructure. Beyond controlled trial settings, these conditions may change, creating technical drift, indication drift, and inequitable adoption. Implementation should therefore be considered a distinct, structured phase of surgical research. The period is particularly vulnerable because landmark trials often evaluate de-escalation or technically complex innovations. Expanding de-escalation beyond trial-tested eligibility can cause undertreatment, whereas diffusion of complex procedures without sufficient expertise or infrastructure can increase morbidity. Disparities in access to specialist surgeons, imaging, pathology, molecular testing, perioperative support, and long-term follow-up amplify these risks. Responsible translation requires trial reports to define the technical, institutional, and patient-selection conditions under which outcomes were achieved. Strategies may include credentialing expectations, operative standards, and risk-appropriate guidelines. Once findings sufficiently resolve equipoise, post-implementation surveillance should determine whether effective procedures are adopted-or ineffective ones abandoned-and whether appropriate use, technical fidelity, safety, equity, and outcomes are maintained as practice spreads. Secondary databases can evaluate utilization, perioperative safety, equity, practice-change attribution, and selected real-world outcomes at scale, but incompletely capture appropriateness, technical fidelity, granular complications, recurrence, and patient-reported quality of life. Surveillance should therefore use a multilevel approach that matches each objective to where information is generated and supplements broad databases with targeted clinical, procedural, and patient-reported data. Treated as an active research phase, surveillance can ensure that surgical innovation reaches the right patients and settings, with outcomes consistent with the supporting evidence.

items.title: How to plan and deliver lung cancer reirradiation: A consensus approach from the ESTRO reirradiation and lung focus groups and ReCOG
items.authors: Hoffmann L, Matrosic CK, Andratschke N, et al.
items.abstract: Lung reirradiation is seeing increased use, yet the evidence base guiding its practice remains limited despite significant technological advances. This paper provides a consensus approach addressing the technical factors underpinning clinical decision-making. It aims to answer the central question: how can clinical teams implement a safe, reproducible, and technically robust workflow for high-dose lung reirradiation? The recommendations are developed by an expert panel of radiation oncologists, medical physicists, and radiation therapists (RTT) from 14 European, American, and Canadian centres, synthesizing a broad range of clinical perspectives. The scope of this work/manuscript is to provide a structured, practical workflow applicable across diverse clinical settings. Using a clinical case, the manuscript demonstrates key conceptual principles, such as the rationale for advanced dose accumulation and the impact of anatomical changes during treatment, with clear, stepwise guidance to support consistent implementation and informed clinical judgement. Key recommended steps include retrieval of prior treatment data; consideration of prior positioning and motion management; and equieffective dose accumulation using deformable image registration or organ-at-risk (OAR)-focused rigid registration. Treatment planning should explicitly incorporate prior dose while balancing target coverage against OAR limits. Daily online volumetric image guidance is central to evaluating both bony and soft-tissue anatomy, enabling setup adjustments to protect critical structures approaching tolerance. Clear documentation and multidisciplinary communication are integral throughout. This consensus approach is intended to support both centres that aim to establish reirradiation practice and experienced teams seeking to harmonize best practices.

items.title: Long-Term Outcomes and Biomarker Correlates of a Multi-Institutional Phase II Study of Hypofractionated Proton Beam Therapy for Unresectable Primary Liver Tumors
items.authors: Roberts HJ, Hong TS, Guan Z, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate long-term outcomes and determine whether longitudinal plasma profiling provides biological insight into disease progression after proton hypofractionated ablative radiation therapy (HART) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC). Patients And Methods: In this single-arm, multi-institutional phase II trial, 92 patients with localized unresectable HCC or ICC with Child-Pugh class A/B liver function received HART (up to 67.5 GyE in 15 fractions). Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Plasma samples were collected at baseline, days 1, 8, 15, and 1-month after treatment for exploratory correlative analyses. Results: Among evaluable patients (44 HCC, 39 ICC), median OS was 29.2 months (HCC) and 20.8 months (ICC), with 5-year OS rates of 25.9% and 12.3%, respectively. Median PFS was 13.8 months (HCC) and 8.4 months (ICC). In-field local failure occurred in 2 HCC (4.5%) and 7 ICC (17.9%) patients, whereas out-of-field intrahepatic/distant progression remained the predominant pattern of failure. No grade >3 treatment-related toxicities were observed. Exploratory plasma profiling identified distinct biological signatures associated with progression: HCC was characterized by markers of hypoxia, inflammation, vascular remodeling, stromal activation, and hepatic regeneration, whereas associations in ICC predominantly involved signatures of hypoxia and vascular remodeling. Conclusions: HART provides durable long-term in-field local control with minimal toxicity, but disease progression remains predominantly out-of-field intrahepatic/distant. Exploratory correlative analyses suggest that biological signatures reflecting vascular remodeling, hypoxia, inflammation, stromal activation, and hepatic reserve are associated with progression despite successful local therapy, informing future translational studies and combination strategies.

items.title: Trends in multi-lesion stereotactic radiosurgery: an IROC survey on the state of the practice
items.authors: Faught AM, Vinogradskiy Y, Agazaryan N, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The last decade has seen an increase in the treatment of multiple lesions within a single course of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS). Hardware, software, and processes have evolved to support the clinical adoption of multi-lesion SRS. An understanding of the current state of the practice is needed to provide proper guidance. Methods: The Imaging and Radiation Oncology Core (IROC) distributed an addendum on SRS practices along with its annual facility questionnaire. Participants were asked 13 questions regarding their SRS program, including: whether single-isocenter multiple target deliveries are performed, delivery equipment used, the maximum number of lesions treated with a single isocenter, quality assurance practices, and the margins used for treatment. Results: The survey generated 879 responses from institutions with an SRS program. Among those programs, 91% (n=789) reported treating multiple lesions within a single course of treatment. Among institutions with equipment capable of treating multiple lesions with a single isocenter, 83% (n=504) reported doing so. Practices varied across clinical programs; for example, expansion margins from gross tumor volume (GTV) to planning target volume (PTV) ranged from 0mm to 2+mm. This variation was partially associated with the use of a six degree-of-freedom (6DOF) couch and the maximum number of lesions treated in a single isocenter. Among programs that treated multiple lesions per isocenter, 84.1% used a 6DOF couch compared to only 50.8% that treated one lesion per isocenter (p<0.01, χ2=64.8). Similarly, among institutions that reported no GTV to PTV margin (n=79), 100% used a 6DOF couch while only 55.3% of institutions that used a 2 mm margin reported the use of a 6DOF couch (p<0.01, χ2=73.0). Conclusion: Treatment of multiple lesions in a single course of SRS has become standard practice. However, when treating with a single isocenter, variability exists in clinical practice, highlighting the need for guidance on best practices.

items.title: Comparative assessment of skin toxicity in prone vs supine positions during postoperative breast radiotherapy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Sawaira F, Khalid AA, Qazi H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Breast-conserving surgery followed by adjuvant whole-breast irradiation (WBI) is the standard of care for early-stage breast cancer. Patient positioning during WBI, prone versus supine, may influence the incidence and severity of radiation-induced skin toxicity. However, existing studies have reported inconsistent findings, and no comprehensive meta-analytic synthesis has been performed to date. Objective: To systematically compare the incidence of acute and late skin toxicity outcomes between prone and supine WBI in patients with early-stage breast cancer following breast-conserving surgery. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Randomized controlled trials and comparative observational studies reporting skin toxicity outcomes for prone versus supine WBI were included. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled using random-effects models and expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic and Cochran's Q test. Results: Nine reports met the inclusion criteria (1128 enrolled patients). Because three reports (Mulliez et al., Veldeman et al., Vakaet et al.) derive from a single randomized trial and one retrospective cohort (De Langhe et al.) overlaps that centre's patients, no cohort contributed more than once to any pooled outcome. Using de-duplicated data and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) random-effects models, prone positioning was not associated with a statistically significant change in any outcome. For moist desquamation, the nominally significant reduction observed in the original analysis was no longer statistically significant after removal of overlapping cohorts and application of HKSJ inference (two randomized trials; RR 0.57; HKSJ 95% CI 0.01-42.55; p = 0.34). No significant differences were found for Grade 2+ acute skin toxicity (RR 0.76; p = 0.37), acute pain (RR 0.75; nominally significant under DerSimonian-Laird [p = 0.04] but not under HKSJ [p = 0.29]), Grade 2 erythema/dermatitis (RR 0.84), Grade 1-2 toxicity (RR 1.05), or fibrosis (RR 0.76). A non-significant trend toward more mild (Grade 1) erythema was seen in the prone group (RR 1.72; HKSJ p = 0.16). Statistical heterogeneity was high for several outcomes.…

items.title: Patient-reported outcome sub-analysis of a phase 2 trial of bladder preservation therapy with atezolizumab and radiation therapy (BPT-ART) for invasive bladder cancer
items.authors: Mathis BJ, Nagumo Y, Kimura T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Impacts on quality of life (QoL) from bladder preservation therapy with atezolizumab and radiation therapy (BPT-ART), as assessed by patient reported outcomes (PROs), remains unanalyzed. We delineated temporal effects of BPT-ART on urinary QoL across multiple domains using established PRO tools. Methods: This was a planned sub-analysis for the Phase 2 BPT-ART trial. PRO instruments included the EuroQol 5-item 5-point questionnaire (EQ-5D-5L), OABSS (Overactive Bladder Symptom Score) and IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score). Forty-four total participants from 9 Japanese hospitals were surveyed from January 2019 to June 2024. Changes from baseline for each PRO tool were summarized over time as mean changes with 95% confidence intervals. Results: EQ-5D-5L utility showed a transient decline during treatment, followed by recovery during follow-up. At the dimension level, pain/discomfort showed the largest transient decrease during radiotherapy (mean change - 0.60, 95% CI -0.90 to -0.31), followed by recovery after treatment. Total OABSS showed a modest increase during radiotherapy and recovered after treatment. Among OABSS components, urgency showed the largest increase (+ 0.95, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.46), followed by urgency incontinence (+ 0.53, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.96) and nighttime frequency (+ 0.33, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.62), while daytime frequency remained stable (+ 0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.26). Baseline symptom burden was associated with absolute scores, but trajectories appeared comparable, and global health status remained stable across subgroups. Conclusion: PROs outlined a temporal pattern of QoL decline but progressive recovery, as measured across patient-reported functional domains. These results support BPT-ART as effective for maintaining patient QoL.

items.title: Bispecific dual T cell agonist invikafusp alfa in solid tumors: the phase 1/2 START-001 trial
items.authors: Sullivan RJ, Tschernia NP, Friedman CF, et al.
items.abstract: Invikafusp alfa (invika), a first-in-class, bispecific, dual T cell agonistic antibody selectively targeting Vβ6/Vβ10 T cell subsets, is being evaluated in START-001, a multicenter phase 1/2 monotherapy trial in participants with mostly immune checkpoint blockade (ICB)-resistant, antigen-rich solid tumors. Primary outcomes were safety/tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) in phase 1 and anti-tumor activity in phase 2. As of 12 March 2025, phase 1 completed dose escalation (n = 34) through dose levels of 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12 and 0.16 mg kg-1 without reaching maximum tolerated dose, and initial phase 2 enrolled 18 participants. Two participants experienced reversible dose-limiting toxicities, one at each of the 0.08 mg kg-1 and 0.16 mg kg-1 dose levels. The most common treatment-related adverse event was cytokine release syndrome, mainly grades 1 and 2. No treatment-related deaths or non-laboratory grade 4 adverse events were reported. At the optimal biological doses (OBDs; 0.08 mg kg-1 and 0.12 mg kg-1) in combined phase 1 and phase 2 cohorts, the overall objective response rate was 14.8% (4/27), including confirmed partial responses in immunologically cold tumors, such as microsatellite stable colorectal cancer and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-negative non-small cell lung cancer. No objective responses were seen at doses lower than 0.08 mg kg-1. Invika selectively and potently expanded peripheral and intratumoral Vβ6/Vβ10 T cells, of a predominantly memory-like phenotype, dose-dependently, peaking at the OBDs. Pharmacodynamic increases in interferon-γ and soluble CD25 followed a similar pattern. Integrated analyses from safety, pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and preliminary anti-tumor data supported the selection of 0.08 mg kg-1 as the RP2D. In conclusion, phase 1 of START-001 met its primary outcomes by demonstrating the acceptable safety profile of invika consistent with its mechanism of action and selecting an RP2D. Initial phase 2 results further corroborated the safety of invika and expanded its preliminary evidence of clinically meaningful anti-tumor activity in ICB-resistant solid tumors, supporting further evaluation in the ongoing phase 2. items.title: Ibrutinib and standard immunochemotherapy in younger, high-risk patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: A phase II study of GLA
items.authors: Shumilov E, Ziepert M, Friedrichs B, et al.
items.abstract: Younger patients with high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) frequently have unfavourable outcomes. We conducted a prospective phase II study evaluating ibrutinib plus rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone (R-CHOEP+I) in patients aged 18-60 years with DLBCL and age-adjusted international prognostic index ≥2. Patients received ibrutinib (560 mg daily, d1-112) combined with eight cycles of R-CHOEP q2w. The primary end-point was 2-year progression-free survival (PFS). Outcomes were compared exploratorily with those of patients with identical inclusion criteria treated with R-CHOEP alone in the R-MegaCHOEP phase III trial (n = 130). Forty patients started R-CHOEP+I. Ibrutinib was administered for a median of 96 days, and 42% of patients completed treatment fully according to protocol. The overall response rate was 92%. Sixty-eight per cent received all R-CHOEP cycles compared with 88% in R-MegaCHOEP; 22% vs. 49% of patients with bulky and/or extranodal disease underwent radiotherapy. With a median follow-up of 31 months, 2-year PFS was 83% (95% CI, 71-95) vs. 75% (95% CI, 67-82) after R-CHOEP alone (p = 0.237). Exploratory cell-of-origin analyses suggested favourable outcomes in activated B-cell-type disease, but these findings remain descriptive. Grade ≥3 haematological adverse events were frequent, although no treatment-related deaths occurred. In this prematurely closed phase II study, the addition of ibrutinib to R-CHOEP showed encouraging activity. However, findings remain exploratory and hypothesis generating only.

items.title: Overall survival from the phase III postMONARCH trial of abemaciclib plus fulvestrant versus placebo plus fulvestrant for HR+, HER2- advanced breast cancer following progression on a prior CDK4/6 inhibitor plus endocrine therapy
items.authors: Kalinsky K, Wander SA, Hamilton E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The phase III postMONARCH trial demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) with abemaciclib plus fulvestrant versus placebo plus fulvestrant in participants with HR+, HER2- advanced breast cancer (ABC) after disease progression on prior CDK4/6i plus endocrine therapy (ET). Here we report the prespecified final overall survival (OS) analysis. Participants And Methods: Eligible patients had disease progression on a CDK4/6i plus aromatase inhibitor as initial therapy for ABC or recurrence on or after adjuvant CDK4/6i plus ET. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive abemaciclib plus fulvestrant or placebo plus fulvestrant. The final OS analysis was pre-specified at 200 OS events (HR boundary 0.753). Time-to-event analyses used the Kaplan-Meier method, and stratified Cox models were used to estimate the HR and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: A total of 368 participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to abemaciclib plus fulvestrant (n = 182) or placebo plus fulvestrant (n = 186). At data cutoff, median follow-up was approximately 37 months; 200 OS events were observed (90 [50%] vs 110 [59%]). Median OS was 32.1 months with abemaciclib plus fulvestrant versus 24.6 months with placebo plus fulvestrant (HR, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.60 to 1.06]; P = 0.11, boundary for significance not reached). OS differences were consistent across subgroups. Updated PFS was consistent with the primary analysis (HR, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.62 to 0.99]; nominal P = 0.039). Time to second progression and chemotherapy-free survival also favored abemaciclib plus fulvestrant. Safety was consistent with the established abemaciclib profile with no new signals identified. Conclusion: Abemaciclib plus fulvestrant resulted in numerically longer median OS versus placebo plus fulvestrant, though statistical significance was not reached. The totality of evidence supports consideration of abemaciclib-based treatment for patients with HR+, HER2- ABC after disease progression on prior CDK4/6i plus ET. items.title: Atirmociclib and fulvestrant for patients with HR+/HER2- advanced/metastatic breast cancer who progressed on a prior cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitor: primary analysis of the randomized FourLight-1 trial
items.authors: Giordano A, Xu B, Yoshinami T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Atirmociclib is a potential first-in-class, highly selective cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 4 inhibitor, demonstrating significantly greater selectivity over CDK6. In a phase 1/2a study, atirmociclib plus endocrine therapy was well tolerated and showed encouraging antitumor activity in patients with HR+/HER2- advanced/metastatic breast cancer (mBC). We present results from a randomized study of atirmociclib plus fulvestrant versus investigator's choice of therapy (ICT) in patients with HR+/HER2- mBC whose disease progressed on prior adjuvant or first-line CDK4/6 inhibitor treatment. Patients And Methods: FourLight-1 is an open-label, phase 2 study. Patients were randomized 1:1 to atirmociclib (300 mg orally, twice daily, continuously) plus fulvestrant or ICT (fulvestrant alone or everolimus plus exemestane). The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), and safety. Results: At the data cutoff (12 January 2026), 263 patients were enrolled (atirmociclib, n = 126; ICT, n = 137; median age: 57 years). PFS was significantly improved with atirmociclib versus ICT (stratified hazard ratio: 0.60; 95% CI, 0.440-0.825; 1-sided P = 0.0007; median: 9.4 vs 6.6 months). A consistent PFS benefit was observed across most subgroups. Patients with baseline measurable disease in the atirmociclib arm had a higher ORR versus the ICT arm (21 [19.3%] vs 13 [11.3%]; nominal 2-sided P = 0.0901) and median DOR was numerically longer (14.8 vs 9.3 months, respectively); CBR was 61.9% versus 46.0%, respectively. The most common any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) in the atirmociclib arm were neutropenia (47.2%), leukopenia (33.6%), and diarrhea (28.0%); 6.4% of patients discontinued atirmociclib due to TEAEs. Conclusions: Atirmociclib plus fulvestrant showed significant and clinically meaningful PFS improvement in patients who progressed on prior CDK4/6 inhibitor treatment with a manageable safety and tolerability profile.

items.title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab with or without visugromab in muscle-invasive bladder cancer: the phase 2a GDFATHER-NEO trial
items.authors: Necchi A, Mercinelli C, Maiorano BA, et al.
items.abstract: Growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) is overexpressed in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) and was recently identified as a potential therapeutic target to overcome resistance to programmed cell death protein 1/programmed death ligand 1 (PDL1) blockade. We investigated the safety and efficacy of GDF-15 blockade in an exploratory, stratified, placebo-controlled, single-blinded, nonrandomized phase 2a trial (GDFATHER-NEO). Thirty-one cisplatin-ineligible or cisplatin-refusing patients with newly diagnosed MIBC (clinical T2-T4aN0M0) were stratified by tumor stage and PDL1 combined positive score (CPS) and allocated sequentially to receive three cycles of neoadjuvant nivolumab (N, 480 mg 4-weekly) plus the GDF-15-neutralizing antibody visugromab (V, 20 mg kg-1 4-weekly; n = 16) or placebo (P, n = 15), followed by radical cystectomy or repeat transurethral resection of the bladder tumor. Locally assessed pathologic complete response (pCR, ypT0N0/x) and Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1-based radiographic response served as dual primary endpoints. pCR was 33% (5 of 15, 95% confidence interval (CI) 12-62%) in patients receiving N + V versus 8% (1 of 13, 95% CI 0-36%) for N + P; major pathologic response was 60% (95% CI 32-84%) versus 23% (95% CI 5-54%), and radiographic overall response rate was 60% (95% CI 32-84%) versus 15% (95% CI 2-45%), respectively. Responses to N + V were associated with higher baseline densities of total and proliferating (Ki-67+) CD8+ T cells, but independent of CPS and baseline GDF-15 levels in serum and tumor. There were no treatment-related discontinuations or treatment-related delays to surgery; grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in two (13%) and three (20%) patients treated with N + V or N + P, respectively. These findings support further evaluation of visugromab in MIBC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06059547 .

items.title: Radiotherapy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A comprehensive update with practical recommendations
items.authors: Ted K. Yanagihara, Laura A. Dawson, Hirokazu Makishima, Andrew M. Moon, Michael Yan
items.abstract: Management of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is evolving rapidly and decisions regarding locoregional therapy are complex. External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is a highly effective and safe intervention with an expanding role in HCC, and major guidelines (BCLC 2026, EASL, AASLD, NCCN, ASTRO) now endorse it across defined clinical settings. However, guidelines largely treat EBRT as a single modality, whereas in practice it encompasses multiple delivery techniques and nuanced technical decisions that directly influence safety and efficacy.

items.title: A simple and interpretable method to predict head and neck offline adaptation needs based on anatomical changes
items.authors: Flühmann T, Guyer G, Vallet V, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Modern radiotherapy techniques do not automatically account for anatomical changes during treatment, which can lead to reduced target coverage, hotspots, or increased dose to healthy tissues. Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) addresses this by updating the treatment plan based on the patient's current anatomy. In routine clinical practice, the decision to replan is often triggered by a suboptimal fit of the immobilization mask, identified by the radiation therapy technologist. Because this process is operator dependent and lacks methodological rigor, a quantitative decision‐support method could substantially improve the replanning decision. Daily image‐guided radiotherapy (IGRT) images provide valuable clinical information but often lack sufficient quality for accurate target contouring or reliable dose calculation to support straightforward clinical decision‐making. This limitation motivates the need for a simpler, more practical, and scalable alternative. Purpose This study develops an automated workflow to predict the need for replanning at every treatment fraction in head and neck (H&N) cancer patients using robust tools, thus requiring minimal manual validation while aiding the radio‐oncologists in their decision‐making. Methods A retrospective dataset of 21 H&N cancer patients treated on a Tomotherapy Radixact system (Accuray, USA) with kVCT daily imaging was analyzed, of whom 14 underwent replanning during treatment. For each patient, the planning CT (pCT) and daily images were processed in RayStation treatment planning system (RaySearch Laboratories AB, Sweden) via scripts. Rigid registrations were used to align daily images to the pCT, and a patient‐specific region of interest (ROI) was defined to consistently capture the same anatomical region across all treatment fractions. ROI volumes were intersected with the external contour and converted to relative volumetric changes with respect to the pCT. By grouping patients according to whether a replanning occurred during treatment, differences in mean volumetric change between replanned and non‐replanned patients were assessed at each treatment fraction. To automatically detect clinically relevant anatomical changes, a simple, interpretable model based on three volumetric features (current volume loss, short‐term trend, and long‐term trend) was evaluated using cross‐validation. Thresholds defining the trigger condition were optimized using a tailored loss function that prioritizes early detection and penalizes false negatives more strongly than false positives.…

items.title: Frailty assessment in ovarian cancer: a systematic review of measurement definitions, methods, and clinical implications
items.authors: Castelo-Loureiro A, Alqaisi H, Fazelzad R, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate how frailty is defined and assessed in ovarian cancer studies, and whether these assessments inform clinical outcomes or are integrated into clinical decision-making. Methods: Studies assessing frailty across surgical, systemic therapy, and surveillance settings were included. The systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidance and was prospectively registered. Frailty assessment approaches were categorized as validated or multidimensional frailty assessments versus single-domain proxies or non-frailty constructs. Results: The search identified 5818 records; 3170 were screened after duplicate removal, 111 full-text articles were assessed, and 61 unique publications representing 54 studies or cohorts met broad eligibility criteria. Thirty-two publications (52.5%) used validated screening tools or multidimensional approaches and were retained for outcome synthesis; the remaining 29 (47.5%) relied on single-domain proxies or non-frailty constructs and were mapped separately. Validated screening tools were used in 6 publications, deficit-accumulation indices in 16 publications from 15 studies, and geriatric assessment-based approaches in 10 publications from 8 studies. Reported associations included post-operative complications, treatment tolerance and delivery, health care use, survival, and quality of life, although heterogeneity precluded quantitative synthesis. Clinical use of findings was seldom reported. Among the 27 studies with outcome comparisons, frailty or vulnerability was consistently associated with adverse outcomes. One study prospectively used a geriatric assessment-derived vulnerability score to define eligibility for a randomized treatment comparison. However, no study tested a multidomain care pathway in which individual geriatric deficits triggered targeted interventions and reassessment. Conclusions: Frailty assessment in ovarian cancer remains heterogeneous, but it is consistently associated with adverse outcomes. The major gap is not the absence of assessment tools but their limited translation into clinical care. Future studies should distinguish chronic geriatric vulnerability from potentially reversible, tumor-related impairment and should test whether linking multidomain assessment findings to targeted interventions improves patient and treatment outcomes.

items.title: Fecal Immunochemical Test Outreach for Colorectal Cancer Screening in Community Health Centers: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Martinez ME, Roesch S, Largaespada V, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening is suboptimal among people in traditionally underserved populations, many of whom receive primary care at federally qualified health centers (FQHCs). Mailed fecal immunochemical test (FIT) outreach improves screening, especially in underserved populations, but questions remain about impact over time. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of centralized annual mailed FIT outreach delivered over 3 years to increase CRC screening in FQHCs. Design, Setting, And Participants: This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted between June 1, 2021, and May 31, 2024. Sixteen clinics from 2 FQHCs in Southern California were randomly assigned to mailed FIT outreach or usual care for patients aged 50 to 75 years and not up to date with screening. Intervention: Intervention components followed best practices for mailed FIT outreach and included educational primers, FIT kits, and telephone reminders. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of individuals up to date with any CRC screening after 3 years of intervention (point prevalence); screening at 2 years was a secondary outcome. Due to a resource constraint-related protocol modification, mailed FIT outreach began earlier in year 3, such that some individuals who completed screening in year 2 were not yet due for repeat FIT. Results: Among 16 clinics serving 20 250 patients, 6 clinics serving 8334 individuals at baseline (4435 aged 55-64 years [53.2%]; 4896 female [58.7%]; 341 Asian [4.1%], 238 Black [2.9%], 2390 Hispanic [28.7%], and 4371 non-Hispanic White [52.4%]) were randomized to intervention and 10 clinics serving 11 916 individuals at baseline (6443 aged 55-64 years [54.1%]; 7250 female [60.8%]; 699 Asian [5.9%], 355 Black [3.0%], 4635 Hispanic [38.9%], and 4436 non-Hispanic White [37.2%]) were randomized to usual care. At year 3, screening was 39.4% (95% CI, 36.3% to 42.6%) in intervention clinics vs 36.5% (95% CI, 31.2% to 42.2%) in usual care clinics, which was not a statistically significant difference (2.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.2 to 9.0 percentage points). At year 2, screening was 37.8% (95% CI, 35.2% to 40.4%) in intervention clinics vs 27.0% (95% CI, 21.8% to 32.9%) in usual care clinics (difference, 10.8 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.9 to 16.7 percentage points).…

items.title: Long-term oncological outcomes of robotic versus laparoscopic total mesorectal excision for rectal cancer: COLRAR randomized clinical trial
items.authors: Song SH, Min BS, Park JS, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Long-term oncological equivalence of robotic total mesorectal excision (R-TME) and laparoscopic total mesorectal excision (L-TME) remains unproven. The 5-year outcomes of the COLRAR RCT are reported. Methods: Adults with cT1-4a Nx M0 rectal adenocarcinoma within 10 cm of the anal verge were randomized 1 : 1 to L-TME or R-TME at three Korean tertiary centres between July 2011 and February 2016. Pre-specified secondary endpoints were 5-year overall, relapse-free, local recurrence-free, and distant recurrence-free survival. Analyses were on a modified intention-to-treat basis. Results: Of 295 analysed patients (144 L-TME patients and 151 R-TME patients; median follow-up of 72.6 months), 5-year overall survival (92.6% versus 92.4%; P = 0.838) and relapse-free survival (81.9% versus 83.0%; P = 0.801) were similar. Local recurrence occurred in 4.9% (L-TME) and 1.3% (R-TME); 5-year local recurrence-free and distant recurrence-free survival did not differ (P = 0.076 and P = 0.655). In a post-hoc analysis of 146 patients who received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, 5-year local recurrence-free survival was 98.6% in R-TME patients versus 90.7% in L-TME patients (P = 0.039). Conclusion: R-TME and L-TME produced equivalent 5-year oncological outcomes. A post-hoc analysis suggested improved local control with robotic surgery after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, requiring confirmation in prospectively designed studies. Registration Number: NCT01423214 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov).

items.title: The double jeopardy effect of socioeconomic barriers on guideline-concordant postoperative radiation in oropharyngeal cancer
items.authors: Ramanan S, Ashji G, Chadha N, et al.
items.abstract: Receipt of timely adjuvant radiation after primary surgery for head and neck cancer is a well-established quality benchmark. The social and structural drivers of suboptimal care, however, remain incompletely characterized. Very little work has been done on understanding the combined and interacting effects of social determinants on postoperative radiation therapy (PORT) receipt and timing. Upon examining PORT delivery among intermediate- and high-risk oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma patients, we identified that patients who are both uninsured and live far from a treatment center are at the highest risk for not receiving adjuvant radiation therapy. By identifying which specific patient subpopulations are most vulnerable to delayed or omitted treatment, this analysis provides actionable data to guide institutional interventions, optimize resource allocation, and support advocacy efforts aimed at closing equity gaps in head and neck cancer care.

items.title: A Phase 1 Trial Investigating the Addition of Papaverine to Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT) for Hypoxic Radiosensitization of Lung Tumors
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Brownstein J, Williams T, Xu-Welliver M, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: Tumor hypoxia has been recognized as a barrier to effective radiotherapy. Preclinical work identified the FDA approved smooth muscle relaxant papaverine (PPV) as having an "off target" activity as a mitochondrial inhibitor that reduces hypoxia and radiosensitizes model tumors. Methods: We conducted an IRB-approved phase 1 clinical trial to evaluate safety and feasibility of adding PPV to stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for tumors of the lung. Eligible patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or limited lung metastases who were candidates for SBRT (50 Gy in 4 or 5 fractions) were enrolled. Based on a Bayesian Optimal Interval (BOIN) design, patients were allocated to receive PPV 30-90 minutes prior to each SBRT fraction at 3 dose levels (DL): 0.5 mg/kg (DL-1), 1 mg/kg (DL1), or 2mg/kg (DL2). Results: Nineteen patients enrolled and 18 completed study treatment and were evaluable, with a median follow up of 33.4 months. Among 18 evaluable patients, 7 had early-stage NSCLC, 2 had metastatic NSCLC, and 8 had lung metastases from other histologies. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was determined to be DL2, which had a dose limiting toxicity (DLT) rate posterior estimate of 0.17 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.53). The 2-year controls rates for local, regional and distant control were 100%, 94% and 82%, respectively. Conclusions: We demonstrate the feasibility and safety of PPV as a hypoxic radiosensitizer for SBRT. The MTD for this patient population is at least 2 mg/kg of PPV. Encouraging clinical results indicate that further investigation of PPV's utility as a tumor-selective radiosensitizer is warranted.

items.title: Streamlining Liver SABR: Validation and Initial Experience of Bulk Density Override Based Single-Session, Simulation-Free Adaptive Workflow
items.authors: Gao Y, Hsu E, Pham D, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Conventional liver stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) typically requires a CT simulation visit followed by multiple treatment fractions, which can increase patient burden and limit access. We propose an approach that consolidates imaging, planning, adaptation, and delivery into one session, utilizing an MR-guided adaptive workflow. We report here the workflow and dosimetric validation of a streamlined bulk density override (BDO) strategy and the initial clinical implementation of this simulation-free approach. Methods And Materials: A single-institution phase II trial was designed to deliver liver SABR (30-40 Gy in 1 fraction) in a single-session using an MR-guided Linac for patients with liver cancers using BDO strategy. To validate dosimetric accuracy, 17 previously treated single-fraction liver SABR plans were recalculated retrospectively using (1) CT-based electron density and (2) BDO-based density. DVH endpoints and 3D gamma analysis (1%/1mm) were compared. Early clinical experience from the first five trial patients is reported, including dose comparisons between BDO-based calculations and diagnostic CT-based calculations. Results: For the retrospective analysis, BDO-based calculation closely matched the CT-based calculation. For the PTV and GTV, the median percent differences were close to zero for all evaluated metrics and the maximum percent differences were all within 2%. For organ-at-risk (OAR) endpoints (chest wall, bowel, liver minus GTV, spinal cord), mean and maximum dose differences were within 0.1 Gy and 0.6 Gy, respectively. The average 3D gamma pass rate was 99.2%. For the first 5 patients treated on trial, BDO- and diagnostic CT-based reference plan metrics agreed within 1.5% for PTV coverage and within 0.5 Gy for key OAR endpoints. The mean gamma pass rate was 98.8%. Conclusions: The BDO strategy provides dosimetric agreement comparable to CT-based calculation and supports an efficient and patient-centric single-visit delivery model. Our results support further investigation of simulation-free, single-session MR-guided adaptive liver SABR.

items.title: Two-Year Outcomes of the XXX Trial: Longitudinal Analysis of Safety, PSA Kinetics, and Patient-Reported Outcomes
items.authors: Arcangeli S, Faccenda V, Ferrario F, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To assess the 2-year incidence and longitudinal trajectory of grade (G) ≥2 genitourinary (GU) and gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events (AEs) following single-dose ablative radiotherapy (SDRT) for organ-confined prostate cancer (PCa), alongside associated changes in patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and PSA kinetics. Methods: XXX (XXX) is a single-institution prospective study enrolling patients with unfavorable intermediate-risk or selected high-risk organ-confined PCa treated with SDRT delivering 24 Gy in one fraction to the prostate and seminal vesicles. Treatment incorporated urethra-sparing and intrafraction motion control and was delivered on a linear accelerator using a 10-MV flattening filter-free single partial arc in combination with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). AEs were graded using CTCAE v5.0. PSA and testosterone were monitored longitudinally, and scheduled multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) were performed to assess radiological response. PROs were assessed using EORTC QLQ-C30, QLQ-PR25, IPSS, and IIEF questionnaires. Mixed-effects models evaluated longitudinal trajectories and associations with baseline and dosimetric factors. Results: Thirty patients were treated. At 2 years, no ≥G3 AEs were observed. Cumulative G2 GU and GI AEs were 23% and 7%, respectively. Two years point prevalent G2 GU and GI AEs were 10% and 3%, respectively. Longitudinal analysis showed an overall stable safety profile, with higher baseline IPSS and bladder trigone D1cc significantly associated with higher GU AEs. PRO analyses demonstrated statistically significant changes in urinary domains, although effect sizes remained below minimal important difference thresholds, indicating no clinically meaningful deterioration. Baseline symptom burden strongly predicted long-term PROs trajectories. Biochemical relapse-free survival was 100% at 2 years, with a consistent and significant PSA decline over time and local radiological control confirmed by mpMRI. Testosterone recovery occurred in 76% of patients receiving ADT. Conclusions: Single-fraction 24 Gy SDRT combined with ADT was feasible and well tolerated, with low rates of ≥G2 AEs and largely maintained quality of life at 2 years in patients with unfavorable localized prostate cancer. Early oncologic outcomes are encouraging but require confirmation with longer follow-up and comparative validation.

items.title: Sexual dysfunction in men after radiotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the Anus: A danish anal cancer group DACG study
items.authors: Krogstrup MJ, Steffensen JH, Serup-Hansen E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Sexual dysfunction, particularly erectile dysfunction (ED), is well documented after pelvic radiotherapy, but evidence in men with squamous cell carcinoma of the anus (SCCA) remains sparse. Purpose: To assess erectile and ejaculatory function, and sexual interest up to five years after curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA, based on physician-graded toxicity and validated patient-reported outcomes (PROs). Methods: This sub-study of the prospective DACG-I cohort (NCT05570279) included men treated with curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA (2015-2020). PROs (EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-CR29) and physician-graded toxicity (CTCAE v4.0) were collected at baseline, 1, 3, and 5-years. Symptom prevalences were described descriptively. Longitudinal changes were assessed using linear mixed-effects models on linearly transformed EORTC scores. Results: Of 80 enrolled men, baseline data were available for 76. At baseline, majority were symptom-free. Erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction emerged mainly within 1-3 years after treatment and persisted through 5 years. For the total cohort, ejaculatory dysfunction increased from 4.5% at baseline to 12.3% at 3 years. Physician-assessed ED (NCI-CTCAE grade ≥ 2) increased from 11.9% to 39.3% at 3 years. PROs indicated greater deterioration in erectile function at parallel time points. EORTC scores confirmed moderate-to-major clinically important deterioration at 1 and 3 years. Sexual interest remained stable over time. Conclusion: Sexual dysfunction, particularly ED, represents an increasingly prevalent and persistent late adverse effect in men treated with curative-intent radiotherapy for SCCA. The early onset of symptoms and the limited extent of recovery underscore the need for structured assessment based on PROs to support timely identification and supportive care.

items.title: Overall survival with adjuvant ribociclib plus nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor in patients with high-risk HR+/HER2- early breast cancer: Six-year follow-up of the NATALEE trial
items.authors: Slamon DJ, Hortobagyi GN, Stroyakovskiy D, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Ribociclib plus nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor (NSAI) demonstrated a statistically significant invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) benefit over NSAI alone in patients with hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HR+/HER2-) early breast cancer (EBC) at the primary efficacy analysis of the phase 3 NATALEE trial. This prespecified 6-year analysis assessed overall survival (OS) and other efficacy outcomes as well as safety. Patients And Methods: Eligible patients were adults with HR+/HER2- EBC and anatomic stage IIA (N1 or N0 with high-risk factors), IIB, or III disease. Enrolled patients were randomized 1:1 to ribociclib 400 mg/day (3 weeks on/1 week off for 3 years) plus NSAI (letrozole 2.5 mg/day or anastrozole 1 mg/day for 5 years) or NSAI alone. Premenopausal women and men also received goserelin. The primary endpoint was iDFS, and secondary/exploratory endpoints included OS, distant disease-free survival (DDFS), and distant recurrence-free survival (DRFS). Results: With a median OS follow-up of 66.5 months, ribociclib plus NSAI demonstrated an OS benefit over NSAI alone (6-year ΔOS, 2.1%; HR, 0.809 [95% CI: 0.661-0.989]; nominal 1-sided P = .019), which was generally consistent across key subgroups. An increasing iDFS benefit with ribociclib plus NSAI was also observed (6-year ΔiDFS, 5.3%; HR, 0.741 [95% CI: 0.646-0.849]; nominal 1-sided P < .0001), which was also generally consistent across key subgroups. DDFS (HR, 0.744 [95% CI: 0.646-0.858]) and DRFS (HR, 0.738 [95% CI: 0.634-0.858]) results supported these findings. No new safety signals were observed. Conclusions: This prespecified descriptive 6-year OS analysis demonstrated positive OS results with a clinically relevant benefit of ribociclib plus NSAI, consistent with the increasing reduction in recurrence risk. These results reinforce the benefit of ribociclib plus NSAI in the adjuvant setting across the broad NATALEE-eligible population. Clinical Trial Registration: NCT03701334 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

items.title: Electronic patient-reported outcome assessment at inpatient admission: a descriptive analysis of real-world data for 1423 radiotherapy patients
items.authors: Schollmeyer M, Schmidt H, Müller JA, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Patient-reported outcomes (PRO) capture patients' self-reported and treatment-related experiences, including functional impairment, symptoms, and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Although PRO have shown benefits in many studies and are recommended by guidelines, systematic PRO assessment is still rarely integrated into routine cancer care. This paper describes results of the long-term implementation of electronic PRO assessment (ePRO) in the routine workflow of a radiation oncology inpatient clinic by analyzing patients' HRQOL at admission. Methods: Admission ePRO included the EORTC QLQ-C30. PRO data were analyzed descriptively and stratified by sex, age, and primary tumor diagnosis. Results: The sample included 1,423 patients. More than half reported clinically important burden in physical and emotional functioning and fatigue. Male patients tended to report better functioning and lower symptom burden. Older patients reported greater burden in physical functioning, appetite loss, and constipation but less burden in social functioning and financial problems. Global health status showed little to no differences by sex, age, or tumor diagnosis. Conclusions: The analyses showed substantial self-reported functional impairment and symptom burden at admission in inpatient radiation oncology and highlight the value of ePRO for identifying needs early, when patients' clinical status is not yet well known to the care team. At the organizational level, these results can help set priorities for supportive care during hospitalization and support more efficient resource allocation. Trial Registration: Not applicable, the analysis used only PRO data collected as part of routine care in the inpatient radiation oncology clinic (see also the declaration of no objection).

items.title: Final prespecified analysis of the phase 3 LITESPARK-011 study: belzutifan plus lenvatinib versus cabozantinib for advanced renal cell carcinoma after anti-PD-(L)1 therapy
items.authors: Heng DYC, Schmidinger M, McDermott R, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The phase 3, randomized, open-label LITESPARK-011 trial (NCT04586231) investigated belzutifan plus lenvatinib versus cabozantinib in participants with advanced clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma (ccRCC) following anti-PD-(L)1 therapy. At earlier analyses, belzutifan plus lenvatinib significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) and objective response rate (ORR) versus cabozantinib. Overall survival (OS) was tested but did not reach significance. We present the final analysis of LITESPARK-011. Participants And Methods: Adult participants with advanced ccRCC that progressed on or after anti-PD-(L)1 therapy were randomly assigned (1:1) to 120 mg belzutifan plus 20 mg lenvatinib or 60 mg cabozantinib orally once daily until disease progression or unacceptable adverse events. Dual primary endpoints were PFS by blinded independent central review (BICR) and OS. ORR by BICR was a key secondary endpoint; safety and duration of response (DOR) by BICR were secondary endpoints. Results: At final analysis, median time from randomization to data cutoff date (2 February 2026) was 38.8 months (range, 29.1-59.0). 371 participants were assigned to belzutifan plus lenvatinib and 376 to cabozantinib. Belzutifan plus lenvatinib continued to demonstrate benefit versus cabozantinib in PFS (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.88), ORR (53.1% vs 40.2%), and DOR (22.0 vs 11.9 months). Mature OS results did not reach statistical significance at final analysis (median 33.7 versus 28.6 months; HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.70-1.03; one-sided P=0.04689 [prespecified boundary 0.0223]). Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 85.4% of the belzutifan plus lenvatinib group versus 83.0% of the cabozantinib group. Conclusions: Belzutifan plus lenvatinib continued to demonstrate PFS, ORR, and DOR benefit versus cabozantinib with additional follow-up; OS favored the combination but did not reach statistical significance at final analysis. Safety profile of belzutifan plus lenvatinib remained consistent with each drug as monotherapy. These findings continue to support belzutifan plus lenvatinib as a treatment option in advanced ccRCC following anti-PD-(L)1 therapy.

items.title: [Comment] Multiple standards of care in non-small-cell lung cancer after EGFR-TKI therapy: progress, fragmentation, or inevitability?
items.authors: Stephanie P L Saw, Mihaela Aldea
items.abstract: The treatment landscape of EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations has advanced remarkably over the past two decades. Although acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) is inevitable in most patients, novel compounds such as bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded the armamentarium of options after EGFR-TKI therapy. Following the global MARIPOSA-2 trial that showed superior progression-free survival (PFS) of amivantamab plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy alone in patients who have progressed on osimertinib,1 this is the second-line option preferred by major guidelines including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the European Society for Medical Oncology.

items.title: A fast and reliable quality assurance framework for CBCT-based synthetic CTs for adaptive proton radiotherapy
items.authors: Galapon A, Smolders AJ, Wagenaar D, et al.
items.abstract: Cone beam CT based synthetic CTs (sCTs) enable online adaptive proton therapy by preserving daily patient anatomy without additional acquisition of diagnostic-quality CTs. However, clinical adoption is limited by the lack of fast, reliable quality assurance (QA) methods. This study proposes and evaluates a practical QA workflow to assess sCT suitability for proton dose optimization. Approach:A two-step sCT-QA workflow was developed in which a candidate sCT intended for reoptimization (sCTref) is compared with an independently generated secondary sCT (sCTtest). The workflow combines image based metrics and dose based metrics, with doses derived from recalculating a template proton plan on both sCTs. In this study, the framework was evaluated using a deformably propagated virtual CT (vCT) as sCTref and either a deep learning-based sCT (sCTDL) or an analytically corrected CBCT (CBCTcorr) as sCTtest. Same-day CTs were deformably registered to the CBCT and used as ground truth (CTGT) for evaluation. Thresholds were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation on 182 head and neck (H&N) CT-CBCT pairs. Dose calculation suitability was defined as a gamma pass rate (2%, 1mm) exceeding 95% between dose distributions computed on sCT and CTGT. The method was further tested on an external H&N dataset and on abdominal cases.Main Results:Optimal classification performance was achieved using a combination of image mean absolute error (MAE) and dose MAE. On the H&N test set, the workflow achieved balanced accuracies of 91.2% and 89.7% for the vCT-CBCTcorr and vCT-sCTDL comparisons, respectively, while maintaining a low false positive rate. When applied without modifications to the external H&N and abdominal datasets, balanced accuracy was 94.7% (HN) and 85.0% (abdominal) for vCT-CBCTcorr, and 37.9% (HN) and 61.1% (abdominal) for vCT-sCTDL.Significance:This study introduces a clinically feasible sCT QA workflow for CBCT based adaptive proton therapy and showed promising transferability across datasets.

items.title: Colonoscopy screening outcomes in Lynch syndrome and differential colorectal cancer paths among MLH1/MSH2 carriers
items.authors: Briollais L, Choi YH, Semotiuk K, et al.
items.abstract: Backgroud: Lynch syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes increases the risk of colorectal cancer, which remains elevated even under active colonoscopy surveillance. A deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving CRC development under colonoscopy surveillance in individuals with LS is crucial for evaluating its effectiveness. The goal of this study is to better understand the differential patterns of CRC development focusing more specifically on MLH1 and MSH2 carriers. Methods: Patients with Lynch syndrome were identified through the Familial Gastrointestinal Cancer Registry in the Zane Cohen Centre at Mount Sinai hospital, Toronto. This study proposed a general model integrating colonoscopy screening visits, adenoma counts, and CRC occurrence (a joint model) and which accounts for their interdependencies when modelling CRC risk. Results: More frequent colonoscopy screenings resulting in an increased number of adenomas detected effectively reduces CRC risk in those with a pathogenic variant in MSH2, potentially due to a risk-reducing effect. MLH1 carriers did not experience the same benefit. After 10-year follow-up, among individuals with adenomas, CRC risk was much higher in MLH1 compared to MSH2 carriers, 7.9% [95% CI = 3.9-15.8%] vs. 4.0% [95% CI = 1.6-9.6%] in males and 4.2% [95% CI = 2.2-8.2%] vs. 1.6% [95% CI = 0.7-3.5%] in females. Conclusions: Our study identified differences in MLH1 and MSH2 cancer development which may suggest distinct mechanisms impacting CRC. The inverse relationship between adenoma detection and CRC risk in MSH2 carriers enhances our understanding of the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, while the lack of association in MLH1 carriers suggests alternative carcinogenic pathways requiring further study.

items.title: Selection and Management of Patients With Resectable Gastric or Gastroesophageal Junction Cancer Receiving Perioperative FLOT: A Modified Delphi Consensus Approach
items.authors: Saeed A, Janjigian YY, Gibson MK, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, and docetaxel (FLOT) is a guideline-recommended standard for patients with resectable gastric cancer or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma globally. Guidance is limited on patient selection, nutritional optimization, and toxicity management within existing guidelines. This study aimed to develop an international consensus to address these management gaps. Methods: A modified Delphi methodology, informed by the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method, was conducted virtually between March and August 2025. A multidisciplinary panel of 16 experts independently rated draft clinical statements across multiple domains. Responses were anonymized, with structured, iterative rounds of feedback and re-rating. Consensus was defined a priori as a median score of 7-9 (appropriate) or 1-3 (inappropriate) with a disagreement index ≤1.0. Results: Consensus was reached on 66.3% of the statements. Experts agreed that patients aged >70 years should not be routinely excluded from perioperative FLOT but require comprehensive assessment; inclusion of Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) 0-1 is appropriate, and ECOG PS 0-2 may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Adequate organ function, correction of baseline conditions, hepatitis B screening, and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase testing are appropriate before FLOT initiation. Universal baseline nutritional screening and support, proactive intervention for malnourished patients, and structured physical activity were endorsed. Surgical planning was supported through multidisciplinary input, with defined perioperative windows, individualized dosing, and flexibility in pre-/postoperative cycles. For toxicity management, the panel supported dose modification over drug omission, where possible. Conclusion: This Delphi consensus provides expert-driven, practice-oriented advisories codifying fitness-based selection, nutrition-forward optimization, and pragmatic toxicity management. The resulting guidance builds on current standards and provides internationally applicable consensus statements to ultimately enhance patient care.

items.title: DAG-informed analysis of muscle characteristics and overall survival in patients receiving radical treatment for bladder cancer
items.authors: Vickers AJ, McSweeney DM, Choudhury A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Reduced skeletal muscle (SM) quantity and quality may influence outcomes in bladder cancer, but most studies are associative and vulnerable to confounding and inconsistent covariate adjustment. We applied a directed acyclic graph (DAG)-informed framework to evaluate associations between computed tomography-derived SM characteristics and overall survival (OS) in patients receiving curative-intent radiotherapy-based bladder preservation or radical cystectomy. Methods: This retrospective two-centre cohort study included patients treated between 2014 and 2024. Computed tomography imaging closest to definitive local therapy was analysed using an automated segmentation pipeline to quantify SM quantity, expressed as skeletal muscle index (SMI), and quality, expressed as intramuscular adipose tissue ratio (IMATR). A DAG was used to prespecify the adjustment strategy, and Cox models were fitted separately within radiotherapy and surgical cohorts. Results: The final cohorts comprised 353 radiotherapy-treated and 117 surgically treated patients. In the radiotherapy cohort, higher SMI was associated with improved OS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66-0.94, p = 0.007), while higher IMATR was associated with worse OS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.04-1.48, p = 0.014). In the smaller surgical cohort, point estimates were directionally discordant with the radiotherapy findings and imprecise: SMI HR 1.35 (95% CI 0.99-1.85, p = 0.057) and IMATR HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.62-1.21, p = 0.39). Conclusions: In this DAG-informed analysis, higher SMI and lower IMATR were associated with improved OS in radiotherapy-treated patients. Surgical estimates were imprecise and should be considered exploratory. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further evaluation of CT-derived muscle characteristics as prognostic markers within radiotherapy-treated populations but cannot yet establish a differential benefit for radiotherapy vs cystectomy.

items.title: Disease-free survival and overall survival after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer in the Netherlands: results of the single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial
items.authors: Chalabi M, van den Dungen LDW, de Gooyer PGM, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade induces high pathological response rates in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer, yet long-term survival outcomes have not been established. Previously, we reported safety (a primary endpoint) and pathological response (a secondary endpoint) data from the NICHE-2 trial. Here, we report the primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival and the exploratory endpoint of 5-year overall survival. Methods: In this single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial, patients with previously untreated, clinical stage 2 or 3, resectable dMMR colon cancer received a single dose of intravenous ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) on day 1, and two doses of intravenous nivolumab (3 mg per kg) on days 1 and 15, followed by surgery in one of the six participating hospitals in the Netherlands. Here, we report the independent primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival (time from surgery until disease recurrence or death from any cause) and the secondary endpoint of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) analysis. Overall survival (time from study enrolment until death from any cause) is reported as an exploratory post-hoc analysis. All endpoints were assessed in the per-protocol population (patients who met the eligibility criteria and received at least one cycle of therapy). The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03026140, and has completed accrual. Findings: From July 4, 2017, to July 18, 2022, 123 patients were screened, of whom 115 were treated and 111 were included in the per-protocol population. At the data cutoff (June 19, 2026), the postoperative median follow-up was 58·7 months (IQR 49·0-72·9). The 3-year disease-free survival was 100% (97·5% CI 100-100). After a median follow-up of 60·4 months (IQR 50·6-74·1), calculated from time of study enrolment, the 5-year overall survival was 100% (95% CI 100-100). In patients with available plasma samples, ctDNA was detected in 99 (92%) of 108 patients at baseline, and ctDNA clearance was observed in 44 (45%) of 98 patients after the first cycle in week 2 and in 80 (82%) of 97 patients after the second cycle before surgery. In patients with a pathological near-complete response and complete response, presurgery ctDNA clearance was observed in 19 (70%) of 27 patients and 60 (92%) of 65 patients, respectively. Assessment for minimal residual disease after surgery revealed that all patients were ctDNA negative.…

items.title: Planned versus accumulated dose in radiotherapy of oropharyngeal carcinoma - Do recurrences occur in unintended cold spots?
items.authors: Lindegaard AM, Enocson H, Georgiev H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Locoregional recurrence (LRR) in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) most often occurs within the high-dose target volume. Anatomical changes during RT may potentially lead to unintended target underdosage, which could contribute to the risk of treatment failure. This study aimed to quantify differences between planned and accumulated dose in the regions of later LRR. Methods: Patients treated with curatively intended RT for OPSCC between 2009 and 2017 at Rigshospitalet with biopsy-proven LRR were identified. Recurrence volumes were delineated on follow up imaging and mapped to the planning CT. The point of origin (PO) of each recurrence was determined using the nidus method. Dose accumulation was performed using synthetic CTs based on daily cone beam CT, followed by recalculation and summation of daily dose distributions. Planned and accumulated doses at the PO were compared. Additional analyses evaluated effect of deformable registration methods. Results: Forty patients with 54 recurrence volumes were included. The accumulated dose was higher than the planned dose in 57% of recurrences. The mean difference between accumulated and planned dose at the PO was - 0.04 Gy (SD: 0.81; 95% CI: -0.26 to 0.18 Gy; p = 0.72). Neither PO localization nor the dose accumulation process was sensitive to the use of an alternative deformation software. Conclusions: Within the evaluated setting, no evidence was found that regions of later LRR were systematically underdosed. Dose differences were small and within clinically acceptable limits. This suggests that anatomical changes during RT were unlikely to cause clinically relevant compromised target dose coverage.

items.title: Carboplatin Plus Mirvetuximab Soravtansine In Platinum-Sensitive Ovarian Cancer: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Konecny GE, Lim PC, Santin AD, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Evaluate efficacy and safety of carboplatin plus mirvetuximab soravtansine (MIRV) in folate receptor alpha (FRa)-expressing recurrent PSOC. Patients And Methods: This phase 2, single arm trial enrolled patients with recurrent FRa-expressing (≥25% of tumor cells with ≥2+ membrane intensity) PSOC and 1 prior platinum-based therapy. Patients received up to 6-8 cycles of carboplatin (AUC 5) plus MIRV (6mg/kg AIBW) Q3W, followed by single-agent MIRV. Primary and key secondary endpoints were investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v1.1 in the FRa ≥50% group and FRa ≥25% group (ie, overall population), respectively. Results: Among 125 enrolled patients (102 FRα ≥50%; 61 prior PARPi), ORR by end of 6 combination cycles was 62.7% (95% CI, 52.6-72.1) in the FRα ≥50% group and 62.4% (95% CI, 53.3-70.9) in the overall population. Most patients (n=101; 81%) transitioned to single-agent MIRV continuation with durable responses. Patients with FRa ≥25% had median duration of response of 11.2 months (95% CI, 8.5-13.6) and median progression-free survival of 11.0 months (95% CI, 9.8-13.1). Most common adverse events (AEs) were blurred vision (81%) and corneal events (74%); 96.7% of corneal cases resolved or had final grade 1. Treatment-emergent AEs led to MIRV and carboplatin discontinuation in 15% and 9%, respectively. Adjudicated treatment-related pneumonitis occurred in 19 (15.2%) patients: 14 grade 1-2; 3 grade 3-4, and 2 fatal cases. Conclusions: Carboplatin plus MIRV was manageable with dose modifications for AEs and showed meaningful activity, including in PARPi-exposed patients, supporting further evaluation in PSOC.

items.title: Serial circulating tumour DNA monitoring in first-line advanced NSCLC (COPE): a randomized, two-arm non-comparative phase II trial
items.authors: Tambaoan CFB, Phan L, Cousin S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: COPE evaluated serial circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling with molecular tumor board (MTB) review during first-line therapy for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Experimental Design: COPE was a multicenter, randomized (2:1), noncomparative phase II trial. Arm A underwent serial plasma profiling with every report reviewed at a weekly virtual MTB; Arm B received standard management. The primary endpoint was 18-month overall survival (OS) in Arm A versus a prespecified 40% historical benchmark; no between-arm comparison was planned. Results: Among 176 patients, 117 were assigned to Arm A and 59 to Arm B. Eighteen-month OS was 53.8% (95% CI, 44.3-62.5) and 65.7% (95% CI, 52.0-76.3), respectively. Baseline plasma profiling provided contributory information in 32 of 35 patients with noncontributory or unavailable tissue, increasing genotyping success from 69% to 97%. Paired baseline and early on-treatment samples were available in 90 patients (median, 21 days; range, 19-64). ctDNA clearance was associated with higher objective response rate (83% vs. 52%), longer progression-free survival (22.9 vs. 5.4 months; P<0.001), and longer OS (not reached vs. 17.1 months; P=0.004) than persistent detection. Conclusions: Serial ctDNA profiling with weekly MTB review was operationally feasible and complemented tissue genotyping. Clinical benefit was not demonstrated; early ctDNA kinetics require validation in interventional trials.

items.title: Circulating Immune and Cancer Driver Gene Biomarkers Precede Prostate Cancer Diagnosis by over 10 yr
items.authors: Huang Z, Parsaeian M, Viallon V, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Objective: Prospective proteomic and proteogenomic studies may enhance the understanding of proteins associated with prostate cancer (PCa) development. Methods: In a case-cohort study within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC), baseline plasma samples from 982 incident PCa cases and 1573 subcohort participants were profiled using the SomaScan 7k platform (over 6000 proteins). Associations were estimated using Prentice-weighted Cox models. The coprimary end points were incident overall PCa and aggressive PCa (n = 290). Findings were evaluated in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study and supported by Mendelian randomization (MR) and exome gene-burden analyses. Key Findings And Limitations: ACP3, FLT4, and KLK3 were associated with overall PCa risk (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 standard deviation [SD] increase were 1.20 [1.10-1.31], 1.26 [1.13-1.40], and 2.28 [1.96-2.65], respectively). Seven proteins were associated with aggressive PCa risk, with ANKRD1 consistently associated across multiple clinically relevant disease subtypes. Twelve proteins were associated with PCa diagnosed >15 yr after blood draw, including ANXA2, GZMK, and OSCAR. ACP3, ANXA2, APOC2, and KLK3 showed consistent associations in both EPIC and ARIC. Additionally, four proteins had support from MR analyses and eight from rare-variant burden tests. Circulating products of established PCa driver genes, including ERBB3, KRAS, and NRAS, were associated with future aggressive disease. Limitations include incomplete external replication and differences in end point availability across cohorts. Conclusions And Clinical Implications: Prospective plasma proteomic analyses identified circulating proteins associated with future PCa risk, including proteins related to immune, adhesion, angiogenesis, and PCa driver-gene pathways. These findings identify candidate protein risk factors for overall and clinically significant PCa, and warrant further validation and mechanistic evaluation.

items.title: Low-grade serous ovarian cancer: 2026 expert consensus report
items.authors: Grisham RN, Slomovitz B, Podder V, et al.
items.abstract: Low-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (LGSOC) is a rare epithelial malignancy characterized by frequent mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway alterations, hormone receptor expression, relative resistance to cytotoxic chemotherapy, and a prolonged, relapsing clinical course. Since publication of the 2023 international expert consensus, significant advances have reshaped the management of both newly diagnosed and recurrent disease. The 2026 LGSOC Consensus Conference convened an international multidisciplinary panel of experts in the field to review emerging evidence and update recommendations across pathology, molecular testing, translational biology, frontline and recurrent treatment, imaging, treatment-associated toxicity, regulatory strategy, patient advocacy, and future research priorities. Recommendations were informed by contemporary clinical evidence, multidisciplinary discussion, and patient perspectives. The updated consensus incorporates practice-changing data from NRG-GY019 supporting chemotherapy-containing postoperative therapy as the current reference approach for stage II-IV disease while recognizing selected circumstances in which endocrine monotherapy may represent individualized de-escalation. It also integrates recent advances in recurrent disease, including the US Food and Drug Administration's accelerated approval of avutometinib in combination with defactinib for KRAS-mutated LGSOC, emerging evidence supporting endocrine therapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibition, and refined guidance for biomarker-directed treatment selection, imaging assessment, toxicity management, and patient-centered survivorship. The panel emphasizes treatment-specific biomarker interpretation, multidisciplinary care, central pathology review for clinical trials, and the continued need for prospective studies addressing treatment sequencing, predictive biomarkers, and quality-of-life outcomes. This updated international consensus provides an evidence-based framework for the diagnosis and management of LGSOC while identifying priorities for future clinical research and drug development.

items.title: Modeling the survival impact of the Inflation Reduction Act out-of-pocket cap in multiple myeloma
items.authors: Zhao H, Teng S, Dong C, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Oral immunomodulatory imide drugs (IMiDs) have become standard of care for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM), but high out-of-pocket (OOP) costs may hinder treatment adherence. In 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act introduced a $2,000 annual OOP cost cap (IRAOOPcap) for Medicare Part D beneficiaries. In the absence of post-implementation data, we used comparative modeling to predict its survival impact. Methods: The survival submodels of two independent Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network (CISNET) natural history of multiple myeloma models were used. The models were parameterized using data from Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare, 2012-2021. We simulated survival among Medicare Part D beneficiaries with NDMM aged 66-75 and ≥76 years, under hypothetical scenarios shifting 0% (pre-IRAOOPcap) to 100% (best-case) of patients to IMiD use with high adherence and a realistic scenario using published data. We computed life-years gained (LYG) by comparing life expectancy (LE) under each scenario with that of the pre-IRAOOPcap scenario. Results: Across models, the realistic/best-case scenario yielded LYG of 0.17-0.18/1.10-1.35 among patients aged 66-75 years, and 0.20-0.26/1.29-1.53 for those aged ≥76 years. These translated into 4,164-5,005/26,893-32,347 LYG at the population level for beneficiaries with NDMM in 2025. Conclusion: The IRAOOPcap may improve survival through increasing IMiD utilization and adherence among Medicare Part D beneficiaries with NDMM. The projected gains represent a meaningful proportion of contemporary survival for patients. Future research should validate these gains when real-world data are available and inform future policy adaptation and extension.
