items.title: Phase II Study of Neoadjuvant Cemiplimab for Stage II to IV Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Final Analysis
items.authors: Gross ND, Miller DM, Khushalani NI, et al.
items.abstract: We previously reported the results of a multicenter phase II trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04154943) of neoadjuvant cemiplimab in resectable stage II to IV cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), in which the pathologic complete response (pCR) rate was 51%. At the 19-month follow-up, estimated 12-month event-free survival (EFS) was 89%, with 11 EFS events. In this study, we report final EFS and overall survival (OS) at a median follow-up of 54 months. Overall, 16 EFS events occurred at final analysis. There were no new disease recurrence events. The five new EFS events were all comorbidity-related deaths without CSCC recurrence. Overall estimated 54-month EFS was 76.2% (81.5% in patients with pCR, 88.9% in patients with major pathologic response, 100% in patients with partial pathologic response, and 45.7% in nonresponders/not-evaluable patients). Among 40 patients with pCR, none had experienced disease recurrence. Overall estimated 54-month OS was 79.4%. No new grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred. The final analysis demonstrates durable EFS and OS, no late recurrences, and no new safety signals with neoadjuvant cemiplimab.

items.title: Pembrolizumab Plus Chemotherapy for HR+/HER2- PD-L1‒Positive Advanced Breast Cancer: Final Analysis of the Phase 3 KEYNOTE-B49 Study
items.authors: Rugo HS, Kok M, Goncalves A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: We evaluated pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in participants with PD-L1‒positive, hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/HER2- advanced breast cancer after progression on prior endocrine-based therapy (ET). Patients And Methods: Participants with locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic HR+/HER2- breast cancer with PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥1 who had prior ET and were candidates for first-line chemotherapy were randomized to pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo Q3W plus chemotherapy. The primary and key secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS) per RECIST v1.1 by blinded independent central review and overall survival (OS), respectively, in participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥1. PFS and OS in participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥10 and safety were secondary endpoints. Following protocol amendment, the sample size was reduced due to low PD-L1 prevalence. Results: 342 participants were randomized. At interim analysis (median follow-up, 29.1 months), the hazard ratio (HR) for PFS was 0.74 (95% CI, 0.58‒0.95; P=0.0089 [significance criterion met]) favoring pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus placebo plus chemotherapy (median [95% CI] PFS, 6.7 [6.2‒8.3] versus 6.0 [4.2‒8.1] months). HR for PFS in participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥10 numerically favored pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (0.59; 95% CI, 0.35‒0.98). At final analysis (median follow-up, 34.9 months), HR for OS was 1.04 (95% CI, 0.81‒1.33; P=0.6185) for pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus placebo plus chemotherapy (median [95% CI] OS, 21.0 [18.9‒22.9] versus 22.2 [17.6‒26.3] months). Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs occurred in 38% of participants in the pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy arm and 33% in the placebo plus chemotherapy arm; 11% and 5% discontinued treatment due to treatment-related AEs, respectively. Conclusion: In participants with PD-L1‒positive (CPS ≥1) HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy demonstrated statistically significant improvement in PFS, with no new safety signals observed. A numerical effect favoring pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy for PFS was observed in participants with PD-L1 CPS ≥10. No significant OS improvement was observed. items.title: Pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib with belzutifan or quavonlimab as first-line therapy for advanced renal-cell carcinoma: randomized open-label phase 3 LITESPARK-012 study
items.authors: Rini BI, Choueiri TK, Voss MH, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib is a first-line standard of care for advanced clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma (ccRCC). The phase 3 LITESPARK-012 study (NCT04736706) evaluated efficacy and safety of adding belzutifan (HIF-2α inhibitor) or quavonlimab (anti-CTLA-4) to this regimen. Participants And Methods: Adults with previously untreated advanced ccRCC were randomized 1:1:1 to 400 mg pembrolizumab IV Q6W plus 20 mg lenvatinib orally daily and 120 mg belzutifan orally daily (Arm A); coformulated quavonlimab/pembrolizumab 25 mg/400 mg IV Q6W (collectively called MK-1308A) plus lenvatinib (Arm B); or standard-of-care pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib (Control). Treatment continued until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal from study; pembrolizumab or quavonlimab/pembrolizumab were administered for a maximum of ∼2 years. Progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review and overall survival (OS) were dual primary endpoints, tested in all randomized participants for Arm A versus Control, and in participants with IMDC intermediate/poor risk or all participants for Arm B versus Control. Safety was a secondary endpoint. Results: Overall, 560 participants were randomized to Arm A, 562 to Arm B, and 566 to Control. As of the data cutoff date (February 4, 2026), median follow-up was 43.6 months (range, 31.8-57.4). Among all participants, median PFS was 20.8 months in Arm A (HR vs Control: 1.08, 95%CI 0.93-1.26; P=0.8408), 20.7 months in Arm B (HR vs Control: 1.07, 95%CI 0.92-1.25; nominal P=0.8174), and 23.7 months in the Control arm; median OS was 52.0 months in Arm A (HR vs Control: 1.04, 95%CI 0.87-1.25; P=0.6622), not reached (NR) in Arm B (HR vs Control: 1.12, 95%CI 0.94-1.35; nominal P=0.8955), and NR in the Control arm. Among participants with intermediate/poor risk, median PFS was 20.5 months in Arm B and 23.5 months in the Control arm (HR 1.12, 95%CI 0.94-1.33; P=0.8954); median OS was 39.1 versus 46.2 months (HR 1.17, 95%CI 0.96-1.42; P=0.9419). Any-grade all-cause adverse events led to any-drug discontinuation in 51.6%, 51.4%, and 36.2% of participants in the A, B, and Control arms. Conclusions: Neither addition of the HIF-2α inhibitor belzutifan nor the CTLA-4 inhibitor quavonlimab to pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib improved outcomes in participants with previously untreated advanced RCC versus pembrolizumab and lenvatinib alone. Higher drug discontinuation rates due to adverse events occurred in the investigational arms.…

items.title: Dalmelitinib Plus Aumolertinib in Advanced NSCLC Patients With EGFR-TKI Resistance and MET Amplification: A Randomized Phase 3 Trial
items.authors: Li Z, Dong X, Yu Y, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: MET amplification accounts for up to 30% of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKI, especially following third-generation EGFR-TKI treatment, yet precision-targeted therapeutic options remain limited. Early-phase studies demonstrated promising antitumor activity with the MET-TKI dalmelitinib combined with the third-generation EGFR-TKI aumolertinib. This phase 3 trial compared dalmelitinib-aumolertinib with platinum-based chemotherapy in EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified advanced NSCLC after EGFR-TKIs progression. Patients And Methods: This randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial (NCT06110663) enrolled patients with locally advanced or metastatic EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified NSCLC after EGFR-TKI progression. MET amplification was defined by fluorescence in situ hybridization as a mean MET copy number ≥5 or MET/CEP7 ratio ≥2. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to dalmelitinib-aumolertinib or platinum-based chemotherapy groups. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review per RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included overall survival, objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DoR), and safety. Results: A total of 314 enrolled patients were assigned to dalmelitinib-aumolertinib (n=156) or platinum-based chemotherapy (n=158). Median follow-up was 11.2 months at the data cutoff date (December 10, 2025). Median PFS was 6.2 months with dalmelitinib-aumolertinib and 4.4 months with chemotherapy (HR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.45 to 0.81; P <0.001). Corresponding ORRs were 59.6% and 38.6%, and median DoRs were 9.7 months and 4.4 months, respectively. Overall survival data were immature. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 50.0% and 51.0% of patients, respectively. Toxicity profiles differed, with more hepatic laboratory abnormalities with dalmelitinib-aumolertinib and more hematologic toxicities with chemotherapy. Conclusion: The dalmelitinib-aumolertinib combination significantly improved PFS versus chemotherapy, with a manageable safety profile in advanced EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified NSCLC after progression on EGFR-TKI. These findings support dual EGFR/ MET inhibition as a new treatment option in this biomarker selected population.

items.title: Three-dimensional deep learning nomogram for post-plan quality assurance in high-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy
items.authors: Beaudry J, Wang T, Enger SA, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Classical nomograms for high-dose-rate (HDR) prostate brachytherapy quality assurance (QA) evaluate agreement between planned and expected total dwell time but do not directly assess the three-dimensional treated volume. This study's aim was to develop a deep learning-based 3D nomogram to predict institution-specific clinical 100% isodose volumes from anatomy and dwell positions for post-plan QA. Methods: A total of 2394 single-fraction 15 Gy HDR prostate brachytherapy plans were included. Input label maps encoded the 3D prostate, urethra, rectum, and dwell positions. The prediction target was the clinical 100% isodose volume. A five-fold cross-validation strategy was used for model development, with 2155 plans used for training and validation and 239 plans held out for testing. A 3D U-Net was trained using combined Dice and binary cross-entropy loss. Agreement was evaluated using prostate V100%, 100% isodose volume, Dice similarity coefficient, and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). Validation-derived thresholds were used for outlier screening and targeted review. Results: The model predicted prostate V100% with a mean error of 0.73 percentage points. Predicted and clinical 100% isodose volumes showed strong agreement, with R2 = 0.990, slope = 0.99, and intercept = 0.77 cm3. Median Dice similarity coefficient was 0.960, and median ASSD was 0.48 mm. A 95% threshold flagged 6.3% of plans as atypical relative to validation data. Conclusions: A deep learning-based nomogram predicted an institution-specific 100% isodose volume with low coverage error and high spatial agreement. This geometry aware post-plan QA tool can complement equation-based nomograms by directly evaluating the spatial treated volume.

items.title: An interim analysis of acute treatment adverse events and patient reported quality of life for functional imaging guided salivary gland sparing radiation therapy using diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging
items.authors: Cahill K, Hargrave C, Miller K, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Evolving evidence suggests that regional sparing of the parotid gland during radiation therapy could reduce radiation-induced xerostomia in head and neck cancer. This interim analysis investigates the functional relationship between the diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) derived parotid gland biological at-risk volume (BRV) dose and acute adverse events, including patient-reported quality of life (QoL). Materials And Methods: Twenty-four head and neck cancer patients underwent MRI-simulation to delineate parotid gland BRVs using DW-MRI derived apparent diffusion coefficient measurements. Dose was optimised, sparing the parotid gland BRV. Clinician-reported acute adverse events (xerostomia, dysphagia, oral pain) were recorded and patient-reported QoL was assessed using University of Washington QoL Questionnaire v4.1 with Radiation Therapy Oncology Group modification. Adverse events were quantified using area under the curve and time to side effect peaks were calculated and analysed. Results: A moderate positive correlation trend was observed between contralateral BRV mean dose and xerostomia area under the curve, although this did not reach statistical significance (r = 0.34, p = 0.13). There was a strong relationship between the contralateral BRV sector and days to peak dysphagia (r = 0.56, p = 0.005). Low- and high-dose grouped analysis revealed a trend toward significance for time to peak xerostomia (p = 0.059). There were no significant associations with the ipsilateral parotid gland BRVs. Conclusion: Findings suggest a potential functional-dose relationship between the contralateral BRV mean dose and acute xerostomia. Ongoing follow-up will determine whether the suggestive trends observed in the acute phase strengthen with long-term recovery time.

items.title: MRI-Based Machine Learning to Differentiate True Progression from Pseudoprogression in Glioblastoma: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.authors: Zhang X, Guo X, Wang Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Differentiating true progression (TP) from pseudoprogression (PsP) after chemoradiation for glioblastoma remains clinically difficult. We evaluated externally validated diagnostic performance of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based machine learning models and appraised study quality and transparency. Methods: PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and Cochrane Library were searched through October 1, 2025 (PROSPERO registration CRD420251144894). Eligible adult glioblastoma studies used MRI-based machine learning to distinguish TP from PsP against histopathology and/or clinicoradiologic follow-up. The primary meta-analysis included external test cohorts with extractable 2 × 2 data; internal and combined internal and external test analyses were secondary. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with bivariate random-effects models. Results: Thirty-one studies including 2,344 patients undergoing imaging assessment were included. Seven external test cohorts, including 219 patient observations, entered the primary meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.63-0.88), specificity was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.63-0.84), and summary area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.81 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.69-0.91). Internal test cohorts showed higher apparent performance than external cohorts (AUC, 0.91 vs 0.81), but the difference was not statistically significant (difference, -0.09; 95% CI, -0.22 to 0.02; P = 0.12). Risk of bias was frequently high or unclear, and reporting transparency was heterogeneous. Conclusions: MRI-based machine learning showed moderate-to-good external validation performance for TP-versus-PsP discrimination, but evidence remains limited by small external test cohorts, bias, and incomplete reporting. Larger transparent multicenter validations are needed before routine clinical implementation.

items.title: Cost Effectiveness Analysis of the Presto-Trial: A Three-Armed RCT Evaluating Prophylactic Swallowing Exercises in Head and Neck Cancer Patients During (Chemo)radio Treatment
items.authors: Vergauwen A, Van den Steen L, Baudelet M, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Research on oropharyngeal head and neck cancer (HNC) patients indicates that prophylactic swallowing exercises (PSE) during (C)RT can positively affect muscle strength, swallowing function and quality of life (QOL). Primary analyses of the PRESTO‐trial showed higher adherence rates for PSE when exercising daily with a speech‐language pathologist (SLP), compared to self‐guided exercises with either an exercise diary or a digital application. Additionally, higher adherence rates were related to greater improvements in swallowing function and QOL. However, given limited healthcare resources, cost‐effectiveness analyses are essential to inform the implementation of such rehabilitation strategies in dysphagia care. This secondary analysis of the PRESTO‐data compares the costs and health effects of the three different service models: app‐based, therapist‐led (daily face‐to‐face, 20 sessions during (C)RT), and paper‐led therapy. Methods One hundred fifty patients receiving (chemo)radiotherapy (C)RT for oropharyngeal HNC were randomly assigned to one of the three exercise groups. All performing the same PSE protocol. The treatment protocol required daily training during the first 4 weeks of the (C)RT treatment program. Patients in the therapy group thereby received a total of 20 face‐to‐face therapy sessions. Health outcomes were expressed as utilities based on the EQ5D5L instrument measured at baseline, post (C)RT and 3 months post (C)RT. Costs were estimated from a health service perspective, including staff time, therapy resources and consumables. Incremental cost‐effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were calculated as ΔCosts/ ΔQALYs. Results No significant between‐group differences were found for utilities. Only significant time effects were observed, with a significant decrease in utilities from baseline to post (C)RT and a significant increase from post (C)RT to 3 months post (C)RT. The therapist‐led intervention was associated with the highest costs. The app‐group intervention was dominated by the paper group in terms of cost‐effectiveness as the utilities were comparable but at a higher cost in the app‐group. Consequently, the ICER was computed between the paper‐group and therapist‐group and resulted in € 124 061,54/QALY. Conclusions Despite the overall positive HR‐QOL effects post 3 months, the daily therapist‐led delivery of PSE therapy was not cost‐effective relative to paper‐based self‐management. Under current resource constraints, low‐cost delivery models represent the most economically efficient option.…

items.title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios
items.authors: Ariel D, Endelman S, Laban G
items.abstract: Background: The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). Objective: To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Design: Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Setting: Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. Participants: No human participants were involved. Measurements: Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). Results: The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Limitations: Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. Conclusion: The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. Primary Funding Source: None.

items.title: Predicting taste alteration in head and neck cancer patients using 3D transformer-based deep learning model
items.authors: Neh H, MacRae DC, de Vette SPM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Taste alteration is a common post-treatment side effect of head and neck cancer (HNC) radiotherapy. Accurate normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models can support treatment planning aimed at reducing side effects that impair quality-of-life. Deep learning (DL) offers opportunities to incorporate full 3D dose, CT, and organofinterest (OOI) data. Using a large prospective cohort, this study explores whether CNN and transformerbased DL models can outperform a conventional logistic regression model for predicting taste alteration 6 months after radiotherapy. Material/Methods: Data from 972 patients was used, with the endpoint being moderatetosevere patientreported taste alteration at six months (EORTC QLQH&N35). DL models were trained using 3D dose distributions, planning CT, OOI segmentations and clinical features. A conventional NTCP model using oral cavity mean dose, parotid mean dose, and age served as reference. Attention maps were evaluated for the transformer-based DL model to quantify the model attention to specific regions of the head and neck area. In addition, two cropping approaches for the 3D data were compared. Results: The CNN and transformer DL models performed comparable to the reference NTCP model in the test set (Reference: AUC = 0.71; ResNet: AUC = 0.68; TransRP: AUC = 0.71), though calibration was best for the reference model. Shifting the crop improved DL performance and transformer attention focused on supraglottic and submandibular regions. Conclusion: This study showed that the prediction of taste alteration can be achieved using DL models, particularly transformer-based models which, in contrast to CNNs, can account for global features of comprehensive 3D information of dose distribution, CT-images and organs-of-interest segmentations.

items.title: Prospective phase 2 trial of high- and intermediate-intensity myeloablative conditioning for cord blood transplantation
items.authors: Colgan JN, Gooley TA, Pedersen JB, et al.
items.abstract: Umbilical cord blood transplantation (UCBT) is an important alternative donor strategy for patients with high-risk hematologic malignancies. While myeloablative conditioning (MAC) is associated with superior disease control following UCBT compared to reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC), its benefits can be offset by non-relapse mortality (NRM). Intermediate-intensity MAC may preserve the anti-leukemic effects of historically high-intensity MAC while reducing NRM. We conducted a prospective phase 2 trial evaluating outcomes of patients undergoing UCBT following either high-intensity or intermediate-intensity MAC. A total of 132 patients were enrolled between 2006 and 2022, with acute leukemia being the predominant indication. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS), with secondary endpoints including relapse-free survival (RFS), relapse and NRM. For the overall study population at 1 year, OS was 78% (95% CI, 70-85%) and RFS was 72% (95% CI, 64-79%). Outcomes were comparable between conditioning regimens, with encouragingly low NRM observed in patients receiving intermediate-intensity conditioning, including in the pediatric cohort. Among patients with acute leukemia, measurable residual disease (MRD) positivity at transplant was not associated with an increase in relapse, supporting enhanced GVL following UCBT. These findings were particularly notable in patients with AML. These data demonstrate that UCBT following intermediate intensity MAC is a viable strategy that may reduce toxicity while preserving disease control in selected patients. Collectively, these findings support the unique anti-leukemic properties of UCBT and reinforce its role as a highly effective donor platform for high-risk leukemia in children and adults. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT00719888.

items.title: Comments on Cardiac Risk After Heart-Sparing Breast Radiotherapy Study
items.authors: Lui JCF, Chan JCH, Jimenez RB
items.abstract: To the Editor We were eager to read the publication by Quirk and colleagues, which addresses an important topic regarding dose metrics that may best predict cardiac risk after breast radiotherapy. In summary, they conclude from their cohort of patients with left-sided breast cancer treated with radiation therapy that maximum dose to the left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) was a better predictor of cardiac events than mean heart dose. Specifically, they identified that a maximum LAD dose of 12-Gy equivalent dose in 2-Gy fractions (EQD2) best stratified cardiac risk.

items.title: Trastuzumab Rezetecan in ERBB2-Low Advanced Breast Cancer: The HORIZON-Breast06 Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Fan Y, Liu Y, Wang Y, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Trastuzumab rezetecan (SHR-A1811) has demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity in a global phase 1 trial involving heavily pretreated patients with erythroblastic oncogene B (ERBB2)-low metastatic breast cancer. Objective: To compare trastuzumab rezetecan vs physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer. Design, Setting, And Participants: This open-label, randomized, multicenter phase 3 trial was conducted at 73 hospitals across China. Eligible patients were females aged 18 to 75 years with centrally confirmed ERBB2-low (immunohistochemistry [IHC] 1+ or IHC 2+/in-situ hybridization [ISH]-negative) unresectable locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer who had received 1 or fewer prior lines of chemotherapy for metastatic disease, with prior endocrine therapy required for hormone receptor-positive disease. Enrollment began on June 30, 2023, and ended on August 20, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the final analysis for progression-free survival in the current study was March 20, 2026. Interventions: Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive trastuzumab rezetecan (6.4 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks; n = 277) or physician's choice of chemotherapy (n = 274). Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary end point was progression-free survival assessed by blinded independent central review in chemotherapy-naive patients and the overall population. Results: Between June 30, 2023, and August 20, 2025, a total of 551 patients were randomized, with a mean (SD) age of 54.9 (9.9) years. At the data cutoff (March 20, 2026), trastuzumab rezetecan significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared with chemotherapy in the chemotherapy-naive patients (median, 16.6 [95% CI, 14.0-19.4] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-7.0] months; hazard ratio, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.19-0.33]; P < .001) and the overall population (median, 16.4 [95% CI, 14.0-16.8] months vs 6.8 [95% CI, 5.7-6.9] months; hazard ratio, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.21-0.34]; P < .001). The benefit was consistent in hormone receptor-negative disease (median progression-free survival: 16.5 vs 6.8 months; hazard ratio, 0.34, [95% CI, 0.22-0.54]) and hormone receptor-positive disease (median progression-free survival: 16.4 vs 6.7 months; hazard ratio, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.18-0.33]). Grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 84.1% of patients (232/276) with trastuzumab rezetecan and 67.9% (184/271) with chemotherapy, most commonly decreased neutrophil count (180 [65.2%] vs 147 [54.2%]).…

items.title: Microbeam radiotherapy - clinical and dosimetric investigation of a first clinical application
items.authors: Kraus KM, Day LR, Wilkens JJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Microbeam Radiotherapy (MRT) is an emerging radiotherapy technique which delivers spatially fractionated beams on a micrometre scale. In preclinical studies MRT has demonstrated superior normal tissue sparing compared to conventional radiotherapy while maintaining tumour control. However, MRT has traditionally been achievable only at large synchrotron facilities which has impeded clinical translation. The development of a compact line-focus X-ray tube (LFXT) provides a pathway for clinical MRT, but identification of clinically and dosimetrically suitable patient scenarios is required for first-in-human trials. Materials And Methods: Potentially eligible patients were selected from our patient cohort based on clinical criteria including palliative treatment indication, superficial tumour location, reproducible and safe positioning, minimal interference from other therapies, and expected benefit from MRT. Three-dimensional forward treatment planning was performed in Eclipse using gantry rotations, collimator positioning, and conformal masks to treat the clinical target volume (CTV). Dose was calculated in Eclipse using a custom Monte Carlo-based hybrid algorithm adapted for the compact LFXT system with a 300 kVp beam and an eccentric focal spot. A single-fraction equivalent uniform doses (EUD) of 3 Gy was prescribed to the target volume. Dose distributions were analysed using dose-volume histograms (DVHs), peak and valley depth dose profiles, and peak-to-valley dose ratios (PVDRs). Results: Selected cases included primary lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and superficial soft tissue metastases. Dosimetric analysis under exploratory assumptions demonstrated dosimetrically feasible treatment plans with optimal target coverage and organ-at-risk (OAR) sparing for gluteal, nuchal, and inguinal tumours. Maximum OAR doses remained below 8.5 Gy, except in bone or overlapping high-density regions. The mean peak and valley dose across all plans was 57.2 Gy and 3.9 Gy, respectively, with a mean PVDR of 15.4. Dose inhomogeneities were observed due to tissue heterogeneity, kilovoltage beam interactions, and a limited range of suitable gantry angles. Tumours in anatomically complex regions, including those in proximity to OARs or tissue inhomogeneities, showed less favourable trade-offs between target coverage and OAR sparing. Conclusion: This study identifies clinically and dosimetrically suitable scenarios for first-in-human MRT trials, highlighting superficial tumours as optimal initial indications.…

items.title: Examining reliance patterns on AI advice in medical imaging: a mixed-methods, randomised, crossover experiment
items.authors: Gaube S, Jussupow E, Kokje E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) holds significant potential to support diagnostic decision making; however, the collaboration between clinicians and AI systems often does not surpass the performance of unaided humans or standalone AI. This study aimed to examine the effect of AI advice on diagnostic decision making among experts and novices, focusing on the occurrence of AI over-reliance and under-reliance and the potential mitigating effect of explainable AI. Methods: We used a mixed-methods, randomised, crossover experimental design. Participants (50 task experts [radiologists] and 75 novices [non-radiologist physicians and medical trainees]) were randomly assigned in equal proportions to one of six groups, which determined the order in which the three conditions were presented across the three sessions. In each session, participants read 50 head CT scans with or without the presence of an intracranial haemorrhage, under one of three experimental conditions: control, no AI prediction; basic AI advice, AI prediction without annotations; and explainable AI advice, AI prediction with scan annotations. 80% of cases with basic or explainable AI advice received correct advice, and 20% received incorrect advice. The main outcomes were diagnostic performance (the correct identification of intracranial haemorrhage), confidence in the diagnosis, case reading time, and AI advice usefulness ratings. We defined under-reliance as a final decision that did not align with correct AI advice, and over-reliance as a final decision that aligned with incorrect AI advice. All elements of the project were preregistered and are available on the project's Open Science Framework repository. Findings: Data were collected between Feb 16, 2023, and Aug 10, 2023. Both over-reliance on incorrect advice and under-reliance on correct advice occurred. Under-reliance was associated with high uncertainty and, in absolute terms, had a more detrimental effect on diagnostic performance than over-reliance. Correct explainable AI advice reduced under-reliance and improved performance (OR=1·84, p<0·0001, 95% CI 1·49-2·28) and confidence (b=0·15, p<0·0001, 0·09-0·22) compared with no advice, particularly when reviewing more difficult cases with intracranial haemorrhage. Correct explainable AI did not reduce reading time compared with the no-advice condition (b=-1·81, p=0·071, -3·78 to 0·16). Explainable AI was perceived as more useful than basic AI advice (b=0·12, p=0·0029, 0·04-0·20), especially among novices.…

items.title: Supraclavicular Lymph Node Delineation for Regional Nodal Irradiation in Breast Cancer and Considerations for the Posterior Neck When Using Conformal Modalities
items.authors: Rummel KA, Jimenez RB, Corbin KS
items.abstract: A 61-year-old female was diagnosed with a 2.7 cm invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) of the left breast, clinical stage cT2 cN0 (ER+/PR+/HER2–, Ki-67 15%). She underwent lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Final pathology demonstrated a grade 3, 2.8 cm IDC with lymphovascular invasion and negative margins. Two of four lymph nodes were positive. Oncotype DX score was 21 and chemotherapy was not recommended. Endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor were recommended after radiotherapy. She received adjuvant whole-breast radiation with regional nodal irradiation (RNI) to the ipsilateral supraclavicular (SCLN), internal mammary (IMN), and axillary lymph nodes.

items.title: Recommendations for the Multimodal Management of Malignant Bowel Obstructions: Results of a North American Multidisciplinary Delphi Consensus
items.authors: Shariff F, Bogach J, Sriskandarajah A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Malignant bowel obstruction (MBO) is a challenging clinical problem requiring teams to balance complex oncologic disease, limited treatment options, and patient prognosis and values as they approach end of life. Presently, there is limited high-quality evidence to guide decision-making for MBO patients. Objective: A multidisciplinary modified Delphi process was undertaken to create guidance and support clinical decision-making in the medical and surgical care of this patient population. Methods: Multidisciplinary experts from all specialties regularly caring for MBO in Canada and the United States were invited for participation, including Acute Care Surgery, Surgical Oncology, Gynecologic Oncology, Gastroenterology, Radiology, Medical Oncology, and Palliative Care. Statements were evaluated through two rounds of surveys and a consensus meeting, with an a priori threshold of 80% agreement for approval. Results: Forty-nine final evidence-informed statements were included following expert consensus review pertaining to Patient Assessment, Medical Management, Surgical Management, and Palliative Management, in addition to a unifying definition of MBO. Consensus statements address aspects of complex MBO care, including but not limited to, optimal preoperative evaluation and multidisciplinary review; timing and use of steroids, motility, and antisecretory agents; contraindications to surgery; key facets of consent and perioperative decision making; framework for the nuanced use of gastrostomies and IV fluids in the end-of-life setting. Conclusions: This Modified Delphi consensus provides multidisciplinary evidence-based recommendations for the care of patients with this challenging problem. These expert approved statements provide much-needed clinical guidance to support best care balanced with patient values and avoidance of undue harm.

items.title: From Diagnosis to Destruction: The Rise of Radioligand Therapeutics as Oncology’s New Pillar
items.authors: Ken Herrmann
items.abstract: Once regarded by mainstream oncology as a predominantly diagnostic discipline, nuclear medicine stands on the threshold of redefining systemic cancer care. Highlighting this evolution, a European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) keynote lecture addressed radioligand therapeutics and theranostics as an emerging pillar of cancer management. The presentation traced how theranostics—the clinical pairing of diagnostic imaging agents with cytocidal therapeutic radionuclides—has advanced from an academic salvage option into an established, disease-modifying treatment paradigm across multiple malignancies.

items.title: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence
items.authors: Cui C, Magge R, Schwartz TH, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra‐tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia‐driven radio‐resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium‐Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non‐enhancing regions. Purpose This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual‐tracer PET using a combined dose of 18FMISO (hypoxia) and 18FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI. Methods Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH‐mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual‐[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post‐injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast‐enhanced T1 (T1‐Gd), and T2‐FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow‐up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET‐defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites. Results Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET‐defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1‐Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2‐FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET‐defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI‐defined contours (mean non‐overlap 6.4 cc vs T1‐Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2‐FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET‐avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET‐defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression‐free‐survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months. Conclusions Dual‐[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2‐FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual‐tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

items.title: Segment anything model (SAM)-driven prompt-guided interactive delineation of gross tumor volume for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy
items.authors: Wu S, Geng J, Bai L, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt‐guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user‐defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. Purpose This study proposes a feasible prompt‐guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. Methods A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding‐box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine‐tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state‐of‐the‐art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle‐slice selection and box‐prompt margins was analyzed. Results Compared to other fine‐tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle‐slice prompt exhibited negligible impact (p > 0.05). The finalized SAM‐driven workflow outperformed end‐to‐end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. Conclusions The proposed SAM‐driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.

items.title: A dual-prompt framework combining spatial-mask priors and clinical-text conditioning for CT-only GTV delineation in esophageal cancer: A multicenter study
items.authors: Sun H, Chen C, Chen J, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Accurate gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation is essential for esophageal cancer radiotherapy, but CT‐only automatic delineation remains difficult because of indistinct tumor boundaries. Purpose This study aimed to develop and validate a two‐stage dual‐prompt framework combining a spatial‐mask prior with LLaMA3‐encoded clinical‐text conditioning for primary esophageal GTV delineation. Methods: This multicenter study included 857 patients: 500 for development, 125 for internal validation, 50 for ablation analysis, and 182 for external validation. The proposed framework consists of two stages: (1) a CT‐based automatic segmentation network generating an initial GTV as a spatial mask prompt, and (2) a refinement network that jointly incorporates spatial mask prompt and LLaMA3‐encoded clinical text prompt derived from structured clinical information. Performance was evaluated using overlap, surface distance, and volumetric metrics, and compared with multiple state‐of‐the‐art deep learning models. Ablation and radiomics analyses assessed component contributions and downstream consistency. Results In internal validation, the framework achieved a DSC of 80.32 ± 6.65%, an HD95 of 11.42 ± 8.90 mm, and an absolute volume difference of 9.99 ± 10.49 mL; all Holm‐adjusted p values were <0.001 versus the comparison models. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the external cohorts. Mean DSCs were 78.60 ± 13.39% and 78.36 ± 15.54% in the two external cohorts, respectively. In external cohort A, ContextUNETR showed a lower mean HD95 than the proposed model (10.93 ± 8.03 vs. 13.44 ± 18.90 mm), although the paired difference was not statistically significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.906). Compared with the direct Stage‐1 output, the complete framework consistently improved overlap, boundary‐distance, and volumetric‐agreement metrics across the internal and both external validation cohorts (all adjusted p < 0.001). LLaMA3 encoding improved DSC versus an MLP using the same variables (adjusted p = 0.009), whereas ASSD did not differ significantly. Automatic and manual GTVs showed high radiomic concordance and comparable prognostic performance. Conclusion The framework improved overlap and volumetric agreement for CT‐only primary esophageal GTV delineation across multicenter validation cohorts, although boundary‐distance performance varied across external cohorts.

items.title: Population-level diagnostic and radiation treatment trends of low-risk prostate cancer
items.authors: Monda SM, Odayar V, Yin M, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Overtreatment of low‐risk prostate cancer (PC) undermines screening efforts. Active surveillance is preferred for low‐risk PC, but declining treatment may reflect diagnostic or treatment‐selection changes. We assessed diagnostic risk‐group trends among localized PC and low‐risk trends among radiation‐treated patients since 2010. Methods We analyzed localized PC in Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program (SEER; 2010–2023); Veterans Affairs (VA; 2010–2024); and Michigan Radiation Oncology Quality Consortium (MROQC; 2021–2025). Low‐risk PC was defined as grade group 1, prostate‐specific antigen <10 ng/mL, and clinical stage ≤T2a. Diagnosis‐based analyses described risk‐group trends among all localized PC diagnoses in SEER and VA and treatment among low‐risk patients. The primary outcome was the proportion of radiation‐treated patients classified as low‐risk, evaluated using logistic regression. Results Among localized PC, low‐risk disease at diagnosis declined from 28.8% to 24.0% in SEER and from 32.3% to 21.9% in VA. Among diagnosed low‐risk patients, receipt of neither radiation nor prostatectomy increased from 33.6% to 83.4% in SEER and from 51.6% to 96.3% in VA. Among 207,196 patients treated with radiation for localized PC (170,213 SEER; 34,635 VA; and 2348 MROQC), the proportion with low‐risk disease declined from 33.7% to 6.5% in SEER, from 22.9% to 2.0% in VA, and remained ≤4.2% in MROQC. Declines persisted after adjustment. Conclusion Since 2010, low‐risk PC has become less common at diagnosis, whereas diagnosed low‐risk patients increasingly avoid treatment. Radiation for low‐risk PC has markedly declined, paralleling surgical trends and reflecting a nationwide shift toward active surveillance.

items.title: A novel automatic real-time motion tracking method in MRI-guided radiotherapy using enhanced Tracking-Learning-Detection framework with automatic segmentation
items.authors: Chen S, Wang Z, Dai J, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Accurate motion tracking in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRIgRT) is essential for effective treatment delivery. This study aimed to enhance motion tracking precision in MRIgRT through an automatic real-time markerless tracking method using an enhanced Tracking-Learning-Detection (ETLD) framework combined with automatic segmentation, eliminating the need for pre-training. Methods: We developed a novel motion tracking and segmentation method by integrating the ETLD framework with an improved Chan-Vese (ICV) model, termed ETLD + ICV. The ETLD framework was upgraded for real-time MRIgRT, including search process optimization, an enhanced median-flow tracker, and dynamic detection region adjustments. It receives 3.5D MRI data as input and outputs the location prediction of the target volume for each frame. Based on this, ICV was used for precise target volume coverage, refining the segmented region frame by frame using tracking results, with optimized key parameters. The method requires no pre-training and was tested on 3.5D MRI scans from 10 patients with liver metastases. No-reference image quality assessment and manual verification were used to filter out low-quality image data. Comprehensive statistical analyses were performed to assess the statistical significance of differences between experimental outcomes (p < 0.05). In addition, comparative experiments based on an external benchmark dataset were conducted to further evaluate the performance of the proposed method. Results: Evaluation across 106,000 frames from 77 treatment fractions demonstrated sub-millimeter tracking errors of less than 0.8 mm, with over 99% precision and 98% recall for all patients in the Beam Eye View (BEV)/Beam Path View (BPV) orientation. The ETLD + ICV method achieved a Dice global score of more than 82% for all patients, demonstrating the method's extensibility and precise target volume coverage. Comparisons based on the external dataset further showed that the proposed method achieved a balanced trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. Conclusion: This study successfully developed an automatic real-time markerless motion tracking method for MRIgRT. The novel method not only delivers exceptional precision in tracking and segmentation but also shows enhanced adaptability to clinical demands, making it an indispensable asset in improving the efficacy of radiotherapy treatments.

items.title: TACTICAL1 Trial Protocol: Targeted Abdominal CT in Conjunction with Lung Cancer Screening to Identify Kidney Cancer and Other Abdominal Conditions: A Randomised Controlled Pilot Study
items.authors: Rossi SH, Kitt J, Clark M, et al.
items.abstract: Screening for kidney cancer and other serious abdominal conditions in conjunction with lung cancer screening (LCS) is potentially feasible and cost-effective. Targeted Abdominal CT in Conjunction with Lung Cancer Screening (TACTICAL1) aims to pilot this integrated screening model in a real-world setting to inform a future large-scale randomised controlled trial (RCT). TACTICAL1 is a pilot study, with embedded process evaluation, of adding abdominal noncontrast computed tomography (CT; ANCCT) to low-dose CT (LDCT) thorax amongst ever smokers aged 55-70 yr at high risk of lung cancer who were attending the first round of LCS in Yorkshire, UK. There are two points of randomisation. First, participants are randomised 1:1 at the individual level to receive either an LCS invitation letter (invitation control) or an invitation letter for LCS with potential for an additional ANCCT (invitation intervention). Participants in the latter group are then cluster randomised 1:1 to be offered either LDCT thorax alone (scan control) or both LDCT thorax and ANCCT (scan intervention). TACTICAL1 has four primary endpoints and will assess the following: (1) whether the invitation intervention affects LCS uptake, (2) feasibility of cluster randomisation, (3) impact of adding ANCCT to LCS on scanning throughput, and (4) acceptability to participants and screening staff. Strengths include the real-world setting and robust randomisation. TACTICAL1 is a pilot study; therefore, it does not aim to evaluate the prevalence or stage of screen-detected findings nor survival. TACTICAL1 will inform the development of a future large-scale RCT assessing outcomes such as stage shift, earlier detection, and potential survival benefits. A previous study showed that it is possible to offer an additional computed tomography scan of the abdomen at the same time as lung cancer screening. This extra scan may help detect kidney cancer and other serious abdominal conditions early. TACTICAL1 is a pilot research study in which people are randomly assigned to different groups. Its aim is to test how this combined screening approach could work in practice. The results will help design a much larger future study to find out whether combining these scans can save lives.

items.title: A Comprehensive Beam-Level Assessment of Pencil-Beam Scanning Migration and Utilization at a Multi-System Proton Therapy Center
items.authors: Johnson PB, Willoughby T, Alvarez J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To provide a beam-level comparison of pencil-beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy at a high-volume center operating both the ProteusPLUS (P-PLUS) and ProteusONE (P-ONE) platforms and to evaluate how system capabilities influenced room utilization during a multi-year transition to PBS. Methods And Materials: Log files were analyzed for three rooms: P-PLUS Gantry Room 2 (GTR2; 2018-2024), P-PLUS Gantry Room 1 (GTR1; mid-2023-2024), and P-ONE Compact Gantry Room (CGTR; 2020-2024). A script was written to extract beam parameters while clinical and demographic information were obtained from the MOSAIQ database. Data streams were merged, then grouped and analyzed by site, age, and temporal factors. Results: The final dataset included 120,367 beams for the P-PLUS and 95,587 for the P-ONE. During an 18-month comparative period, mean throughput was 27.4 ± 5.4 patients/day (GTR2), 22.9 ± 5.1 (GTR1), and 27.0 ± 4.6 (CGTR), with mean session times of 28.2 ± 2.5, 25.6 ± 1.7, and 26.9 ± 2.4 minutes, respectively. Case allocation reflected platform/nozzle differences: GTR2 primarily treated prostate, breast, and thorax/abdomen targets, while GTR1 and CGTR focused on prostate, head-and-neck, brain, and CNS cases. CGTR treated more pediatric patients (25.2% vs 7.1% in GTR2 and 5.8% in GTR1) and cases involving anesthesia. Maximum cyclotron energy was used more on GTR2 compared to CGTR (7.5% vs 0.4%), while range-shifter use was similar (71.1% vs 67.0%); couch flips occurred in 77% of P-ONE treatments. Conclusions: Expanding PBS capacity substantially shifted room utilization and case mix, driven mainly by differences in spot and field size, and secondarily by imaging, layer-switching, and pediatric-oriented room features. The P-ONE's smaller field size did not materially constrain prostate treatment with involved lymph nodes, frequent couch flips did not inhibit high operational capacity, and the P-ONE's lower minimum energy reduced range-shifter reliance and the need for maximum cyclotron energy. This real-world analysis provides guidance for case selection, workflow optimization, and future proton system design.

items.title: Clinicoepidemiologic Profile of Oral Kaposi Sarcoma in People Living With HIV: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.authors: Otávio E, Badaró RF, Rodrigues DPM, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background To characterize the clinicoepidemiologic profile of HIV‐associated oral Kaposi sarcoma (OKS) and quantitatively synthesize its frequency, anatomical distribution, and temporal patterns across antiretroviral therapy (ART) eras. Methods Six databases and gray literature were searched. Eligible observational, descriptive, and quasi‐experimental studies were appraised using JBI tools. Random‐effects meta‐analyses of patient‐based proportions and treatment‐era subgroup were performed when compatible study‐level denominators were available (PROSPERO: CRD420251105061). Results Forty‐eight studies comprising 1661 individuals were included, and 31 contributed to at least one meta‐analysis. Pooled proportions were 0.85 (95% CI: 0.76–0.91) for palatal involvement and 0.44 (95% CI: 0.23–0.68) for OKS as a sentinel presentation of HIV. Pooled prevalence of OKS among people living with HIV was 0.06 (95% CI: 0.02–0.12). Compared with the pre‐combination ART era, the combination ART era showed lower palatal (0.72 vs. 0.89; p = 0.0034) and gingival involvement (0.07 vs. 0.30; p = 0.0003), but more sentinel presentations (0.72 vs. 0.32; p = 0.0195). Methodological quality was moderate, with substantial heterogeneity. Conclusions Pooled evidence confirms strong palatal predilection of HIV‐associated OKS. Temporal subgroup findings suggest changes in oral distribution across ART eras while reinforcing its persistent role as a sentinel manifestation of HIV infection and persistent clinical relevance despite ART.

items.title: Real-World Adoption of Adjuvant Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Stage IIB/IIC Melanoma Following FDA Approval
items.authors: Jakub JW, Doonan BP, Day CN, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Adjuvant immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) for stage IIB/IIC melanoma was approved in December 2021 based on recurrence-free survival benefit without mature overall survival data. Given uncertainty regarding the risk-benefit balance in this population, we evaluated real-world utilization of adjuvant ICI in the first year following FDA approval and compared uptake with historical patterns observed in stage III melanoma. Methods: The National Cancer Database (NCDB) and Mayo Clinic Cancer Registry were queried for patients with stage IIB/IIC melanoma diagnosed in 2019-2020 (pre-approval) and 2022 (post-approval). Utilization was compared with historical patterns for stage III melanoma surrounding its December 2017 FDA approval. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with receipt of adjuvant ICI. Results: Among 7039 patients with stage IIB/IIC melanoma in NCDB, adjuvant ICI use increased from 5% pre-approval to 32% post-approval (P < .0001), with higher utilization in stage IIC (40%) than IIB (27%). Younger age was the only consistent patient-level factor associated with treatment. Within our tertiary care system, 21% of eligible patients received adjuvant ICI post-approval. By comparison, stage III utilization at NCDB sites increased from 27 to 58% in the first year following its FDA approval. Conclusions: Adjuvant ICI use for stage IIB/IIC melanoma increased following FDA approval; however, most eligible patients did not receive therapy, and overall utilization remained lower than historical patterns observed for stage III disease, suggesting selective adoption driven by risk-benefit considerations.

items.title: Clinical Outcomes of Bladder-sparing Management Versus Early Radical Cystectomy in cT1 Micropapillary Bladder Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.authors: Patel SR, Rauf M, Geng Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Clinical T1 micropapillary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is an aggressive variant histology for which early radical cystectomy (RC) is commonly recommended. However, there remain conflicting data on whether conditions in carefully selected patients may be managed with initial bladder-sparing approaches without compromising oncologic outcomes. Objective: The objective is to systematically review and synthesize the available literature comparing bladder-sparing approaches, such as Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) therapy, and early RC outcomes in clinical stage 1 primary tumor (cT1) micropapillary carcinoma of the bladder. Design, Setting, And Participants: A systematic search was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement and Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Outcome Measurement And Statistical Analysis: The primary end points were overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS). The included articles were descriptively assessed and time-to-event analysis was performed for select endpoints. Results And Limitations: Among 461 identified reports, nine retrospective studies met the criteria for quantitative analysis, encompassing 9402 patients of whom 9287 (99%) had non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) and 1033 (11%) had a micropapillary subtype. A total of 625 patients (62%) underwent bladder-sparing approaches, whereas 392 (39%) underwent early RC. Of the bladder-sparing approaches, 88% of patients received intravesical BCG therapy. For a bladder-sparing approach for cT1 disease with a micropapillary component, pooled unadjusted hazard ratios were not statistically significant for CSS (hazard ratio [HR] 1.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60-2.88, p = 0.5) and OS (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.68-1.07, p = 0.16) compared with early RC. Data evaluating bladder-sparing strategies beyond BCG were limited. Conclusions: NMIBC with micropapillary features is an aggressive disease conventionally managed with early RC. In retrospective cohorts of selected patients with micropapillary cT1, available unadjusted data did not provide clear evidence of statistically significant differences in CSS or OS between initial bladder-sparing approaches and early RC.

items.title: An experimentally calibrated nanodosimetry-based framework for predicting LET-dependent relative biological effectiveness in proton boron capture therapy
items.authors: Wu J, He Z, Sun Z, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Proton boron capture therapy (PBCT) studies focus on physical dose enhancement or biological observations, while quantitative prediction of biological effectiveness remains limited. This study aimed to establish a framework combining Monte Carlo (MC) simulation, nanodosimetry, and radiobiological experiments to evaluate the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) of PBCT. Approach: Geant4-based MC simulations and a pre-calculated nanodosimetric database were used to determine mixed-field nanodosimetric parameters, including M1, M2, and F2. Clonogenic survival experiments were performed using a clinical 70 MeV proton beam and a 6 MV photon beam. U-87 MG cells were irradiated with photons, protons, and PBCT at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 Gy using boronophenylalanine (BPA, 21.0 ppm 11B). Survival data were fitted with the linear-quadratic model, and the resulting α and β values were used to optimize the Logistic Nanodosimetry Model (LNDM) for depth-dependent RBE prediction. Main Results: The LNDM, combined with MC-derived nanodosimetric parameters and experimental survival data, reproduced the measured radiobiological response with differences in α and β below 0.5% at the experimental cell position, corresponding to a water-equivalent depth (WED) of 3.9 cm and located on the rising edge of the Bragg peak. PBCT consistently exhibited higher α and RBE values than proton irradiation across the investigated LET range. At 3.9 cm, PBCT increased RBE by 8.7% compared with protons. For the 70 MeV beam, PBCT yielded α = 0.116 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.023 Gy⁻², and RBE = 1.25, compared with α = 0.076 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.023 Gy⁻², and RBE = 1.15 for proton therapy. Significance: An experimentally calibrated framework integrating MC simulation, nanodosimetry, radiobiological experiments, and the LNDM was established for LET-dependent PBCT RBE prediction based on biological calibration data. PBCT showed consistently higher RBE than proton therapy, with a greater advantage at higher LET, supporting future biological optimization of PBCT.

items.title: Concurrent Versus Sequential Postoperative Radiotherapy and CDK4/6 Inhibitors in Breast Cancer with Positive Regional Nodes: A Multi-Center Safety and Toxicity Study
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Liu J, Lin X, Yu J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Our purpose was to compare the safety and toxicity profiles of concurrent versus sequential administration of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) and postoperative radiotherapy (RT) in patients with Positive regional nodes, operable, hormone receptor-positive (HR+), HER2-negative breast cancer (HER2-). Methods: We conducted a real-world, multicenter retrospective cohort study enrolling 364 patients with node-positive, operable HR+/HER2- breast cancer who received postoperative radiotherapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors between January 2019 and December 2024. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed to balance baseline covariates between the two arms, yielding 87 patients in each matched group. The primary endpoint was permanent CDK4/6i discontinuation, and secondary endpoints included dose reduction, drug substitution, grade ≥3 toxicities, and symptomatic radiation-induced lung injury (sRILI). Results: No significant intergroup differences were observed in CDK4/6i discontinuation rates before or after PSM (unmatched: 10.4% vs. 8.4%, P=0.536; PSM-matched: 10.3% vs. 9.2%, P=0.798). Similar non-significant findings were identified for dose reduction and drug substitution across unmatched and matched cohorts. For severe toxicities, univariate analysis of the unmatched cohort revealed a significantly higher rate of grade ≥3 drug eruption in the concurrent arm (4.3% vs. 0.4%, unadjusted P=0.013), while this association attenuated to borderline statistical significance after covariate balancing via PSM (4.6% vs. 0.0%, unadjusted P=0.059). No significant between-group differences were detected in sRILI, interstitial pneumonia, grade ≥3 radiation dermatitis, grade ≥3 diarrhea, or hematologic toxicities pre- and post-matching. All grade ≥3 drug eruptions occurred outside radiation fields and presented as diffuse maculopapular rashes involving the trunk and extremities, consistent with CDK4/6i-related hypersensitivity. Conclusions: Concurrent CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy and postoperative RT demonstrate a manageable safety and tolerance profile. Given that treatment discontinuation due to ≥G 3 toxicities was observed in both groups, close toxicity monitoring and comprehensive management throughout the treatment course should be implemented when combining RT with CDK4/6i.

items.title: Consensus on current clinical workflow and future use of 3D models in parotid gland tumor surgery: A Delphi study
items.authors: Moll MCM, Karssemakers LHE, Braun LMM, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: MRI-based 3D models provide patient-specific spatial information on the relationship between parotid gland tumors and the facial nerve. However, their potential role in clinical practice and the level of support for their implementation remain unclear. This study aimed to assess the level of consensus among surgeons on the current clinical workflows in parotid gland surgery and the future role of 3D models. Study Design: We used a three-round Delphi study to explore consensus among surgeons performing more than five parotid surgeries annually. Round 1 consisted of semi-structured interviews about parotid surgery, innovations, and the use of 3D models. Inductive analysis was used to formulate statements and questions for round 2. In rounds 2 and 3, participants rated the questions and statements on a 7-point adjective scale. Results: A panel of 15 surgeons, including 9 otolaryngologists and 6 oral and maxillofacial surgeons from nine Dutch hospitals, completed all study rounds. Partial consensus was observed for 10% of statements in round 3. Trends toward greater importance of both MRI scanning and 3D model use were identified in cases involving malignancy, facial nerve dysfunction, deep lobe tumors, fixed tumors, non-palpable tumors, and indications for a mastoidectomy. Stronger trends toward importance were observed for using 3D models in preoperative planning and patient counseling than in their use during surgery. Conclusion: Although consensus was limited, this study identified indications for MRI use and highlighted the perceived value of 3D models in parotid gland tumor surgery.

items.title: Spot-wise compensation of proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation in the transverse magnetic field of an in-beam MR scanner using a research version of a commercial treatment planning system
items.authors: Cobanaj M, Traneus E, Horst F, et al.
items.abstract: ObjectiveMagnetic resonance-integrated proton therapy (MRiPT) offers the potential for high-precision, image-guided particle therapy but is challenged by magnetic field (MF)-induced proton beam deflection and radiation field deformation. Unless compensated for, these effects compromise dose conformity and prohibit clinical implementation. This work aims to develop and experimentally validate a spot-wise compensation method capable of restoring proton dose distributions in the presence of a measured 3D magnetic vector field map within a clinical treatment planning system (TPS).ApproachA spot-wise compensation framework was implemented in a research version of RayStation, a TPS commercially available for clinical use. The method compensates both lateral beam deflection and MF-induced radiation field deformation by shifting individual pencil-beam spots based on displacement vectors derived from dose calculations in water phantoms using the measured MF of an in-beam MR scanner integrated with a horizontal proton beamline. Two complementary strategies were implemented: a patient-specific approach based on plan-specific displacement calculations, and a generic approach using precomputed displacement maps derived from a reference phantom. Compensation performance was evaluated in representative clinical cases. Dose distributions were experimentally validated using 2D ionisation chamber array measurements.Main ResultsBoth compensation methods effectively restored target coverage, dose homogeneity, and organ-at-risk sparing to the level of no-MF reference plans. The patient-specific method generally achieved a higher performance, whereas the generic compensation method enabled rapid automated correction with sufficient accuracy for clinical workflows involving deep-seated tumours. Local γ-analysis demonstrated excellent agreement between measured and calculated doses, with pass rates exceeding 98.5% for 3%/3 mm criteria.SignificanceThis work demonstrates that compensation of MF-induced proton beam deflection and field deformation can be achieved entirely within a research version of the RayStation TPS using measured, MR scanner-specific MF data. The proposed method provides a scalable, robust framework for future MRiPT clinical applications.&#xD.

items.title: An International Randomized Prospective Trial Comparing a Supine MRI-based Guidance System, The Breast Cancer Locator(TM), to Wire Localization for Breast-Conserving Surgery for Non-palpable Breast Cancer
items.authors: Gass JS, Pesek S, Czerniecki B, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Positive margins after breast-conserving surgery (BCS) require additional surgery, a negative patient experience that also adds costs to care. Pilot trials indicate the Breast Cancer LocatorTM (BCL), a novel supine magnetic resonance imaging-based guidance system, helps surgeons resect cancers with a low positive margin rate (PMR). Our objective was to evaluate BCL noninferiority and superiority compared with wire localization (WL) in reducing the PMR with BCS. Methods: Patients with nonpalpable, magnetic resonance imaging-visualized invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ undergoing BCS were prospectively randomized to either BCL or WL. Results: In total, 418 randomized patients underwent surgery. The PMR was 14.4% (30/209) in the BCL group and 21.1% (44/209) in the WL group, a relative decrease of 32%. In primary analysis, the treatment difference was -7.1% (95.4% confidence interval [CI] -14.3 to 0.1). Noninferiority was demonstrated (p = 0.011). The one-sided p-value for superiority (p = 0.025) slightly exceeded the prespecified significance level of 0.023. In prespecified analysis stratified by final tumor type, the PMR was significantly lower in the BCL group (p = 0.019). Fewer BCL patients underwent re-excision: 12.9% versus 19.6%, a relative decrease of 34%. The PMR for all tumor types was lower in the BCL group, with a > 60% relative reduction in PMR in patients with ductal carcinoma in situ (20.6% vs. 53.3% [95% CI -52.1 to -9.1]) and invasive lobular carcinoma (9.1% vs. 25.6% [95% CI -32.9 to -0.2]). Adverse event rates were similar. Conclusions: BCL was noninferior to WL and superior in analysis stratified by final tumor type. Clinically meaningful relative reductions in PMR and re-excision rates were observed.

items.title: Phase II study of cabozantinib in recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer after progression on platinum-based chemotherapy (CABOCOL)
items.authors: Coquan E, Vion R, Colomba-Blamemble E, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: The antiangiogenic pathway is an effective target for recurrent uterine cervical carcinoma (rCC). This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of cabozantinib monotherapy for rCC. Patients & Methods: This open-label phase II study (NCT04205799) enrolled patients with rCC who previously received platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients received oral cabozantinib (60 mg daily) until progression or discontinuation from any cause. The main objective was based on joint primary endpoint of efficacy (3-month disease control rate, DCR3) and safety (proportion of patients with grade ≥ 2 (CTCAE v5.0) gastro-intestinal (GI) perforation, GI-vaginal and/or genito-urinary (GU) fistula events) according to a Bryant-and-Day design. Key secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DOR) and safety. Results: Among 57 patients enrolled, 54 received cabozantinib: median age was 55.5 years, 18 patients (33.3%) had received more than two prior lines of treatment; 28 patients (51.9%) had been previously treated with bevacizumab. Median duration of follow-up was 8.9 months. DCR3 was 46.3% [95% CI, 32.8-60.3]. Fistula/perforation occurred in 5 (9.3%) patients. Objective response rate was 9.3%, with a median DOR of 2.5 months. Median PFS was 2.8 months (95% CI, 2.5-4.6). Grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 51.9% of patients, most commonly asthenia (15%), hypertension (9%) and mucositis (6%). Dose reductions and treatment interruptions were reported in 26 (48%) and 24 (44%) patients, respectively. Conclusions: Cabozantinib demonstrates efficacy comparable to other anti-angiogenic monotherapy in rCC; however, modest benefit and toxicity do not support further monotherapy development.

items.title: Mind the data: pitfalls and perspectives in acquiring and interpreting preclinical evidence for the FLASH effect
items.authors: Böhlen TT, Sesink A, Adrian G, et al.
items.abstract: FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) has rapidly emerged as a promising approach to widen the therapeutic window through differential sparing of normal tissue. However, despite substantial experimental activity, uncertainties remain regarding the magnitude, reproducibility, and determinants of the FLASH effect. This work reviews common pitfalls and sources of ambiguity in the acquisition and interpretation of preclinical FLASH data to support clinical application. In particular, the widespread use of fixed single-dose study designs, over-reliance on differential endpoint-based metrics, and limited quantification of effect size may obscure the true magnitude and clinical relevance of observed effects. Moreover, small dose-modifying effects are highly susceptible to experimental and biological variability, including dosimetric uncertainties, endpoint sensitivity, and environmental factors such as oxygenation. Heterogeneity in experimental protocols and endpoints further complicates cross-study comparisons. Addressing these challenges through improved quantitative characterisation, harmonised methodologies, and transparent reporting will be essential to enable robust interpretation and support the clinical translation of FLASH-RT.

items.title: Clinical Complete Response with Dostarlimab Monotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: First Results from the Global AZUR-1 Trial
items.authors: Cercek A, Bachet JB, Folprecht G, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Multimodal treatment with chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) is a standard of care (SOC) associated with significant toxicity/morbidity. After TNT, clinical complete response (cCR) ranges between 21-41%, highlighting the need for novel approaches. dMMR/MSI-H tumors are exceptionally responsive to PD-1 blockade: in a pilot study, patients with dMMR/MSI-H LARC achieved durable responses after neoadjuvant dostarlimab. AZUR-1 is the first global registrational study evaluating dostarlimab monotherapy in adults with previously untreated stage II/III dMMR/MSI-H LARC. Methods: Dostarlimab 500 mg was administered intravenously Q3W for 9 cycles. Key endpoints include rate of sustained cCR for 12 months (cCR12) following end of treatment (EOT) with dostarlimab alone by investigator and independent central review (ICR), and composite rate of cCR12 (INV) + pathological CR (pCR). Results: At data cutoff (April 20, 2026), 154 patients were enrolled (median follow-up [range]: 26.3 [2-36] months). Of 144 patients with ≥12 months follow-up, 68% achieved cCR12 (INV). pCR was achieved in 12/15 patients (80%) who underwent surgery after dostarlimab alone: cCR12+pCR rate was 76%. cCR12 (ICR) was less mature than investigator, as first cCR (ICR) was identified at later timepoints. 98% who achieved cCR maintained cCR for ≥12 months. Overall, 93% of patients were on study with no evidence of disease progression after treatment (dostarlimab ± SOC); 71% achieved this outcome with dostarlimab alone. There were no reported recurrences for patients in cCR or pCR. Safety was acceptable; grade ≥3 immune-mediated AEs occurred in 4 (3%) patients. PROs showed meaningful improvements from baseline to EOT for several domains. Conclusions: In this AZUR-1 interim analysis, 68% of patients achieved cCR12 and 76% achieved cCR12+pCR with dostarlimab alone and had no disease recurrences. These durable responses indicate the potential to eliminate the need for current SOC and redefine the curative-intent treatment paradigm with dostarlimab in dMMR/MSI-H LARC. items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI-accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy
items.authors: Xiao F, Delopoulos N, Wahl N, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)‐guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real‐time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam‐level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. Acquisition and validation methods The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI‐linear accelerator (MRI‐linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre‐processing included deformable image registration, air‐cavity correction and resampling. Ground‐truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open‐source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT‐MRI images, beam‐level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient‐specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY‐NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. Potential applications The DoseRAD2026 dataset enables benchmarking and development of fast dose calculation methods for radiotherapy applications. Potential use cases include rapid beam‐level dose estimation for photon and proton therapy, MRI‐based dose calculation in MRI‐only and MRI‐guided radiotherapy workflows, and support for real‐time adaptive radiotherapy strategies.
