items.title: Impact of daily machine performance check on prediction models for patient-specific quality assurance of multiple-target stereotactic radiosurgery
items.authors: Lambri N, Reggiori G, Nicotera L, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Single-isocenter multiple-target (SIMT) stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivered with standard linear accelerators (linacs) achieves high dose conformity through modulated fields with small multi-leaf collimator (MLC) apertures, making patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA) a critical component of radiotherapy programs. Complexity metrics are established predictors of PSQA results, while daily quality control checks of linacs represent an additional potential source of predictive information. Purpose: To investigate whether integrating machine performance check (MPC) parameters with complexity metrics improves machine learning model prediction of the gamma passing rate (GPR) in SIMT SRS PSQA. Methods: A total of 1054 volumetric modulated arcs from 245 consecutive patients treated with SIMT SRS were included. The median total planning target volume was 5.03 cc (range 0.31-119.65 cc) treated with 10MV-FFF beams in 1 fraction of 20 or 24 Gy, or in 3-5 fractions of 27-32 Gy. PSQA was performed field-by-field using an electronic portal imaging device (EPID) with a gamma criterion of 3%/1 mm and a 95% tolerance limit. Eighteen arc-specific plan complexity metrics (aPCM) and ten MPC features were considered. Feature selection based on hierarchical clustering of the Spearman's rank correlation matrix yielded fourteen features (five aPCM, nine MPC). Data were split chronologically according to the QA session date, with the earliest 80% of arcs used for training and the most recent 20% for testing. Four histogram gradient boosting models were trained to predict the GPR of each arc: model A (aPCM and MPC), model B (aPCM only), model C (MPC only), and model D (MPC predicting the residuals of model B). Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Differences between models A and B were assessed with Cohen's f2 and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on residuals. Model explainability was obtained with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). Results: Model A showed the best performance (MAE = 1.7% [1.5, 1.9]; AUC = 0.87 [0.79, 0.93]), closely followed by model B (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.75, 0.89]) and model D (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.76, 0.90]). Model C performed markedly worse, particularly in classification ability (MAE = 2.0% [1.7, 2.2]; AUC = 0.64 [0.58, 0.71]). The incremental effect of adding MPC features was small-to-medium but not significant on residuals (f2 = 0.13 [0.02, 0.27]; Wilcoxon p = 0.213).…

items.title: Impact of dose reduction and multi-parametric harmonization on multi-organ radiomics robustness in total-body PET imaging: Methodological implications for quantitative theranostics
items.authors: Azimi MS, Cheraghi M, Zaidi H
items.abstract: Abstract Background Radiomic features derived from positron emission tomography (PET) are sensitive to count statistics and acquisition protocol variability, thereby limiting quantitative reliability in low‐dose and multi‐center total‐body PET imaging. Purpose This study evaluated dose robustness of PET radiomics and assessed the impact of multi‐parameter ComBat harmonization on feature reproducibility. Methods A multi‐center total‐body PET dataset comprising 550 patients from two institutions was retrospectively analyzed. Seven dose levels were simulated from list‐mode data (Standard; dose reduction factors (DRF) of 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, and 100). Automatic deep learning–based segmentation was applied. A total of 107 Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)‐compliant radiomic features were extracted from standardized uptake value (SUV)‐normalized images. Feature‐level ComBat harmonization was performed under five configurations (scanner manufacturer, pixel spacing, radiopharmaceutical, scatter correction, and non‐harmonized baseline). Reproducibility was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC (2,1)) across dose levels, organs, and harmonization settings. Results Dose reduction produced organ‐ and feature‐dependent effects. Overall, 32.7% of the features achieved good or excellent reproducibility (ICC ≥ 0.75) in at least one anatomical region. Selected first‐order and intensity‐associated features retained good reproducibility in several anatomical regions under moderate dose reduction (DRF ≤ 20), whereas severe count reduction (DRF 50–100) was associated with greater organ‐ and feature‐dependent instability, particularly among higher‐order texture features in vascular and lower‐contrast soft‐tissue regions. Harmonization produced organ and feature‐dependent changes but did not uniformly improve cross‐dose reproducibility or compensate for noise‐induced instability. Conclusion Radiomics robustness in total‐body PET is strongly influenced by dose level, anatomy, and acquisition variability. Moderate dose reduction preserves selected intensity‐based features, while extreme count reduction compromises higher‐order textures. Harmonization altered reproducibility patterns but did not uniformly improve cross‐dose agreement or fully offset noise‐induced instability, underscoring the need for dose‐aware feature selection in multi‐center PET radiomics.

items.title: Artificial intelligence apps for medical image analysis using pyCERR and cancer genomics cloud
items.authors: Apte AP, LoCastro E, Iyer A, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose To provide a software resource that enables medical researchers and practitioners to develop and apply reproducible, out‐of‐the‐box, AI‐based analysis workflows for radiological and radiotherapy data. Development and validation methods The framework comprises two main components: the Python‐native computational environment for radiological research (pyCERR) for radiological image processing, and the cancer genomics cloud (CGC), a National Cancer Institute–funded resource that supports cloud‐hosted collaborative projects, with tools for managing collaborators and compute‐hardware from providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. pyCERR is open‐source (GNU GPL) and distributed at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr; it provides user‐friendly data structures, simplified access to metadata across radiological imaging modalities, and tools for data transformation, AI‐based image segmentation, radiomics, dynamic contrast‐enhanced MRI analysis, radiotherapy dose–volume histogram (DVH) feature extraction, and normal‐tissue complication and tumor‐control models. Radiomics features comply with the Image biomarker standardization initiative (IBSI) standards and are validated against published reference values. Unit tests covering data input/output, radiomics, DVH features, and visualization run on every code update. Workflows are containerized for reproducible, identical execution on the CGC and on local hardware. The CGC enables AI inference from radiological images to be combined with other data types such as genomics and proteomics. Our public CGC project (https://cgc.sbgenomics.com/u/sevenbridges/pycerr‐radiological‐radiotherapy‐imageanalysis), accessible with free registration, currently includes apps for organ‐at‐risk (OAR) and lung‐nodule segmentation based on published models trained in‐house and clinically validated. These apps can be run interactively from a web browser or programmatically via a REST API with client support for multiple programming languages. Notebooks demonstrating the CGC API and pyCERR capabilities are provided at https://github.com/cerr/pycerr‐notebooks. Potential applications The framework facilitates end‐to‐end radiological image analysis and reproducible research, including data access from public and private repositories, training and inference with AI models, and utilities for data management, visualization, and simplified access to image metadata.

items.title: ROECSG report: Real-world implementation patterns and perceptions of artificial intelligence in radiation oncology
items.authors: Sohn JJ, Knill C, Bossart E, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: While international surveys have examined radiation oncology professionals' attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) and documented generally low early utilization, actual implementation patterns and the depth of integration among engaged practitioners remain unclear. This multi-institutional survey aims to characterize current AI implementation, identify critical barriers to optimization, and evaluate the psychological factors driving clinical trust. Methods And Materials: A de-identified survey covering six domains was developed by a multi-institutional working group and distributed via a widely subscribed medical physics listserv and at the 2025 American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM) Annual Meeting. The instrument assessed adoption rates, specific workflow applications, and user perceptions (trust and understanding) using 6-point Likert scales to reduce central tendency bias. Quantitative data were analyzed using Pearson correlation coefficients and Welch's two-sample t-tests, while qualitative responses underwent inductive thematic analysis (κ = 0.78). Results: In this convenience sample of 80 respondents (46.3% radiation oncologists, 37.5% medical physicists), 85.0% (68/80) reported current AI use. Adoption is heavily concentrated in auto-contouring (88.2% of AI users), whereas diagnosis/prognostication (14.7%) and treatment planning (23.5%) remain limited. Most users (60.3%) employ AI for task automation without influencing clinical judgment. Trust in AI (3.55 ± 1.02) correlates positively with perceived time savings (r = 0.57), clarity of use (r = 0.54), and technical understanding (r = 0.51, all p < 0.001), with no significant difference among these correlations (Williams test, both p > 0.59). Notably, self-rated understanding averaged near the scale midpoint (3.44 ± 1.22), yet 88.8% welcomed greater AI integration. Qualitative analysis identified transparency (38%) and validation protocols (31%) as the primary barriers to deeper implementation. Conclusions: AI use was common within this sample (85.0%), although self-selection likely inflates this figure relative to the broader field. However, implementation remains "broad but shallow," focused on workflow automation rather than clinical intelligence. The gap between enthusiasm and understanding necessitates a shift toward active institutional governance and standardized AI-literacy education.

items.title: Comparison of two close-packing methods for vertex placement in lattice radiotherapy (LRT)
items.authors: Song Y, Ma P, Dai J
items.abstract: Background: Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT) is characterized by its 3D-mouldated spatial dose distribution of vertices inside the lattice volume with high peak-to-valley dose ratio (PVDR) for enhancing tumor control and reducing normal tissue toxicity. While face-centered cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP), both achieving maximum spatial packing density, have been used for vertex placement, a direct comparative analysis of their dosimetric performance is lacking. Purpose: This study aimed to systematically compare FCC and HCP methods for vertex placement under identical conditions to determine which yields superior dosimetric outcomes, specifically regarding the peak-to-valley dose ratio (PVDR), and to provide data supporting the standardization of LRT planning. Materials And Methods: This study was retrospectively conducted on 10 patients with large gross tumor volumes (GTV) (GTV; median [IQR] GTV volume: 916.59[609.37] cm3). For each patient, an identical inward margin was applied to the GTV to create the lattice volume for placing LRT vertices. Within this lattice volume, two sets of spherical vertices were generated: one arranged in a HCP lattice and the other in a FCC lattice, both vertices of same diameter. The initial diameter and volume of vertices were determined based on GTV volume. Vertex positions were optimized using an Adaptive Simulated Annealing (ASA) algorithm to maximize inter-vertex distance, with the total volume of all vertices constrained to approximately 1% of the GTV. All plans were optimized using identical dose-volume objectives. Plan quality was evaluated using GTV dose metrics (D5%, D10%, D50%, D90%, Dmean, V50%), normal tissue mean dose (NT Dmean), maximum point doses (Dmax) to serial organs at risk and PVDR defined by both GTVD10/D90 and lattice volume D10/D90 ratios. Results: Vertex parameters (number, volume, spacing) showed no significant difference between Plan_FCC and Plan_HCP (P > 0.05). Dosimetric analysis revealed a statistically significant increase in PVDR (lattice volume D10/D90) for Plan_FCC compared to Plan_HCP (median [IQR]: 6.95 [3.38] vs. 4.48 [2.00], p = 0.019). No other evaluated metrics demonstrated significant differences, including other GTV metrics NT Dmean or the maximum point doses to serial OARs.…

items.title: End-to-end film-based characterization of gated delivery latencies in a spot-scanned synchrotron-based proton therapy system
items.authors: Stottler ZS, Kruse JJ, Deisher AJ
items.abstract: Background: Temporal mismatches between gating signals and beam activation-beam-on and beam-off latencies-in gated particle beam therapy can compromise dose integrity. Yet standardized measurement techniques are lacking, and system-specific characterization, particularly for synchrotron-based proton systems, remains limited. Purpose: To implement a novel strategy for precise end-to-end gating latency measurements of a spot-scanned proton beam using Gafchromic film. Methods: Gating latencies have been measured for a Hitachi ProBeat accelerator equipped with a Varian RPM gating system. EBT4 films were positioned within a stack of acrylic blocks on a QUASAR respiratory motion platform operated with a 1.5 cm amplitude and 12 bpm sinusoidal pattern. A stainless-steel ball bearing (BB), positioned atop the film, facilitated localization. During irradiation, the BB produced a dose shadow on the film that indicated the phantom position. A proton plan consisting of a single 85.3 MeV spot was delivered to isocenter during a single gate-on/off interval initiated near the 25% phase, to maximize phantom velocity. Fifty-one measurements were made with a variety of gating intervals. Beam-on latency and delivery time produced a separation between the BB-shadow and the centroid of the Gaussian proton spot. Spot duration information was extracted from accelerator log files. BB-shadow/spot separation is modeled analytically based on phantom motion enabling the direct calculation of the total beam-on and beam-off latencies. Accelerator latency was measured directly with an oscilloscope, enabling isolation of the relative contributions of the RPM gating system. Results: An average beam-on latency of 142 ± 27  ms is observed for the RPM+ProBeat system for the first gate of a delivery, which includes a known 69 ms beam extraction judgment time for the first proton spot in a spill from the Hitachi synchrotron. The corresponding average beam-off latency is 87 ± 30  ms  . The average gate-on and gate-off latencies of the RPM system are calculated as 72 ± 27  ms  and 81 ± 30  ms  , respectively. The associated average contributions of the accelerator to the beam-on latencies are measured as 69.3 ± 0.2  ms  (first gate in new spill) and 0.53 ± 0.07  ms  (subsequent gates in existing spill) and similarly 6 ± 4  ms  for beam-off latency. Conclusion: A novel, high-precision method for gating-latency measurements has been implemented using film to characterize gating latencies in a spot-scanned particle beam.…

items.title: Proton arc therapy reduces the dose delivered to circulating blood compared to intensity-modulated proton therapy for head-and-neck cancer
items.authors: Tattenberg S, Liu P, Cong X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Compared to intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT), proton arc therapy (PAT) has various dosimetric advantages. However, questions have been raised over whether the larger low-dose bath during PAT may increase radiation-induced lymphocyte killing, which is correlated with adverse clinical outcomes. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to quantitatively compare radiation dose delivery to circulating blood during IMPT and PAT. Methods: For each of 10 head-and-neck cancer patients, one IMPT and one PAT treatment plan were created, and the hematological dose (HEDOS) blood dose model was used to simulate radiation dose delivery to circulating blood. HEDOS simulations utilized gantry angle-wise dose distributions (including for PAT) and considered gantry rotation and energy layer switching as well as irradiation times. Blood dose histograms as well as the mean dose to all simulation blood particles (Dmean) and the dose delivered to the 90% and 10% of blood particles receiving the highest dose (D90% and D10%) were then compared between IMPT and PAT. Results: For IMPT, blood dose metrics (in the form of mean over all patients ± one standard deviation) were (0.522 ± 0.204)Gy(RBE) for D90%, (0.563 ± 0.212)Gy(RBE) for Dmean, and (0.605 ± 0.219)Gy(RBE) for D10%. For PAT, D90% was (0.430 ± 0.184)Gy(RBE), Dmean was (0.483 ± 0.195)Gy(RBE), and D10% was (0.538 ± 0.207)Gy(RBE). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated statistically significant (p < 0.05) differences between blood dose metrics of IMPT and PAT for all patients, and IMPT did not increase the percentage of blood particles which received no radiation dose during the delivery of a single treatment fraction. Conclusions: Compared to IMPT, proton arc therapy was associated with significantly lower radiation dose delivery to circulating blood across a variety of different metrics. Proton arc therapy for head-and-neck cancer is therefore not expected to result in higher radiation-induced killing of circulating lymphocytes compared to IMPT.

items.title: Do new guidelines enable a more accurate comparison of [(18)F]FDG PET/CT features with histopathology in primary breast cancer?
items.authors: Sharkey AR, Chen HY, Funso-Fayomi C, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Recent EANM-SNMMI guidelines suggest that quantitative [18F]FDG PET parameters, including standardised uptake values (SUV), metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), provide valuable prognostic information in breast cancer. We aim to evaluate the association between [18F]FDG PET parameters in a large real-world cohort of high-risk breast cancer patients and the four main intrinsic subtypes of breast cancer defined by the EANM-SNMMI guidelines. Methods: All women with newly diagnosed high-risk breast cancer undergoing [18F]FDG PET/CT between 1/8/22  and 17/4/2025 were eligible for inclusion. Primary tumour metabolic parameters (SUVmax/mean/peak, SUV heterogeneity index (HI), MTV, TLG) were measured and compared with histological grade, hormone receptor status (oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR)) and Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) expression. Cases were classified according to EANM-SNMMI histological groupings: Group 1 (G1) representing Luminal A-like (HR+ /HER2- and low-grade/low proliferation), Group 2 (G2) Luminal B-like (HR+ /HER2- and high-grade/high proliferation), Group 3 (G3) HER2+ (HR + or -) lesions, and Group 4 (G4) triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). Hormone receptor status was analysed separately. Results: 185 cases were included for analysis: G1 (n = 48), G2 (n = 35), G3 (n = 54) and G4 (n = 48). Significant differences were observed between groups for SUVmax, SUVmean, SUV HI and MTV; post hoc analysis revealed TNBC, HER2 + and Luminal B tumours exhibited significantly higher SUVmax than Luminal A cancers, with significantly higher SUVmean and SUVpeak in TNBC and Luminal B versus Luminal A. The SUV HI showed significantly lower heterogeneity in the Luminal A group compared with Luminal B (p = 0.02) and HER2-positive tumours (p = 0.03), with no other significant pairwise differences. When looking at MTV, only the Luminal A vs. Luminal B comparison reached significance, with larger MTVs observed in Luminal B tumours. ER + and PR+ tumours showed significantly lower SUV parameters (p < 0.05) when compared with receptor-negative tumours, but no significant differences were observed for volumetric parameters (MTV and TLG) (p > 0.05). HER2 scores (negative/low/positive) showed no significant association with SUV or volumetric PET parameters.…

items.title: Image-Guided Decubitus Craniospinal Irradiation Setup in a Fixed-Beam Proton Room: Accuracy and Efficiency
items.authors: Zeng Q, Han Z, Chhabra A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Recent developments have further demonstrated the feasibility of craniospinal irradiation (CSI) delivery using simplified beam arrangements, such as a single posterior brain beam. Extending these advances, CSI delivered in the lateral decubitus position within a fixed-beam proton room offers an opportunity to improve room utilization and treatment access but introduces unique challenges in patient setup and image guidance. Methods: This study compares 2 image-guided setup workflows for decubitus CSI to evaluate whether meaningful differences exist. We retrospectively analyzed 10 CSI patients treated in the decubitus position between 2024 and 2025 using the fixed-beam ProBeam system with the 3-iso technique. Two setup workflows were evaluated: (1) Continuous Full-Field Image Guidance (CFF-IG), in which all isocenters were aligned prior to treatment delivery, and (2) Selective Field-Based Image Guidance (SF-IG), in which full-field imaging was applied only at the initial fraction, followed by field-specific verification thereafter. Setup accuracy was quantified using translational and rotational deviations derived from oblique kV imaging, and dosimetric robustness was assessed through target coverage and junction dose gradient analysis. Setup efficiency was evaluated using treatment room time stamps. Results: Across all 3 isocenters, mean translational deviations were below 4 mm and mean angular deviations were below 1.5°. Differences in target coverage (ΔD95) and junction dose gradients were small between the 2 workflows. No statistically significant differences in setup accuracy or dosimetric quality were observed. SF-IG was associated with shorter average setup time, with the majority of treatment sessions completed within 30 minutes. Conclusions: Both CFF-IG and SF-IG achieved setup accuracy within institutional action levels and maintained dosimetric robustness for CSI delivered in the decubitus position using pencil beam scanning. The absence of significant differences suggests that either approach may be clinically feasible for decubitus CSI delivery. SF-IG offers a more time-efficient workflow without compromising treatment quality, supporting its use as the preferred default strategy, while CFF-IG may be reserved for select cases requiring enhanced global realignment. These findings support decubitus CSI as a practical extension of modern single-beam and simplified pencil beam scanning CSI techniques.

items.title: Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy for Central and Ultracentral Lung Tumors: A Multicenter Real-world Outcomes Analysis
items.authors: Akgün Z, Ahmadova A, Atalar B, et al.
items.abstract: Aims: The aim of the study is to evaluate real-world clinical outcomes of stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for central (C) and ultracentral (UC) lung tumors, with a focus on toxicity, tumor control, and overall survival (OS). Materials And Methods: This multicenter retrospective analysis included 133 patients with C or UC lung tumors treated with SBRT across multiple participating centers. Patient characteristics, treatment parameters, toxicity outcomes, tumor control, and OS were analyzed retrospectively. Results: Grade 2 toxicity occurred in 30.1% (n = 31/103) of patients with C tumors and 26.7% (n = 8/30) with UC tumors, while grade 3 toxicity was observed in 8.7% and 16.7% of patients, respectively. Median OS was 24 months. Favorable outcomes were observed in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant disease and smaller planning target volumes (PTVs). Delivery of SBRT in conjunction with systemic therapies was feasible and associated with manageable toxicity profiles. Conclusion: In this multicenter real-world cohort, SBRT for C and UC lung tumors was associated with acceptable toxicity and clinically meaningful outcomes when delivered using contemporary techniques and cautious fractionation. Observations in selected subgroups, including patients with EGFR-mutant disease and smaller PTVs, should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and support individualized clinical decision-making in anatomically high-risk settings.

items.abstract: Importance: Skin toxic effects are a common early adverse event of enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab (EVP) therapy, but its association with clinical outcomes in patients receiving first-line therapy remains uncertain. Objective: To evaluate the association between treatment-emergent skin toxic effects and clinical outcomes among patients receiving first-line EVP. Design, Setting, And Participants: This retrospective cohort study was performed at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center among adults with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma receiving first-line EVP therapy between March 3, 2022, and July 31, 2025. Skin toxic effects were used as a time-dependent exposure in Cox proportional hazards regression to account for immortal-time bias. Prespecified sequential adjustment models and 30-day landmark analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the findings. Exposure: Treatment-emergent skin toxic effects (rash or pruritus) were identified from medical records. Main Outcomes And Measures: Primary outcome was overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included progression-free survival and objective response rate (ORR). OS and PFS were measured from EVP therapy initiation to the respective event or last follow-up. ORR was evaluated among patients with a response assessment after the 30-day landmark, according to skin toxic effects status within the first 30 days. Results: Among 185 patients (median age, 73 [IQR, 67-79] years; 140 [75.7%] male), skin toxic effects occurred in 98 (53.0%) at a median of 14 (IQR, 7-28) days after EVP therapy initiation. Skin toxic effects of grade 3 or higher occurred in 10 patients (5.4%). Skin toxic effects resulted in EV dose reduction in 31 patients (16.8%), treatment interruption in 20 (10.8%), and treatment discontinuation in 9 (4.9%). At a median follow-up of 17.7 (IQR, 11.3-24.2) months, Simon-Makuch curves demonstrated longer OS and PFS among all patients and longer OS among patients with visceral metastases in the skin toxic effects stratum than in the no toxicity stratum. In adjusted time-dependent Cox proportional hazards regression, skin toxic effects were associated with longer OS (hazard ratio, 0.34 [95% CI, 0.20-0.57]). The association remained consistent across sequential adjustment models and prespecified 30-day landmark analyses. In the 30-day landmark analyses, associations with PFS and ORR remained directionally favorable but were attenuated after multivariable adjustment.…

items.authors: Haury J, Chanier JB, Renevier B, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Despite organized screening programs, persistent social inequalities undermine cervical cancer screening effectiveness in high-income countries, disproportionately affecting the most socially vulnerable women. Objectives: To identify distinct social vulnerability profiles among pregnant women and examine their associations with cervical cancer screening adherence and intraepithelial lesion detection. Design, Setting, And Participants: This retrospective cohort study assessed all pregnant women 25 years or older who delivered at Centre Hospitalier Intercommunal André-Grégoire, a single tertiary care maternity unit in France, between May 1, 2019, and May 1, 2025. Exposures: Social vulnerability was assessed across 15 indicators spanning administrative, psychological, and violence-related domains. Multiple component analysis and hierarchical clustering on principal components identified 6 distinct vulnerability profiles. Multiple logistic regression examined associations between profiles and cervical screening inadequacy (no cervical sample within the last 3 years, including those never screened) and squamous intraepithelial lesion detection, adjusting for maternal age and body mass index. Main Outcomes And Measures: Cervical screening inadequacy (primary outcome) and low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion detection (secondary outcome). Results: Among 18 253 women (median [IQR] age, 32.3 [29.1-36.0] years; median [IQR] body mass index, 25.9 [22.7-29.4]), 10 248 (56.1%) were up to date with screening. Six vulnerability profiles were identified. Compared with the low-vulnerability reference profile, all profiles showed increased odds of screening inadequacy: substance use and psychological vulnerability (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.33; 95% CI, 1.20-1.48), migrant or linguistic barrier (AOR, 3.40; 95% CI, 3.16-3.66), psychological violence (AOR, 2.01; 95% CI, 1.75-2.32), sexual violence (AOR, 2.08; 95% CI, 1.74-2.48), and physical violence (AOR, 2.54; 95% CI, 2.19-2.95). Violence-exposed and substance use profiles also had significantly higher proportions of women with a detected intraepithelial lesion despite reduced screening participation. Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study of pregnant women, distinct social vulnerability profiles were differentially associated with cervical cancer screening inadequacy; women with migration-related barriers experienced the greatest disadvantage, and violence-exposed women showed both reduced screening and elevated disease burden.…

items.title: Benchmarking intermediate dose spillage in single target stereotactic radiosurgery for brain metastases
items.authors: Nour Y, Wiegreffe S, Tekin T, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Intermediate-dose spillage is central to normal-brain sparing in stereotactic radiosurgery, yet fixed adverse-event and relative indices do not define achievable plan quality for single-target linear accelerator treatments. The aim was to derive a volume-dependent absolute benchmark for the 50% prescription isodose volume (V50%; equivalent to V10 Gy for 20 Gy plans) for brain metastases. Materials And Methods: In total, 276 single-isocenter single-target plans were analyzed: 178 idealized model plans and 98 clinical plans. Power-law regression in log-log space modeled spillage against planning target volume (PTV, cm3). The volume-scaling exponents were 0.83 for the ideal references and 0.75 for the simplified clinical threshold. The clinical upper threshold was derived using q = 0.90 quantile regression. Threshold-exceeding plans were reviewed for anatomical or technical justification. Results: In the model cohort V50% value correlated strongly with PTV (r = 0.994, p < 0.001). The ideal mean model was V50% = 3.71 × PTV0.83, the conservative ideal-planning reference was V50% = 4.10 × PTV0.83, and the clinical upper threshold was V50% = 5.00 × PTV0.75. Ten of 98 clinical plans (10%) exceeded the threshold. Seven lacked anatomical justification and were replanned, reducing V50% by a median of 14% (range 7-29%) without compromising target coverage. Conclusions: A volume-based V50% benchmark provided a complementary quality-assurance reference for single-target linear accelerator radiosurgery for brain metastases. It flagged plans that warranted structured review alongside target coverage, organs of interest, conformity, and gradient metrics.

items.title: Biomarker-guided treatment strategies for patients with gliomas in clinical practice
items.authors: Le Rhun E, Mellinghoff IK, Weiss T, et al.
items.abstract: Targeted therapy has made important contributions to improving outcomes for patients with many solid tumors, but has had only limited activity so far in patients with gliomas, notably glioblastoma. Failure of targeted therapy in glioblastoma is likely due to redundance of oncogenic pathway activation and so far the inability to identify suitable targets and apply biomarker-based enrichment strategies in clinical trial designs. In contrast, in non-glioblastoma tumors, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice: inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) exemplified by vorasidenib, the first approved drug specifically for IDH-mutant gliomas, has changed the landscape for targeted therapy of WHO grade 2 gliomas. Furthermore, dordaviprone, an antagonist of dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3) and an allosteric agonist of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic mitochondrial matrix peptidase proteolytic subunit (ClpP), emerges as a potentially active agent in patients with recurrent K27M-mutant diffuse midline gliomas. Finally, BRAF mutations, neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase ( r fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene fusions continue to raise interest as therapeutic targets at least for subsets of patients with gliomas. Almost no targeted therapy approaches for ependymomas have emerged. Improved clinical trial designs including shared control arms early on and using pharmacodynamic endpoints ideally in enriched patient populations are the path forward towards the identification of further active treatments for patients with gliomas.

items.title: [Comment] Redefining curative treatment for early-stage mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer
items.authors: Sharlene Gill, Jonathan Loree
items.abstract: For decades, the standard of care for patients with resected stage II and III colon cancer has centred on surgery with consideration of postoperative adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce risk of recurrence. Mismatch repair deficiency is seen in 10–15% of non-metastatic colon cancers and is predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibition. The initial report of the single-arm, phase 2 NICHE-2 study of one dose of ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) and two doses of nivolumab (3 mg per kg) before surgery with clinical stage II and III colon cancer generated considerable interest after demonstrating a remarkable 98% pathologic response rate, including a pathologic complete response rate of 68%.

items.title: Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma: A Review
items.authors: Tsilimigras DI, Ntanasis-Stathopoulos I, Pawlik TM
items.abstract: Importance: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is the second most common primary liver malignancy, and incidence is increasing worldwide. Despite advances in multimodal therapy, 5-year overall survival remains approximately 9%, underscoring the urgent need for improved therapeutic strategies and comprehensive understanding of current management approaches. Observations: Surgical resection with regional lymphadenectomy remains the cornerstone of curative therapy, with adjuvant capecitabine established as standard of care after resection. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be strongly considered for patients with iCCA with high-risk features, including at least 1 of the following: tumor size larger than 5 cm, multifocal disease, vascular invasion, lymph node involvement, and elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9. For unresectable, liver-confined disease, locoregional therapies, including transarterial chemoembolization, Y-90 radioembolization, hepatic artery infusion pump chemotherapy, thermal ablation, and radiotherapy, may provide meaningful survival benefits. Liver transplant is emerging as a viable option in highly selected patients with very early iCCA or sustained response to neoadjuvant therapy. In advanced disease, chemoimmunotherapy with gemcitabine/cisplatin plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab has become the first-line treatment. Comprehensive molecular profiling identifies actionable targets in 30% to 40% of patients, including FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements, IDH1 variants, and other alterations amenable to targeted therapies approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Conclusions And Relevance: The management of iCCA has evolved substantially with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for high-risk resectable disease, enhanced locoregional strategies for liver-confined tumors, chemoimmunotherapy as first-line systemic therapy for advanced disease, and precision oncology approaches targeting recurrent molecular alterations. Multidisciplinary evaluation and comprehensive genomic profiling are essential for optimal patient outcomes.
